# Module 5 — Asynchronous JavaScript

# Lesson 5.1 — The JavaScript Execution Model: Execution Context, Call Stack, Browser APIs, Event Loop, Microtask Queue, and Callback Queue

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the Most Asked Topics)

---

# ⚠️ Before We Start

This lesson is arguably **the single most important lesson** in the entire course.

If you truly understand this lesson, you'll understand:

- Why `setTimeout()` doesn't execute immediately.
- Why Promises run before `setTimeout()`.
- Why `async/await` works.
- Why React state updates sometimes appear asynchronous.
- Why Node.js can handle thousands of requests.
- Most asynchronous interview questions.

Many developers memorize the Event Loop.

Very few **understand it**.

Our goal is to build a **mental model**, not just memorize definitions.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain how JavaScript executes code.
- Define an Execution Context.
- Understand the Call Stack.
- Explain the role of Browser APIs.
- Explain the Event Loop.
- Differentiate the Microtask Queue and Callback Queue.
- Predict the output of asynchronous JavaScript code.
- Solve common interview questions on execution order.

---

# 1. The Big Picture

When you run JavaScript in a browser (or in environments like Node.js), you're not just running JavaScript code.

You're working with **multiple cooperating systems**.

```text
                Your JavaScript Code
                        │
                        ▼
              JavaScript Engine (V8, SpiderMonkey, etc.)
                        │
        ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
        ▼                               ▼
   Memory (Heap)                 Call Stack
                        │
                        ▼
              Browser / Runtime APIs
                        │
                        ▼
        Microtask Queue      Callback Queue
                │                 │
                └────────┬────────┘
                         ▼
                    Event Loop
                         │
                         ▼
                    Call Stack
```

Think of JavaScript as the **manager** of a restaurant.

The browser is the **kitchen**.

The Event Loop is the **waiter**.

The queues are the list of completed orders waiting to be served.

---

# 2. JavaScript is Single-Threaded

One of the most common interview questions is:

> **Is JavaScript single-threaded?**

**Answer:**

Yes, JavaScript execution is **single-threaded**.

That means:

- One Call Stack.
- One instruction executes at a time.
- No two JavaScript statements execute simultaneously on the same thread.

Example:

```js
console.log("A");
console.log("B");
console.log("C");
```

Output:

```text
A
B
C
```

It cannot print:

```text
A
C
B
```

because JavaScript executes one line after another.

---

# What Does "Single-Threaded" Mean?

Imagine a cashier with one checkout counter.

```text
Customer A
     │
     ▼
+-----------+
| Cashier   |
+-----------+
     ▲
     │
Customer B
     ▲
     │
Customer C
```

The cashier serves **one customer at a time**.

The same idea applies to JavaScript.

---

# 3. Execution Context

Every time JavaScript starts executing code, it creates an **Execution Context**.

Think of an execution context as:

> **The environment needed to run a piece of code.**

It contains:

- Variables.
- Functions.
- The value of `this`.
- The scope chain.

---

# Types of Execution Context

There are three you'll commonly encounter.

## 1. Global Execution Context

Created when the program starts.

```js
const name = "Lekan";

function greet() {}

console.log(name);
```

Everything initially lives in the Global Execution Context.

---

## 2. Function Execution Context

Every function call creates a new execution context.

```js
function greet() {
    console.log("Hello");
}

greet();
```

When `greet()` runs:

```text
Global Context

↓

Function Context

↓

Destroyed after completion
```

---

## 3. Eval Execution Context

Created by `eval()`.

Rarely used and generally discouraged.

You won't be asked about it often.

---

# Visual Representation

Suppose:

```js
const a = 10;

function foo() {
    const b = 20;
}
```

Memory:

```text
Global Execution Context

Variables

a → 10

foo → function
```

When `foo()` executes:

```text
Function Execution Context

Variables

b → 20
```

---

# 4. The Call Stack

The **Call Stack** is where JavaScript keeps track of which function is currently executing.

Think of it as a stack of plates.

```text
Top
──────
Plate 3
Plate 2
Plate 1
──────
Bottom
```

The last plate placed on top is the first removed.

This is called:

**LIFO**

> **Last In, First Out**

---

# Example

```js
function one() {
    two();
}

function two() {
    three();
}

function three() {
    console.log("Done");
}

one();
```

---

### Step 1

```text
Call Stack

Global
```

---

### Step 2

`one()`

```text
one()

Global
```

---

### Step 3

`two()`

```text
two()

one()

Global
```

---

### Step 4

`three()`

```text
three()

two()

one()

Global
```

---

### Step 5

`console.log()`

```text
console.log()

three()

two()

one()

Global
```

After logging, each function finishes and is popped off the stack in reverse order.

---

# Final Stack

```text
Global
```

Program ends.

---

# Why the Call Stack Matters

An interview favorite:

What happens here?

```js
function recurse() {
    recurse();
}

recurse();
```

Each call adds another execution context to the stack.

Eventually:

```text
Maximum Call Stack Size Exceeded
```

This is a **stack overflow** caused by infinite recursion.

---

# 5. Browser APIs

Here's an important point:

> **`setTimeout()` is NOT part of JavaScript itself.**

Neither are:

- `fetch()`
- `setInterval()`
- DOM events (`click`, `scroll`, etc.)

They are provided by the **browser runtime** (or Node.js runtime).

Common Browser APIs include:

- `setTimeout`
- `setInterval`
- `fetch`
- `addEventListener`
- `requestAnimationFrame`
- DOM manipulation APIs

---

# Example

```js
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("Timeout");
}, 1000);

console.log("End");
```

Execution:

```text
JavaScript

↓

console.log("Start")

↓

Browser handles timer

↓

console.log("End")
```

Notice that JavaScript doesn't wait one second.

Instead, it hands the timer to the browser.

---

# Visual Flow

```text
JavaScript

↓

setTimeout()

↓

Browser Timer

↓

1 second finishes

↓

Callback Queue
```

The callback doesn't execute immediately—it waits until the Call Stack is empty and the Event Loop moves it back.

---

# 6. Callback Queue (Macrotask Queue)

When a Browser API finishes, its callback is placed into the **Callback Queue** (also called the **Macrotask Queue**).

Examples:

- `setTimeout`
- `setInterval`
- DOM events
- `postMessage`

Example:

```js
setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("Hello");
}, 0);
```

Even with `0` milliseconds, the callback does **not** run immediately.

Why?

Because it must wait for:

1. The timer to complete.
2. The Call Stack to become empty.
3. The Event Loop to move it back onto the stack.

---

# 7. Microtask Queue

Promises do **not** go to the Callback Queue.

They go to the **Microtask Queue**.

Sources of microtasks include:

- `.then()`
- `.catch()`
- `.finally()`
- `queueMicrotask()`
- The continuation after an `await`

The Microtask Queue has **higher priority** than the Callback Queue.

---

# Example

```js
console.log("A");

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("B");
});

console.log("C");
```

Execution:

1. Print `A`.
2. Schedule the Promise callback in the Microtask Queue.
3. Print `C`.
4. Call Stack becomes empty.
5. Run microtasks.

Output:

```text
A
C
B
```

---

# 8. The Event Loop

The Event Loop constantly checks:

```text
Is the Call Stack empty?
```

If **No**:

→ Wait.

If **Yes**:

1. Execute **all** Microtasks.
2. Then execute **one** Callback Queue task.
3. Repeat.

---

# Mental Model

Imagine:

```text
Call Stack

↓

Empty?

↓

YES

↓

Run ALL Microtasks

↓

Run ONE Callback

↓

Repeat
```

This priority explains many interview questions.

---

# Example: Promise vs setTimeout

```js
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("Promise");
});

console.log("End");
```

Let's trace it.

### Step 1

Print:

```text
Start
```

### Step 2

`setTimeout` registers with the browser.

### Step 3

Promise callback goes to the Microtask Queue.

### Step 4

Print:

```text
End
```

The Call Stack is now empty.

The Event Loop checks the queues.

- Microtask Queue → contains the Promise callback.
- Callback Queue → contains the timer callback.

Microtasks run first.

Final output:

```text
Start
End
Promise
Timeout
```

---

# Visual Timeline

```text
Main Script
│
├── console.log("Start")
├── setTimeout(...) ──────────────► Browser Timer
├── Promise.then(...) ───────────► Microtask Queue
├── console.log("End")
│
└── Main Script finishes
        │
        ▼
Event Loop
        │
        ├── Run ALL Microtasks
        │       └── Promise
        │
        └── Run ONE Callback Task
                └── setTimeout
```

---

# Common Interview Mistakes

### Mistake 1

> "`setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs immediately."

❌ Incorrect.

It runs **after**:

- the current synchronous code,
- all queued microtasks,
- and when the Call Stack is empty.

---

### Mistake 2

> "Promises go into the Call Stack."

❌ Incorrect.

Only their callback executes on the Call Stack.

Initially, the callback waits in the **Microtask Queue**.

---

### Mistake 3

> "`fetch()` is JavaScript."

❌ Incorrect.

`fetch()` is provided by the browser (or runtime environment), not by the ECMAScript language itself.

---

# Interview Perspective

Interviewers ask this topic to evaluate:

- Your understanding of JavaScript's execution model.
- Whether you truly understand asynchronous behavior.
- Whether you can reason through execution order rather than memorizing outputs.

A common prompt is simply:

> "Without running the code, tell me the output and explain why."

They care about **your explanation** as much as your answer.

---

# Live Coding / Prediction Questions

## Easy

Predict the output:

```js
console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("B");
}, 0);

console.log("C");
```

---

## Medium

Predict:

```js
console.log(1);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(2));

console.log(3);
```

---

## Hard

Predict:

```js
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout 1"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("Promise 1");

  Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("Promise 2");
  });
});

setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout 2"), 0);

console.log("End");
```

(We'll solve even more complex versions in later lessons.)

---

# Practice Exercises

### Knowledge

1. What is an Execution Context?
2. What is the Global Execution Context?
3. What is the Call Stack?
4. Why is JavaScript considered single-threaded?
5. Are Browser APIs part of JavaScript?
6. What is the Event Loop?
7. What is the Microtask Queue?
8. What is the Callback Queue?
9. Which queue has higher priority?
10. Why doesn't `setTimeout(fn, 0)` execute immediately?

---

### Coding

11. Write a function that demonstrates nested function calls and draw the Call Stack.
12. Create an example showing a Promise executing before a `setTimeout`.
13. Create a recursive function and explain why it overflows the stack.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
JavaScript Runtime

┌────────────────────┐
│ Call Stack         │
└────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼
  Browser / Runtime APIs
          │
          ▼
┌────────────────────┐
│ Microtask Queue    │  ← Promises, await
└────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼
┌────────────────────┐
│ Callback Queue     │  ← setTimeout, events
└────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼
      Event Loop
          │
          ▼
      Call Stack

Priority:
1. Synchronous code
2. ALL Microtasks
3. ONE Callback task
4. Repeat
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain what an Execution Context is.
- ✅ Draw the Call Stack for nested function calls.
- ✅ Explain why JavaScript is single-threaded.
- ✅ Explain the role of Browser APIs.
- ✅ Describe how the Event Loop works.
- ✅ Differentiate the Microtask Queue from the Callback Queue.
- ✅ Predict the output of basic asynchronous code.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Without running the code, determine the exact output and explain **every step**:

```js
console.log("1");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("2");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("3");
});

console.log("4");

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("5");
});

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("6");
}, 0);

console.log("7");
```

Answer:

1. What is the final output?
2. Which statements run synchronously?
3. Which callbacks enter the Microtask Queue?
4. Which callbacks enter the Callback Queue?
5. In what order does the Event Loop process them?
6. Draw the Call Stack, Microtask Queue, and Callback Queue after the main script finishes.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 5.2 — Callbacks**, where we'll cover:

- What callbacks are and why they exist.
- Synchronous vs asynchronous callbacks.
- Callback Hell.
- Error-first callbacks.
- How callbacks work under the hood.
- Common interview questions and live coding exercises involving callbacks.

questions.questionText: Where are callbacks of resolved Promises (e.g. .then()) queued?
questions.explanation: Promise callbacks enter the Microtask Queue, which has higher priority than the Callback (macrotask) Queue.

questions.questionText: Which of the following run asynchronously? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: `setTimeout` and Promise callbacks run asynchronously via event queues. `forEach` callbacks run synchronously.

questions.questionText: What queue has higher execution priority: Callback Queue or Microtask Queue?
questions.explanation: The Event Loop empties the entire Microtask Queue before processing any macrotask from the Callback Queue.

lessons.objective: Master callback functions, synchronous vs asynchronous execution, and callback error-first patterns.
lessons.content:
# Module 5 — Asynchronous JavaScript

# Lesson 5.2 — Callbacks

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Intermediate → Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Very High)

---

# Why This Lesson Matters

Before JavaScript had **Promises** and **async/await**, almost all asynchronous code was written using **callbacks**.

Even today, callbacks are everywhere:

- `Array.prototype.map()`
- `Array.prototype.filter()`
- `Array.prototype.reduce()`
- `setTimeout()`
- `addEventListener()`
- Many Node.js APIs
- Third-party libraries

Many developers think callbacks are only for asynchronous code.

**That's incorrect.**

Callbacks can be **synchronous** or **asynchronous**.

Understanding this distinction is something interviewers often test.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what a callback is.
- Distinguish synchronous and asynchronous callbacks.
- Understand why callbacks exist.
- Explain callback hell.
- Understand the Node.js error-first callback pattern.
- Recognize common interview questions involving callbacks.

---

# 1. What is a Callback?

A callback is simply:

> **A function passed as an argument to another function, so it can be called later.**

That's all.

Notice the definition does **not** mention asynchronous code.

---

## Example

```js
function greet(name) {
    console.log(`Hello ${name}`);
}

function processUser(callback) {
    callback("Lekan");
}

processUser(greet);
```

Output:

```text
Hello Lekan
```

---

# Visual Mental Model

```text
processUser()

↓

Receives

greet

↓

Stores It

↓

Later Executes

↓

greet("Lekan")
```

The callback is just another function.

---

# Syntax Deep Dive

```js
processUser(greet);
```

Let's examine every part.

### `processUser`

The function being called.

---

### `(`

Beginning of arguments.

---

### `greet`

Notice:

No parentheses.

We're passing the **function itself**, not calling it.

---

Correct:

```js
processUser(greet);
```

Incorrect:

```js
processUser(greet());
```

Why?

Because:

```js
greet();
```

executes immediately.

The return value gets passed instead.

---

### `)`

End of arguments.

---

# Under the Hood

When JavaScript sees:

```js
processUser(greet);
```

Conceptually:

```text
processUser

↓

callback

↓

Reference to greet function
```

Then later:

```js
callback("Lekan");
```

becomes:

```js
greet("Lekan");
```

---

# Memory Representation

```text
Stack

processUser

↓

callback

───────────────┐
               │
               ▼
Heap

Function greet()
```

The callback variable stores a reference to the function.

---

# 2. Synchronous Callbacks

Not all callbacks are asynchronous.

Example:

```js
const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

numbers.forEach(function(number) {
    console.log(number);
});

console.log("Done");
```

Output:

```text
1
2
3
Done
```

The callback executes immediately during the loop.

---

## Visual Flow

```text
forEach

↓

Take First Element

↓

Run Callback

↓

Take Second Element

↓

Run Callback

↓

Repeat
```

Everything happens synchronously.

---

# More Examples

## `map()`

```js
const doubled = [1,2,3].map(function(number){
    return number * 2;
});
```

The callback runs immediately for every element.

---

## `filter()`

```js
const even = [1,2,3,4].filter(function(number){
    return number % 2 === 0;
});
```

Again:

Synchronous callback.

---

# 3. Asynchronous Callbacks

Now let's use `setTimeout`.

```js
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(function(){
    console.log("Timeout");
},1000);

console.log("End");
```

Output:

```text
Start
End
Timeout
```

The callback executes later.

---

# Why?

Because `setTimeout` hands the callback to the browser.

```text
JavaScript

↓

setTimeout

↓

Browser Timer

↓

Callback Queue

↓

Event Loop

↓

Call Stack

↓

Execute Callback
```

---

# Another Example

```js
button.addEventListener("click", function(){
    console.log("Clicked");
});
```

The callback waits until the click event occurs.

---

# Real-World Example

Imagine ordering food.

```text
You

↓

Order Food

↓

Restaurant

↓

Prepare Food

↓

Call You

↓

You Pick It Up
```

The restaurant "calls you back."

That's exactly where the programming term comes from.

---

# 4. Why Callbacks Exist

Suppose downloading a file takes 10 seconds.

Without callbacks:

```text
Download File

↓

Wait 10 Seconds

↓

Continue Program
```

JavaScript would freeze.

Instead:

```text
Start Download

↓

Continue Program

↓

Download Completes

↓

Execute Callback
```

The program stays responsive.

---

# 5. Callback Hell

One of the biggest problems with callbacks.

Suppose:

1. Login
2. Fetch Profile
3. Fetch Orders
4. Fetch Payments

Using callbacks:

```js
login(function(user){

    getProfile(user,function(profile){

        getOrders(profile,function(orders){

            getPayments(orders,function(payments){

                console.log(payments);

            });

        });

    });

});
```

Notice the shape:

```text
login

↓

getProfile

↓

getOrders

↓

getPayments
```

Visually:

```text
login
  └── profile
        └── orders
              └── payments
                    └── result
```

This deeply nested structure is known as:

> **Callback Hell**

Also called:

> **The Pyramid of Doom**

---

# Why is Callback Hell Bad?

Problems include:

- Difficult to read.
- Difficult to debug.
- Difficult to maintain.
- Hard error handling.
- Hard to reuse code.

This is one of the main reasons Promises were introduced.

---

# 6. Error-First Callbacks (Node.js)

Node.js established a standard callback pattern.

Example:

```js
function callback(error, data){

}
```

The first parameter is always:

```text
Error
```

Second parameter:

```text
Result
```

Example:

```js
fs.readFile("file.txt", function(err, data){

    if(err){
        console.log(err);
        return;
    }

    console.log(data);

});
```

Pattern:

```text
Success?

↓

Yes

↓

err = null

data = File

--------------------

Failure?

↓

err = Error

data = undefined
```

---

# Why This Pattern?

Because JavaScript functions can only return one value.

Instead:

```js
callback(error,data);
```

lets the caller know whether the operation succeeded.

---

# 7. Callbacks and Higher-Order Functions

A **Higher-Order Function** is:

> A function that accepts another function or returns a function.

Examples:

- `map()`
- `filter()`
- `reduce()`
- `setTimeout()`
- `addEventListener()`

Each accepts a callback.

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Calling instead of passing.

Wrong:

```js
setTimeout(print(),1000);
```

Correct:

```js
setTimeout(print,1000);
```

---

## Mistake 2

Thinking callbacks are always asynchronous.

Wrong.

```js
map()
```

uses synchronous callbacks.

---

## Mistake 3

Too much nesting.

Instead of:

```js
login(function(){

    profile(function(){

        settings(function(){

        });

    });

});
```

Prefer Promises or `async/await`.

---

# Under the Hood

Suppose:

```js
setTimeout(callback,1000);
```

Conceptually:

```text
JavaScript

↓

Store callback

↓

Browser Timer

↓

Wait

↓

Move callback

↓

Callback Queue

↓

Event Loop

↓

Call Stack

↓

Execute callback
```

---

# Interview Perspective

Interviewers often ask:

> **"What is a callback?"**

A complete answer is:

> "A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function so that it can be executed later. Callbacks may execute synchronously, such as in `map()` or `forEach()`, or asynchronously, such as with `setTimeout()` or `addEventListener()`."

That's a stronger answer than simply saying:

> "It's a function that runs later."

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Write a function:

```js
repeat(callback)
```

that executes the callback three times.

Example:

```js
repeat(() => console.log("Hi"));
```

Output:

```text
Hi
Hi
Hi
```

---

## Medium

Write a custom implementation of:

```js
forEach()
```

that accepts an array and a callback.

Example usage:

```js
customForEach([1,2,3], console.log);
```

---

## Hard

Convert this callback-based code into Promise-based code:

```js
login(function(user){

    getOrders(user,function(orders){

        console.log(orders);

    });

});
```

(We'll formally learn Promises in the next lesson.)

---

# Time Complexity

Passing a callback itself is **O(1)**.

The complexity depends on what the callback does.

Examples:

| Function | Complexity |
|----------|------------|
| `forEach()` | O(n) |
| `map()` | O(n) |
| `filter()` | O(n) |
| `setTimeout()` registration | O(1) |

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is a callback?
2. Can callbacks be synchronous?
3. Can callbacks be asynchronous?
4. Why were callbacks introduced?
5. What is callback hell?
6. Why is callback hell difficult to maintain?
7. What is the Node.js error-first callback pattern?
8. Why shouldn't you call the callback when passing it?

---

## Coding

9. Write a function that accepts a callback and invokes it with a greeting.
10. Implement a custom `repeat()` function that runs a callback `n` times.
11. Implement a simple version of `forEach()`.
12. Create a `delay()` function that accepts a callback and executes it after two seconds.

---

## Debugging

13. Why doesn't this work?

```js
setTimeout(print(),1000);
```

Fix it.

14. Explain why `forEach()` callbacks execute before `"Done"` is logged.

15. Identify the callback hell in this code and explain how Promises could improve it.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Callback

↓

Function Passed
to Another Function

↓

Executed Later
(or Immediately)

-----------------------

Synchronous

map()
filter()
forEach()
reduce()

-----------------------

Asynchronous

setTimeout()
setInterval()
addEventListener()

-----------------------

Node.js

callback(err,data)

-----------------------

Callback Hell

Deeply Nested
Callbacks

↓

Hard to Read
Hard to Debug
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Define a callback clearly.
- ✅ Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous callbacks.
- ✅ Recognize callback hell and explain why it's problematic.
- ✅ Describe the error-first callback convention in Node.js.
- ✅ Pass a function as a callback without accidentally invoking it.
- ✅ Implement simple higher-order functions using callbacks.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Without running the code, answer the following:

```js
function process(items, callback) {
  for (const item of items) {
    callback(item);
  }
}

function square(num) {
  console.log(num * num);
}

console.log("Start");

process([1, 2, 3], square);

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Done");
}, 0);

console.log("End");
```

Questions:

1. What is the exact output?
2. Which callbacks are synchronous?
3. Which callback is asynchronous?
4. At what point does the `square` function execute?
5. Why is `"Done"` printed last even though the timeout is `0`?

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 5.3 — Promises**, where we'll cover:

- Why Promises were introduced.
- Promise states (`pending`, `fulfilled`, `rejected`).
- `.then()`, `.catch()`, and `.finally()`.
- Promise chaining.
- Error propagation.
- How Promises interact with the Microtask Queue.
- Common interview questions and live coding exercises involving Promises.

questions.questionText: What term describes deeply nested asynchronous callbacks making code hard to read?
questions.explanation: Deeply nested callbacks are commonly referred to as Callback Hell or Pyramids of Doom.

questions.questionText: Which are characteristics of Node-style error-first callbacks? (Select all that apply)
options: The first argument is reserved for an error object.
The callback is the last argument of the function.
questions.explanation: Node.js uses error-first callbacks (`(err, data) => ...`) as the final parameter of asynchronous functions.

questions.questionText: What type of callback runs immediately during the execution of the calling function, like inside Array.prototype.map?
questions.explanation: A synchronous callback is executed immediately during the function's execution rather than being deferred.

lessons.objective: Master Promise states, executors, resolved/rejected handlers, and error catching flows.
lessons.content:
# Module 5 — Asynchronous JavaScript

# Lesson 5.3 — Promises

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely High)

---

# Why This Lesson Matters

If there is one asynchronous JavaScript topic that appears in almost every frontend interview, it's **Promises**.

You'll encounter them when using:

- `fetch()`
- `axios`
- Database APIs
- File APIs
- Authentication
- React Query
- TanStack Query
- GraphQL clients
- Next.js data fetching

Before ES6 (ECMAScript 2015), callbacks were the primary way to handle asynchronous work. As applications grew, deeply nested callbacks became difficult to read and maintain.

Promises were introduced to make asynchronous code:

- Easier to read
- Easier to compose
- Easier to debug
- Easier to handle errors

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what a Promise is.
- Understand the three Promise states.
- Explain the Promise lifecycle.
- Use `.then()`, `.catch()`, and `.finally()`.
- Chain Promises correctly.
- Explain error propagation.
- Understand why Promise callbacks run before `setTimeout()`.
- Solve common Promise interview questions.

---

# 1. What is a Promise?

A **Promise** is an object that represents the **eventual result** of an asynchronous operation.

A Promise doesn't necessarily contain a value **now**.

Instead, it says:

> "I promise to give you a value (or an error) later."

---

## Real-Life Analogy

Imagine you order a custom laptop online.

```text
Today
│
├── Place Order
│
└── Receive Receipt (Promise)

Later
│
├── Laptop Delivered ✅
│
└── Or Order Cancelled ❌
```

The receipt is **not** the laptop.

It represents a future outcome.

A JavaScript Promise works the same way.

---

# Visual Mental Model

```text
Start Async Task
        │
        ▼
     Promise
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   ▼         ▼
Success    Failure
   │         │
   ▼         ▼
.then()   .catch()
```

---

# 2. Promise States

Every Promise is always in **exactly one** of three states.

```text
           Pending
               │
      ┌────────┴────────┐
      ▼                 ▼
 Fulfilled          Rejected
```

---

## Pending

The asynchronous operation is still running.

Example:

```js
const promise = fetch("/users");
```

Immediately after calling `fetch()`, the request is still in progress.

State:

```text
Pending
```

---

## Fulfilled

The operation completed successfully.

Example:

```text
Server Response

↓

Users Data

↓

Promise Fulfilled
```

---

## Rejected

Something went wrong.

Examples:

- Network error
- Server error
- Authentication failure
- Invalid input

State:

```text
Rejected
```

---

# Important Interview Question

Can a fulfilled Promise become rejected later?

**No.**

Can a rejected Promise become fulfilled later?

**No.**

Once a Promise settles (fulfilled or rejected), its state is **immutable**.

---

# Visual Lifecycle

```text
Pending

↓

Fulfilled

OR

↓

Rejected

(never both)
```

---

# 3. Creating a Promise

Syntax:

```js
const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {

});
```

---

## Syntax Deep Dive

```js
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {

});
```

### `new`

Creates a new Promise instance.

---

### `Promise`

The built-in Promise constructor.

---

### `(resolve, reject) => {}`

This function is called the **executor function**.

JavaScript calls it immediately.

It receives two functions:

```text
resolve()

Success

----------------

reject()

Failure
```

---

# Example

```js
const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  resolve("Success!");
});

console.log(promise);
```

The Promise becomes fulfilled with the value `"Success!"`.

---

# Reject Example

```js
const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  reject("Something went wrong.");
});
```

The Promise becomes rejected.

---

# 4. Consuming a Promise

You don't usually inspect a Promise directly.

Instead, you attach handlers.

```js
promise.then(...);
```

---

# `.then()`

Runs when the Promise is fulfilled.

```js
const promise = Promise.resolve("Hello");

promise.then(value => {
  console.log(value);
});
```

Output:

```text
Hello
```

---

## Under the Hood

```text
Promise

↓

Resolved?

↓

Yes

↓

Queue .then() callback

↓

Microtask Queue

↓

Event Loop

↓

Call Stack

↓

Execute callback
```

Notice:

The callback does **not** execute immediately.

It is queued as a **microtask**.

---

# `.catch()`

Runs when the Promise is rejected.

```js
Promise.reject("Error!")
  .catch(error => {
    console.log(error);
  });
```

Output:

```text
Error!
```

---

# `.finally()`

Runs regardless of success or failure.

```js
fetch("/users")
  .then(data => {
    console.log("Success");
  })
  .catch(error => {
    console.log("Failure");
  })
  .finally(() => {
    console.log("Cleanup");
  });
```

Possible output:

```text
Success
Cleanup
```

or

```text
Failure
Cleanup
```

---

# 5. Promise Chaining

One of the biggest improvements over callbacks.

Instead of:

```text
Task 1

↓

Task 2

↓

Task 3
```

being deeply nested, Promises allow a flat chain.

```js
login()
  .then(getProfile)
  .then(getOrders)
  .then(getPayments)
  .catch(handleError);
```

This is much easier to read.

---

# Why Does Chaining Work?

Each `.then()` returns **another Promise**.

```text
Promise

↓

.then()

↓

New Promise

↓

.then()

↓

New Promise
```

This allows the chain to continue.

---

# Example

```js
Promise.resolve(5)
  .then(value => value * 2)
  .then(value => value + 1)
  .then(value => {
    console.log(value);
  });
```

Step-by-step:

```text
5

↓

10

↓

11

↓

Print 11
```

Output:

```text
11
```

---

# 6. Error Propagation

Errors automatically travel down the chain until a `.catch()` handles them.

```js
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => {
    throw new Error("Oops!");
  })
  .catch(error => {
    console.log(error.message);
  });
```

Output:

```text
Oops!
```

---

## Visual Representation

```text
.then()

↓

Error

↓

Skip Remaining .then()

↓

.catch()
```

---

# 7. Promise vs Callback

Callback style:

```js
login(user => {
  getProfile(user, profile => {
    getOrders(profile, orders => {
      console.log(orders);
    });
  });
});
```

Promise style:

```js
login()
  .then(getProfile)
  .then(getOrders)
  .then(console.log);
```

Benefits:

- Less nesting
- Better readability
- Easier error handling
- Easier composition

---

# 8. Promise and the Microtask Queue

Remember from the previous lesson:

- Promise callbacks go to the **Microtask Queue**.
- `setTimeout()` callbacks go to the **Callback Queue**.

Example:

```js
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("Promise");
});

console.log("End");
```

Output:

```text
Start
End
Promise
Timeout
```

---

## Why?

Timeline:

```text
Main Script
│
├── Start
├── Register timeout
├── Queue Promise callback (Microtask)
├── End
│
└── Main Script ends
        │
        ▼
Run ALL Microtasks
        │
        ▼
Promise
        │
        ▼
Run ONE Callback Task
        │
        ▼
Timeout
```

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Forgetting to return a value in a chain.

```js
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(value => {
    value * 2;
  })
  .then(console.log);
```

Output:

```text
undefined
```

Correct:

```js
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(value => {
    return value * 2;
  })
  .then(console.log);
```

or

```js
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(value => value * 2)
  .then(console.log);
```

---

## Mistake 2

Using `.then()` when the operation should be inside the previous callback.

Understand the flow of returned values.

---

## Mistake 3

Ignoring rejected Promises.

Unhandled rejections can cause warnings or terminate Node.js processes depending on configuration.

Always handle errors with `.catch()` or `try...catch` when using `async/await`.

---

# Under the Hood

When JavaScript sees:

```js
Promise.resolve(42).then(console.log);
```

Conceptually:

```text
Create Promise

↓

Fulfill Promise

↓

Queue .then() callback

↓

Microtask Queue

↓

Event Loop

↓

Call Stack

↓

console.log(42)
```

---

# Interview Perspective

Interviewers often ask:

> **"Why were Promises introduced?"**

A strong answer:

> "Promises were introduced to improve asynchronous programming by avoiding callback hell, enabling chaining, centralizing error handling, and making asynchronous code easier to compose and reason about."

Another favorite:

> **"Why does a Promise callback execute before `setTimeout()`?"**

Answer:

> "Because Promise callbacks are scheduled in the Microtask Queue, which the Event Loop completely drains before processing tasks from the Callback Queue."

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Create a Promise that resolves with `"Frontend"` and print the value.

---

## Medium

Chain three `.then()` calls to transform the number `10` into `25`.

Example:

```text
10
↓

20

↓

25
```

---

## Hard

Predict the output:

```js
console.log("A");

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => {
    console.log("B");
    return "C";
  })
  .then(value => {
    console.log(value);
  });

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("D");
}, 0);

console.log("E");
```

---

# Time Complexity

Promise creation and registration are **O(1)**.

The complexity of a Promise chain depends on the work performed inside each callback.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is a Promise?
2. What are the three Promise states?
3. Can a settled Promise change state?
4. What does `resolve()` do?
5. What does `reject()` do?
6. What does `.then()` return?
7. When does `.catch()` execute?
8. When does `.finally()` execute?
9. Why do Promise callbacks run before `setTimeout()`?
10. Why were Promises introduced?

---

## Coding

11. Create a Promise that resolves after one second.
12. Chain three `.then()` calls that modify a string.
13. Create a Promise that rejects and handle it with `.catch()`.
14. Add a `.finally()` block that logs `"Finished"`.

---

## Debugging

15. Why does this print `undefined`?

```js
Promise.resolve(3)
  .then(value => {
    value * 2;
  })
  .then(console.log);
```

Fix it.

16. Explain why `.catch()` can handle errors thrown inside previous `.then()` callbacks.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Promise

↓

Pending

│
├── Fulfilled
│      │
│      ▼
│    .then()
│
└── Rejected
       │
       ▼
    .catch()

.finally()

↓

Runs Always

-----------------------

Promise Callbacks

↓

Microtask Queue

-----------------------

setTimeout

↓

Callback Queue

-----------------------

Each .then()

↓

Returns a New Promise
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, ensure you can:

- ✅ Define a Promise and explain why it exists.
- ✅ Describe the Promise lifecycle.
- ✅ Use `.then()`, `.catch()`, and `.finally()`.
- ✅ Explain Promise chaining.
- ✅ Explain error propagation.
- ✅ Predict execution order involving Promises and `setTimeout()`.
- ✅ Explain why Promise callbacks use the Microtask Queue.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Without running the code, determine the exact output and explain every step:

```js
console.log("Start");

Promise.resolve(1)
  .then(value => {
    console.log(value);
    return value + 1;
  })
  .then(value => {
    console.log(value);
    throw new Error("Boom");
  })
  .catch(error => {
    console.log(error.message);
    return 99;
  })
  .then(value => {
    console.log(value);
  })
  .finally(() => {
    console.log("Finished");
  });

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

console.log("End");
```

Answer:

1. What is the final output?
2. Which callbacks are placed in the Microtask Queue?
3. At what point does the error occur?
4. Why does the chain continue after `.catch()`?
5. Why is `"Timeout"` printed last?

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 5.4 — `async` / `await`**, where we'll cover:

- How `async` and `await` are built on top of Promises.
- What happens under the hood.
- Sequential vs parallel asynchronous execution.
- Error handling with `try...catch`.
- Common interview questions comparing `async/await` with Promise chaining.

questions.questionText: Once a Promise is resolved successfully, what is its state?
questions.explanation: Promises resolve to either the `fulfilled` state or reject to the `rejected` state.

questions.questionText: Which parameters are passed into the executor function when creating a new Promise? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The executor signature is `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)`.

questions.questionText: What method on a Promise instance is called to handle rejection errors?
questions.explanation: The `.catch()` handler is executed when a promise is rejected or throws an error.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.4
lessons.objective: Learn async/await syntax, sequential vs parallel await statements, and try/catch exception handling.
lessons.content:
# Module 5 — Asynchronous JavaScript

# Lesson 5.4 — `async` / `await`

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the Most Frequently Asked JavaScript Topics)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

One of the biggest misconceptions about `async/await` is this:

> **"`async/await` replaced Promises."**

❌ **False.**

Another common one:

> **"`await` pauses JavaScript."**

❌ **Also false.**

The correct understanding is:

- `async/await` is **syntactic sugar** over Promises.
- Promises are still doing the actual asynchronous work.
- `await` pauses **only the current async function**, not the entire JavaScript engine.

This distinction is tested frequently in frontend interviews.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what `async` does.
- Explain what `await` does.
- Understand how `async/await` is built on Promises.
- Understand what happens internally.
- Handle errors with `try...catch`.
- Execute asynchronous operations sequentially and in parallel.
- Predict execution order.
- Answer common interview questions confidently.

---

# 1. Why Was `async/await` Introduced?

Recall Promise chaining:

```js
login()
  .then(getProfile)
  .then(getOrders)
  .then(getPayments)
  .catch(handleError);
```

This is much better than callback hell, but long chains can still become difficult to read.

`async/await` allows us to write asynchronous code that **looks like synchronous code**.

The equivalent becomes:

```js
async function loadData() {
  try {
    const user = await login();
    const profile = await getProfile(user);
    const orders = await getOrders(profile);
    const payments = await getPayments(orders);

    console.log(payments);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}
```

Same behavior.

Much easier to read.

---

# Visual Comparison

## Promise Chain

```text
login()

↓

.then()

↓

.then()

↓

.then()

↓

.catch()
```

---

## async/await

```text
login()

↓

await

↓

profile

↓

await

↓

orders

↓

await

↓

payments
```

Looks like normal top-to-bottom code.

---

# 2. The `async` Keyword

An `async` function always returns a **Promise**.

Even if you return a primitive value.

Example:

```js
async function greet() {
  return "Hello";
}

const result = greet();

console.log(result);
```

Output:

```text
Promise { "Hello" }
```

---

## Under the Hood

JavaScript treats this:

```js
async function greet() {
  return "Hello";
}
```

as if you had written:

```js
function greet() {
  return Promise.resolve("Hello");
}
```

These are effectively equivalent.

---

# Important Interview Question

What does an `async` function always return?

✅ **Answer: A Promise.**

Even this:

```js
async function number() {
  return 5;
}
```

actually returns:

```js
Promise.resolve(5)
```

---

# 3. The `await` Keyword

`await` waits for a Promise to settle before continuing.

Example:

```js
async function getMessage() {
  const message = await Promise.resolve("Hello");

  console.log(message);
}

getMessage();
```

Output:

```text
Hello
```

---

# Syntax Breakdown

```js
const message = await promise;
```

- `const message` → Variable to store the resolved value.
- `=` → Assignment.
- `await` → Pause this async function until the Promise settles.
- `promise` → The Promise being awaited.

---

# Visual Mental Model

```text
Async Function

↓

await Promise

↓

Pause THIS function

↓

Promise Resolves

↓

Resume Function

↓

Continue Execution
```

Notice:

The **JavaScript engine keeps running other work**.

Only this async function pauses.

---

# 4. What Actually Happens Under the Hood?

Consider:

```js
async function example() {
  console.log("A");

  await Promise.resolve();

  console.log("B");
}

example();

console.log("C");
```

Many beginners expect:

```text
A
B
C
```

Incorrect.

Let's trace it.

### Step 1

Call `example()`.

Print:

```text
A
```

---

### Step 2

Encounter:

```js
await Promise.resolve();
```

The Promise is already resolved.

But the continuation after `await` is still scheduled as a **microtask**.

The async function pauses.

---

### Step 3

Continue executing the remaining synchronous code.

Print:

```text
C
```

---

### Step 4

The Call Stack becomes empty.

The Event Loop processes the Microtask Queue.

Resume the async function.

Print:

```text
B
```

Final output:

```text
A
C
B
```

---

# Visual Timeline

```text
Main Script
│
├── example()
│     ├── Print A
│     ├── await Promise
│     └── Pause Function
│
├── Print C
│
└── Main Script Ends
        │
        ▼
Microtask Queue
        │
        ▼
Resume Async Function
        │
        ▼
Print B
```

---

# 5. Sequential Execution

Suppose:

```js
const user = await getUser();

const posts = await getPosts(user.id);

const comments = await getComments(posts);
```

Timeline:

```text
User

↓

Posts

↓

Comments
```

Each operation waits for the previous one.

This is **sequential execution**.

---

# When is Sequential Execution Correct?

When one task depends on another.

Example:

```text
Login

↓

Need Token

↓

Fetch Profile

↓

Need Profile

↓

Fetch Orders
```

You cannot fetch orders before knowing the user.

---

# 6. Parallel Execution

Suppose:

```js
const users = await fetchUsers();

const products = await fetchProducts();

const settings = await fetchSettings();
```

These requests are independent.

The code above runs them one after another, which is slower.

Better:

```js
const [users, products, settings] = await Promise.all([
  fetchUsers(),
  fetchProducts(),
  fetchSettings()
]);
```

---

## Visual Comparison

### Sequential

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
Products
  │
  ▼
Settings
```

Total time:

```text
2s + 3s + 1s = 6s
```

---

### Parallel

```text
Users ─────┐
           │
Products ──┼──► Promise.all
           │
Settings ──┘
```

Total time:

```text
Longest Request

↓

3 seconds
```

Huge performance improvement.

---

# 7. Error Handling

With Promise chaining:

```js
fetchData()
  .then(...)
  .catch(...);
```

With `async/await`:

```js
async function loadData() {
  try {
    const data = await fetchData();

    console.log(data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}
```

---

# How `try...catch` Works

```text
try

↓

Everything OK?

↓

YES

↓

Continue

-------------------

NO

↓

Jump to catch
```

---

# Example

```js
async function test() {
  try {
    await Promise.reject("Boom!");
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);
  }
}

test();
```

Output:

```text
Boom!
```

---

# 8. Mixing `await` and `.then()`

You might see:

```js
const data = await fetchUsers().then(res => res.json());
```

This works, but it's generally less readable.

Prefer one style consistently:

```js
const response = await fetchUsers();

const data = await response.json();
```

---

# 9. Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Using `await` outside an async function.

```js
const data = await fetchUsers();
```

Output:

```text
SyntaxError
```

Correct:

```js
async function load() {
  const data = await fetchUsers();
}
```

*(Modern JavaScript modules support top-level `await`, but interview questions usually refer to standard function contexts unless specified.)*

---

## Mistake 2

Forgetting to `await`.

```js
const data = fetchUsers();

console.log(data);
```

Output:

```text
Promise { ... }
```

Not the fetched data.

---

## Mistake 3

Using sequential execution unnecessarily.

Bad:

```js
const a = await fetchA();
const b = await fetchB();
```

If independent, prefer:

```js
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([
  fetchA(),
  fetchB()
]);
```

---

# Under the Hood

Consider:

```js
const data = await fetch("/users");
```

Conceptually:

```text
Start Fetch

↓

Returns Promise

↓

Pause Async Function

↓

Fetch Completes

↓

Queue Continuation

↓

Microtask Queue

↓

Resume Async Function

↓

data Assigned
```

The continuation after `await` is treated like a Promise callback.

---

# Interview Perspective

Common questions include:

### Why was `async/await` introduced?

Expected answer:

> It improves readability by allowing asynchronous code to be written in a synchronous style while still using Promises under the hood.

---

### Does `await` block JavaScript?

Correct answer:

> No. It pauses only the current async function. The JavaScript engine continues executing other synchronous code and processes the Event Loop normally.

---

### Does `async/await` replace Promises?

Correct answer:

> No. It is built on top of Promises.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Write an async function that returns `"Frontend"`.

---

## Medium

Use `async/await` to fetch a user and print the name.

*(Assume `fetchUser()` returns a Promise.)*

---

## Hard

Refactor this Promise chain into `async/await`:

```js
login()
  .then(getProfile)
  .then(getOrders)
  .then(console.log)
  .catch(console.error);
```

---

# Time Complexity

`async` and `await` themselves are **O(1)** language features.

The overall complexity depends on the asynchronous work being performed.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What does an `async` function always return?
2. What does `await` do?
3. Can `await` be used in a normal function?
4. Does `await` block the JavaScript engine?
5. Why does code after `await` execute later?
6. When should you use sequential execution?
7. When should you use `Promise.all()`?
8. How do you handle errors with `async/await`?

---

## Coding

9. Write an async function that returns `100`.
10. Create a function that waits one second before returning `"Done"`.
11. Fetch two independent resources in parallel.
12. Convert a Promise chain into `async/await`.

---

## Debugging

13. Why does this print a Promise?

```js
const result = fetchUsers();

console.log(result);
```

14. Fix this error:

```js
function load() {
  const data = await fetchUsers();
}
```

15. Explain why this outputs `A C B`:

```js
async function demo() {
  console.log("A");
  await Promise.resolve();
  console.log("B");
}

demo();

console.log("C");
```

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
async Function

↓

Always Returns Promise

-------------------------

await

↓

Wait for Promise

↓

Resume Later

-------------------------

await

Pauses

ONLY

Current Async Function

-------------------------

Continuation After await

↓

Microtask Queue

-------------------------

Independent Tasks

↓

Promise.all()

-------------------------

Errors

↓

try...catch
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain that `async/await` is built on Promises.
- ✅ State that every `async` function returns a Promise.
- ✅ Explain what `await` pauses (and what it doesn't).
- ✅ Choose between sequential and parallel execution.
- ✅ Handle asynchronous errors with `try...catch`.
- ✅ Predict execution order involving `await`, Promises, and synchronous code.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Without running the code, determine the exact output and explain each step:

```js
async function first() {
  console.log("1");

  await Promise.resolve();

  console.log("2");

  return "Done";
}

console.log("Start");

first().then(result => {
  console.log(result);
});

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("3");
});

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("4");
}, 0);

console.log("End");
```

Answer these questions:

1. What is the exact output?
2. Which lines execute synchronously?
3. Which callbacks enter the Microtask Queue?
4. Why is `"End"` printed before `"2"`?
5. Why is `"Done"` printed before `"4"`?
6. Draw the Call Stack, Microtask Queue, and Callback Queue after the main script completes.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 5.5 — Promise Utilities (`Promise.all()`, `Promise.allSettled()`, `Promise.race()`, `Promise.any()`)**, where we'll cover:

- When to use each utility.
- Failure behavior and trade-offs.
- Real-world React examples (fetching multiple APIs).
- Performance optimization patterns.
- Common frontend interview questions involving concurrent asynchronous operations.

lessons.objective: Master Promise static utility functions: all, allSettled, race, and any.
lessons.content:
# Module 5 — Asynchronous JavaScript

# Lesson 5.5 — Promise Utilities (`Promise.all()`, `Promise.allSettled()`, `Promise.race()`, `Promise.any()`)

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Interview Mastery)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Very High)

---

# Why This Lesson Matters

Imagine you're building a dashboard.

When the page loads, you need to fetch:

- 👤 User Profile
- 🛒 Orders
- 🔔 Notifications
- 💳 Wallet Balance

A beginner might write:

```js
const profile = await getProfile();
const orders = await getOrders();
const notifications = await getNotifications();
const wallet = await getWallet();
```

This works, but it's slow because each request waits for the previous one.

If each request takes 1 second:

```text
Profile         1s
Orders          1s
Notifications   1s
Wallet          1s
-------------------
Total = 4 seconds
```

A better solution:

```js
const [profile, orders, notifications, wallet] =
  await Promise.all([
    getProfile(),
    getOrders(),
    getNotifications(),
    getWallet()
  ]);
```

Now all requests start together.

```text
Profile         1s
Orders          1s
Notifications   1s
Wallet          1s
-------------------
Total = 1 second
```

This is exactly why Promise utility methods exist.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain why Promise utility methods exist.
- Use `Promise.all()`.
- Use `Promise.allSettled()`.
- Use `Promise.race()`.
- Use `Promise.any()`.
- Understand when each method should be used.
- Answer interview questions about concurrent asynchronous operations.

---

# 1. Why Promise Utilities Exist

Consider this code:

```js
const profile = await fetchProfile();
const posts = await fetchPosts();
const friends = await fetchFriends();
```

Timeline:

```text
Profile
    │
    ▼
Posts
    │
    ▼
Friends
```

Total:

```text
1 + 1 + 1 = 3 seconds
```

But these requests don't depend on one another.

They can run simultaneously.

```text
Profile ─────┐
             │
Posts ───────┼──► Together
             │
Friends ─────┘
```

Total:

```text
1 second
```

---

# 2. `Promise.all()`

## What is it?

`Promise.all()` takes an iterable (usually an array) of Promises and returns **one Promise**.

That returned Promise:

- fulfills when **all** input Promises fulfill.
- rejects immediately if **any one** Promise rejects.

---

## Syntax

```js
Promise.all([
  promise1,
  promise2,
  promise3
]);
```

---

## Example

```js
const result = await Promise.all([
  Promise.resolve("A"),
  Promise.resolve("B"),
  Promise.resolve("C")
]);

console.log(result);
```

Output:

```text
["A", "B", "C"]
```

---

# Visual Flow

```text
Promise A ─────┐
               │
Promise B ─────┼──► Promise.all
               │
Promise C ─────┘
               │
               ▼
      All Complete?
               │
          Yes
               │
               ▼
   Return Array of Results
```

---

# Real-World Example

React Dashboard

```js
const [user, notifications, orders] =
  await Promise.all([
    fetchUser(),
    fetchNotifications(),
    fetchOrders()
  ]);
```

The page waits until everything is ready.

---

# What if One Promise Fails?

Example:

```js
Promise.all([
  Promise.resolve(1),
  Promise.reject("Oops"),
  Promise.resolve(3)
]);
```

Result:

```text
Rejected

↓

"Oops"
```

Even though the other Promises may still finish in the background, the Promise returned by `Promise.all()` rejects as soon as it observes a rejection.

---

# Interview Question

Does `Promise.all()` cancel the other Promises?

**No.**

It simply rejects early.

The other asynchronous operations may continue unless you explicitly cancel them (for example, using an `AbortController` with `fetch()`).

---

# 3. `Promise.allSettled()`

Sometimes you want every request to finish, even if some fail.

Example:

Dashboard widgets:

- Weather
- Stocks
- Messages
- Notifications

If Weather fails, should everything fail?

Probably not.

---

## Syntax

```js
Promise.allSettled([
  promise1,
  promise2
]);
```

---

## Example

```js
const result = await Promise.allSettled([
  Promise.resolve("A"),
  Promise.reject("Error")
]);

console.log(result);
```

Output:

```js
[
  {
    status: "fulfilled",
    value: "A"
  },
  {
    status: "rejected",
    reason: "Error"
  }
]
```

---

# Visual Flow

```text
Promise A

↓

Success

----------------

Promise B

↓

Failure

----------------

Promise.allSettled()

↓

Wait for BOTH

↓

Return Status of Each
```

---

# When Should You Use It?

Use `Promise.allSettled()` when:

- Every request matters.
- You want to display partial results.
- One failure shouldn't stop the entire process.

Example:

```text
Dashboard

✔ Profile

✔ Orders

✖ Notifications

Still Render Page
```

---

# 4. `Promise.race()`

`Promise.race()` returns the result of the **first Promise to settle**.

That means the first Promise to either:

- fulfill
- reject

wins the race.

---

## Example

```js
const result = await Promise.race([
  new Promise(resolve =>
    setTimeout(() => resolve("Fast"), 500)
  ),

  new Promise(resolve =>
    setTimeout(() => resolve("Slow"), 1000)
  )
]);

console.log(result);
```

Output:

```text
Fast
```

---

# Visual Flow

```text
Promise A

500ms

↓

Winner

------------------

Promise B

1000ms

↓

Too Late
```

---

# Real-World Example

Request timeout.

```js
Promise.race([
  fetch("/users"),

  new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject("Timeout"), 5000)
  )
]);
```

If the fetch takes longer than 5 seconds:

```text
Timeout
```

---

# Important Detail

If the first Promise to settle rejects, the returned Promise rejects immediately.

```js
Promise.race([
  Promise.reject("Error"),
  Promise.resolve("Success")
]);
```

Result:

```text
Rejected

↓

Error
```

---

# 5. `Promise.any()`

`Promise.any()` waits for the **first fulfilled Promise**.

Rejected Promises are ignored until either:

- one Promise fulfills, or
- all Promises reject.

---

## Example

```js
const result = await Promise.any([
  Promise.reject("A"),
  Promise.resolve("B"),
  Promise.resolve("C")
]);

console.log(result);
```

Output:

```text
B
```

---

# Visual Flow

```text
Promise A

Rejected

Ignored

----------------

Promise B

Fulfilled

↓

Winner
```

---

# What if Every Promise Rejects?

```js
Promise.any([
  Promise.reject("A"),
  Promise.reject("B")
]);
```

Result:

An `AggregateError` is thrown because none of the Promises fulfilled.

---

# Real-World Example

Suppose your application has multiple mirror servers.

```text
Server 1

↓

Down

----------------

Server 2

↓

Responds

↓

Done
```

Use:

```js
Promise.any()
```

---

# Comparing All Four

| Method | Waits For | Rejects If | Returns |
|---------|-----------|------------|----------|
| `Promise.all()` | All fulfill | Any reject | Array of fulfilled values |
| `Promise.allSettled()` | All settle | Never rejects because of individual failures | Array of status objects |
| `Promise.race()` | First settles | First settled Promise rejects | First settled value or rejection |
| `Promise.any()` | First fulfills | All reject | First fulfilled value |

---

# Visual Summary

```text
Promise.all()

A ✔
B ✔
C ✔

↓

Success

----------------------

Promise.all()

A ✔
B ✖
C ✔

↓

Reject Immediately

----------------------

Promise.allSettled()

A ✔
B ✖
C ✔

↓

Return Statuses

----------------------

Promise.race()

Fastest Wins

----------------------

Promise.any()

First Success Wins
```

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Using `Promise.all()` when failures are acceptable.

Better:

```js
Promise.allSettled()
```

---

## Mistake 2

Using sequential `await` unnecessarily.

Instead of:

```js
const user = await fetchUser();
const orders = await fetchOrders();
```

Prefer:

```js
const [user, orders] =
  await Promise.all([
    fetchUser(),
    fetchOrders()
  ]);
```

when they are independent.

---

## Mistake 3

Confusing `Promise.race()` with `Promise.any()`.

Remember:

`Promise.race()`

```text
First settles

↓

Success OR Failure
```

`Promise.any()`

```text
First SUCCESS

↓

Ignores rejections
```

---

# Under the Hood

Conceptually:

```js
Promise.all([
  A,
  B,
  C
]);
```

acts like:

```text
Wait for A

Wait for B

Wait for C

↓

All Finished?

↓

Resolve Array
```

For `Promise.any()`:

```text
Wait for A

↓

Rejected

Ignore

↓

Wait for B

↓

Fulfilled

↓

Resolve Immediately
```

---

# Interview Perspective

A common interview question:

> **When would you choose `Promise.allSettled()` instead of `Promise.all()`?**

Strong answer:

> "I'd use `Promise.allSettled()` when I need every asynchronous operation to complete regardless of individual failures, such as rendering independent dashboard widgets where one failed request shouldn't prevent the others from displaying."

---

Another favorite:

> **Why is `Promise.all()` faster than multiple sequential `await`s?**

Answer:

> "Because it starts all asynchronous operations concurrently instead of waiting for each one to finish before starting the next."

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Fetch two independent APIs concurrently using `Promise.all()`.

---

## Medium

Use `Promise.race()` to implement a 3-second timeout around a fetch request.

---

## Hard

Implement a function:

```js
firstSuccessful(promises)
```

using `Promise.any()` that returns the first fulfilled result.

---

# Time Complexity

Creating these utility Promises is **O(n)** with respect to the number of input Promises, because each input Promise must be tracked.

The overall elapsed time depends on the asynchronous operations themselves, not on the utility method.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What does `Promise.all()` do?
2. When does `Promise.all()` reject?
3. What does `Promise.allSettled()` return?
4. When should you use `Promise.allSettled()`?
5. How does `Promise.race()` determine the winner?
6. How is `Promise.any()` different from `Promise.race()`?
7. What happens if every Promise passed to `Promise.any()` rejects?
8. Why is `Promise.all()` often more performant than sequential `await`s?

---

## Coding

9. Fetch three independent resources with `Promise.all()`.
10. Display partial results using `Promise.allSettled()`.
11. Create a request that times out after 5 seconds using `Promise.race()`.
12. Use `Promise.any()` to retrieve the first successful response from three mirror endpoints.

---

## Debugging

13. Explain why this rejects:

```js
await Promise.all([
  Promise.resolve(1),
  Promise.reject("Error"),
  Promise.resolve(3)
]);
```

14. Explain why `Promise.race()` might reject even if another Promise would eventually fulfill.

15. Explain why `Promise.any()` throws an `AggregateError` when every Promise rejects.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Promise.all()

✔ Fastest for Independent Tasks
✔ Returns Array
✖ Fails Fast

-------------------------

Promise.allSettled()

✔ Waits for Everything
✔ Never Fails Because One Task Failed
✔ Returns Status Objects

-------------------------

Promise.race()

✔ First Promise to Settle Wins
✔ Success OR Failure

-------------------------

Promise.any()

✔ First Successful Promise Wins
✔ Ignores Rejections
✖ Throws AggregateError if All Reject
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Choose the appropriate Promise utility for a given scenario.
- ✅ Explain the behavior of `Promise.all()`, `Promise.allSettled()`, `Promise.race()`, and `Promise.any()`.
- ✅ Optimize independent asynchronous operations using `Promise.all()`.
- ✅ Distinguish `Promise.race()` from `Promise.any()`.
- ✅ Explain why `Promise.all()` does not cancel other Promises on rejection.
- ✅ Predict outcomes when one or more Promises reject.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Without running the code, determine the output and explain each step:

```js
const p1 = new Promise(resolve =>
  setTimeout(() => resolve("A"), 1000)
);

const p2 = new Promise((_, reject) =>
  setTimeout(() => reject("B"), 500)
);

const p3 = new Promise(resolve =>
  setTimeout(() => resolve("C"), 1500)
);

Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])
  .then(console.log)
  .catch(console.log);

Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3])
  .then(console.log);

Promise.any([p2, p3])
  .then(console.log)
  .catch(console.log);

Promise.race([p1, p2])
  .then(console.log)
  .catch(console.log);
```

Answer:

1. Which Promise utility settles first?
2. What does each utility output?
3. Why does `Promise.all()` reject?
4. Why does `Promise.allSettled()` still wait for all three Promises?
5. Why does `Promise.any()` resolve with `"C"`?
6. Why does `Promise.race()` reject with `"B"`?

---

# 🎉 Module 5 Complete!

You have now covered the entire **Asynchronous JavaScript** module:

- ✅ Execution Context
- ✅ Call Stack
- ✅ Browser APIs
- ✅ Event Loop
- ✅ Callback Queue
- ✅ Microtask Queue
- ✅ Callbacks
- ✅ Promises
- ✅ `async` / `await`
- ✅ Promise Utility Methods

These concepts form the foundation for writing efficient frontend applications and are among the most heavily tested areas in JavaScript interviews.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** to begin **Module 6 — Browser APIs**, starting with:

**Lesson 6.1 — The DOM (Document Object Model)**

We'll cover:

- What the DOM is.
- How browsers build the DOM tree.
- DOM nodes and element relationships.
- Selecting elements efficiently.
- Creating, updating, and removing elements.
- DOM performance considerations.
- Common DOM interview questions and live coding exercises.

questions.questionText: Which Promise utility rejects immediately if any input promise rejects?
questions.explanation: `Promise.all()` implements an 'all-or-nothing' behavior, rejecting immediately if any promise rejects.

questions.questionText: Which methods return a promise that resolves when the first input promise resolves? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: `Promise.any` resolves with the first successful value. `Promise.race` resolves or rejects with the first settled value.

questions.questionText: What utility returns an array containing objects describing the outcome of each input promise?
questions.explanation: `Promise.allSettled()` waits for all promises to settle and returns their status and value/reason.

lessons.content:
# Module 6 — Browser APIs # Lesson 6.1 — The DOM (Document Object Model) > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Intermediate → Advanced) > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely High) --- # 🚨 Before We Start One of the biggest misconceptions is: > **"HTML is the DOM."** ❌ **Incorrect.** HTML and the DOM are **not** the same thing. Understanding this distinction is something many interviewers expect, especially for frontend roles. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Explain what the DOM is. - Explain how the browser converts HTML into a DOM tree. - Understand the relationship between HTML, the DOM, and JavaScript. - Select DOM elements efficiently. - Read and modify DOM elements. - Create, insert, remove, and replace elements. - Understand reflow and repaint. - Answer common DOM interview questions. --- # 1. What is the DOM? **DOM** stands for: > **Document Object Model** The DOM is a **JavaScript representation** of your HTML document. When a browser downloads an HTML file, it **parses** (reads) it and builds a tree of JavaScript objects. JavaScript does **not** manipulate the HTML file directly. It manipulates the DOM. --- ## Visual Flow ```text index.html ↓ Browser downloads HTML ↓ HTML Parser ↓ DOM Tree (JavaScript Objects) ↓ JavaScript Manipulates DOM ↓ Browser Updates Screen ``` --- # HTML vs DOM Suppose we have: ```html

Hello

``` Many people think JavaScript edits this HTML. Not exactly. Instead, the browser creates something like: ```text Document │ └── body │ └── h1 │ └── "Hello" ``` Each item is an object in memory. --- # Mental Model Imagine HTML is a blueprint. ```text Blueprint (HTML) ↓ Architect Reads It ↓ 3D Building (DOM) ``` JavaScript edits the **building**, not the blueprint. --- # 2. How the Browser Builds the DOM When you visit a website: ### Step 1 Browser downloads: ```html

Hello

``` --- ### Step 2 The HTML Parser reads it. --- ### Step 3 The browser creates objects. ```text Document ↓ html ↓ body ↓ h1 ↓ Text Node ``` This becomes the DOM Tree. --- # Why a Tree? HTML is hierarchical. ```html

Hello

``` Tree: ```text Document │ └── html │ └── body │ └── div │ └── p │ └── "Hello" ``` Every element has relationships: - Parent - Child - Sibling --- # 3. Nodes Everything inside the DOM is a **Node**. Examples: ```html
Hello
``` Contains: ```text div ↓ Text Node ``` Types of nodes include: - Document Node - Element Node - Text Node - Comment Node - Attribute Nodes (historically treated as nodes; in modern DOM they're represented differently but still accessible via the element's attributes) --- # Visual Example ```html

Hello

World

``` Tree: ```text Document │ └── html │ └── body │ ├── h1 │ │ │ └── "Hello" │ └── p │ └── "World" ``` --- # 4. Selecting Elements The browser exposes the DOM through the global `document` object. --- ## `getElementById()` ```html

Frontend

``` ```js const heading = document.getElementById("title"); ``` --- ### Syntax Breakdown ```js document.getElementById("title"); ``` - `document` → The root DOM object. - `.` → Access a property or method. - `getElementById` → Built-in method. - `("title")` → ID to search for. Returns: ```text

``` or ```text null ``` if not found. --- # `querySelector()` Returns the **first** matching element. ```js const button = document.querySelector(".btn"); ``` Works with CSS selectors: ```js document.querySelector("#title"); document.querySelector(".card"); document.querySelector("button"); document.querySelector("nav ul li"); ``` --- # `querySelectorAll()` Returns **all** matching elements. ```js const buttons = document.querySelectorAll(".btn"); ``` Returns a `NodeList`. --- # Interview Question Difference between: ```js querySelector() ``` and ```js querySelectorAll() ``` Answer: | Method | Returns | |---------|----------| | `querySelector()` | First matching element | | `querySelectorAll()` | All matching elements (`NodeList`) | --- # 5. Reading and Updating Content Suppose: ```html

Frontend

``` --- ## `textContent` ```js const heading = document.getElementById("title"); console.log(heading.textContent); ``` Output: ```text Frontend ``` Update: ```js heading.textContent = "JavaScript"; ``` --- ## `innerHTML` ```js heading.innerHTML = "Hello"; ``` Now: ```html

Hello

``` --- ## Interview Question Difference: ```js textContent ``` vs ```js innerHTML ``` | textContent | innerHTML | |-------------|-----------| | Plain text | Parses HTML | | Safer | Can introduce XSS if used with untrusted content | | Faster for text-only updates | More work because HTML must be parsed | --- # 6. Updating Attributes Example: ```html ``` JavaScript: ```js const image = document.getElementById("logo"); image.src = "logo.png"; image.alt = "Company Logo"; ``` --- Generic methods: ```js image.setAttribute("src", "logo.png"); image.getAttribute("src"); image.removeAttribute("src"); ``` --- # 7. Working with Classes ```js element.classList.add("active"); element.classList.remove("active"); element.classList.toggle("active"); element.classList.contains("active"); ``` --- Visual: ```text Initial ↓ btn ↓ add() ↓ btn active ↓ remove() ↓ btn ``` --- # 8. Creating Elements ```js const div = document.createElement("div"); ``` Now: ```text div ↓ Exists Only in Memory ``` It is **not** yet visible. --- Add text: ```js div.textContent = "Hello"; ``` --- Append to page: ```js document.body.appendChild(div); ``` Now the DOM updates. --- # 9. Removing Elements ```js const item = document.querySelector(".card"); item.remove(); ``` Gone from the DOM. --- # 10. Replacing Elements ```js const newDiv = document.createElement("div"); oldDiv.replaceWith(newDiv); ``` --- # 11. Traversing the DOM Suppose: ```html

``` Relationships: ```text div │ ├── h1 └── p ``` Useful properties: ```js element.parentElement element.children element.firstElementChild element.lastElementChild element.nextElementSibling element.previousElementSibling ``` --- # 12. Reflow vs Repaint This is an advanced interview topic. ## Reflow (Layout) Occurs when layout changes. Examples: - Width - Height - Margin - Padding - Font size The browser recalculates positions and sizes. --- ## Repaint Occurs when appearance changes but layout doesn't. Example: ```css color: red; ``` The browser repaints pixels without recalculating layout. --- ## Visual ```text DOM Change ↓ Need New Layout? ↓ YES ↓ Reflow ↓ Repaint ---------------- Need Only Color? ↓ Repaint Only ``` Reflow is generally more expensive than repaint. --- # 13. Real-World Example Imagine an e-commerce cart. When the user clicks: ```text Add to Cart ``` JavaScript: - Creates a new cart item element. - Updates the cart count. - Changes the total price. - Adds an animation class. All of these are DOM manipulations. --- # Common Mistakes ## Mistake 1 Using `innerHTML` when only text is needed. Prefer: ```js element.textContent = "Hello"; ``` --- ## Mistake 2 Querying the same element repeatedly. Bad: ```js document.getElementById("title").textContent = "A"; document.getElementById("title").style.color = "red"; ``` Better: ```js const title = document.getElementById("title"); title.textContent = "A"; title.style.color = "red"; ``` --- ## Mistake 3 Creating many DOM updates one by one. Each update can trigger layout work. Batch updates when possible to improve performance. --- # Under the Hood When you write: ```js element.textContent = "Hello"; ``` Conceptually: ```text JavaScript ↓ Update DOM Node ↓ Browser Detects Change ↓ Recalculate (if needed) ↓ Paint Screen ``` --- # Interview Perspective Common questions: ### Is HTML the DOM? **Answer:** No. HTML is the source markup. The browser parses it into a DOM tree of JavaScript objects. --- ### Why is the DOM a tree? Because HTML elements are nested, creating parent-child relationships. --- ### Why is manipulating the DOM expensive? Because changes may trigger style recalculation, layout (reflow), and repaint, especially if many updates are made individually. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Select an element with ID `title` and change its text to `"Interview Ready"`. --- ## Medium Create a `
  • ` element, set its text, and append it to an existing `
      `. --- ## Hard Implement a function: ```js function highlightActive(id) { // Remove "active" from all nav links // Add "active" to the link with the given id } ``` Use efficient DOM selection and `classList`. --- # Time Complexity Approximate complexities (browser implementations may vary): | Operation | Complexity | |-----------|------------| | `getElementById()` | O(1) (typically optimized) | | `querySelector()` | Depends on selector; often efficient but can be O(n) | | `querySelectorAll()` | O(n) in the worst case | | `appendChild()` | O(1) for the insertion itself (layout cost is separate) | --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. What is the DOM? 2. Is HTML the same as the DOM? 3. Why is the DOM represented as a tree? 4. What is a node? 5. What is the difference between `querySelector()` and `querySelectorAll()`? 6. When would you use `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`? 7. What is reflow? 8. What is repaint? 9. Why is reflow generally more expensive than repaint? 10. What does `classList.toggle()` do? --- ## Coding 11. Change the text of a heading. 12. Add a new paragraph to the page. 13. Remove the last item from a list. 14. Toggle a `dark-mode` class on the ``. 15. Replace an image with another one using DOM methods. --- ## Debugging 16. Why does this return `null`? ```js document.getElementById("main"); ``` (Assume the element doesn't exist yet when the script runs.) 17. Explain why using `innerHTML` with user input can be dangerous. 18. Optimize this code: ```js for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) { document.body.innerHTML += `

      ${i}

      `; } ``` (Hint: repeated `innerHTML +=` reparses and recreates the DOM repeatedly. We'll discuss better approaches, such as building elements or using a `DocumentFragment`, in a later lesson.) --- # Interview Cheatsheet ```text HTML │ ▼ Browser Parses │ ▼ DOM Tree │ ▼ JavaScript Manipulates DOM │ ▼ Browser Updates Screen ------------------------- Selectors getElementById() querySelector() querySelectorAll() ------------------------- Content textContent innerHTML ------------------------- Classes add() remove() toggle() contains() ------------------------- DOM Updates createElement() appendChild() remove() replaceWith() ------------------------- Performance Reflow → Layout + Paint Repaint → Paint Only ``` --- # Mastery Checklist Before moving on, make sure you can: - ✅ Explain the difference between HTML and the DOM. - ✅ Draw a simple DOM tree from HTML. - ✅ Select elements using common DOM APIs. - ✅ Update text, attributes, and classes. - ✅ Create, insert, remove, and replace elements. - ✅ Explain reflow vs repaint. - ✅ Describe why excessive DOM manipulation can affect performance. --- # Mini Interview Challenge Given this HTML: ```html
      • Study JavaScript
      • Practice TypeScript
      ``` Write JavaScript to: 1. Select the `
        `. 2. Create a new `
      • ` with the text `"Learn React"`. 3. Append it to the list. 4. Add the class `completed` to the first `
      • `. 5. Remove the second `
      • `. 6. Explain which DOM methods you used and why. --- ## Coming Next Reply **Next** for **Lesson 6.2 — Events and Event Propagation**, where you'll learn: - Event listeners - Event bubbling - Event capturing - `event.target` vs `event.currentTarget` - Preventing default behavior - Stopping propagation - Event delegation (a favorite interview topic) - Real-world React comparisons (`onClick`, synthetic events, and delegation)
