lessons.content:
# Module 6 — Browser APIs # Lesson 6.2 — Events and Event Propagation > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced) > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the Most Asked Frontend Topics) --- # 🚨 Before We Start Most developers know how to write: ```javascript button.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Clicked"); }); ``` But during interviews, they struggle when asked: - Why did the event fire twice? - Why did the parent receive the click? - What's the difference between `event.target` and `event.currentTarget`? - Why use event delegation instead of adding listeners everywhere? - What is the event propagation lifecycle? This lesson will make those questions straightforward. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Explain what an event is. - Register event listeners. - Explain the three phases of event propagation. - Understand Event Capturing. - Understand Event Bubbling. - Explain `event.target`. - Explain `event.currentTarget`. - Use `preventDefault()`. - Use `stopPropagation()`. - Implement Event Delegation. - Answer common interview questions confidently. --- # 1. What is an Event? An **event** is something that happens in the browser that JavaScript can respond to. Examples include: - Mouse click - Double click - Keyboard press - Form submission - Page load - Scrolling - Window resize - Drag and drop - Clipboard actions - Touch gestures Think of the browser as constantly listening for user interactions and system events. --- # Real-Life Analogy Imagine a restaurant. ```text Customer Rings Bell ↓ Waiter Notices ↓ Waiter Takes Action ``` The bell ringing is the **event**. The waiter responding is the **event listener**. --- # 2. Event Listener The browser provides the method: ```javascript element.addEventListener() ``` This tells the browser: > "When this event happens, execute this function." --- ## Syntax ```javascript element.addEventListener(type, listener, options); ``` --- ### Syntax Breakdown ```javascript button.addEventListener("click", handleClick); ``` Breakdown: ```text button ↓ DOM Element ---------------------- . ↓ Access Method ---------------------- addEventListener ↓ Built-in Browser Method ---------------------- ( Start Arguments ---------------------- "click" ↓ Event Type ---------------------- handleClick ↓ Callback Function ---------------------- ) End Arguments ``` --- # Example ```javascript const button = document.querySelector("button"); button.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Clicked!"); }); ``` When the user clicks: ```text User Click ↓ Browser Detects Click ↓ Creates Event Object ↓ Calls Listener ↓ Console ``` --- # 3. Common Event Types Mouse Events: ```javascript click dblclick mousedown mouseup mousemove mouseenter mouseleave ``` Keyboard Events: ```javascript keydown keyup ``` Form Events: ```javascript submit change input focus blur ``` Window Events: ```javascript load resize scroll ``` --- # 4. The Event Object Every event listener receives an **Event Object**. Example: ```javascript button.addEventListener("click", function(event) { console.log(event); }); ``` The browser automatically creates this object. It contains information like: - Mouse position - Pressed key - Target element - Timestamp - Event type - Modifier keys (Ctrl, Shift, etc.) --- # Visual ```text User Click ↓ Browser Creates Event Object ↓ { type: "click", target: ``` Tree: ```text Document ↓ html ↓ body ↓ div ↓ button ``` Question: When you click the button... Which listener executes first? The answer depends on the **propagation phase**. --- # The Three Phases Whenever an event occurs, it travels through **three phases**. ```text 1. Capturing Phase ↓ 2. Target Phase ↓ 3. Bubbling Phase ``` --- # Visual Journey ```text Document ↓ html ↓ body ↓ div ↓ button ↓ button (Target) ↓ div ↓ body ↓ html ↓ Document ``` Notice: The event travels **down** first. Then **back up**. --- # 6. Capturing Phase The browser starts at: ```text Document ``` and walks down toward the clicked element. ```text Document ↓ html ↓ body ↓ div ↓ button ``` By default, listeners do **not** execute during this phase. They only do if you explicitly enable capturing. Example: ```javascript parent.addEventListener( "click", () => console.log("Parent Capture"), true ); ``` The third argument (`true`) enables capturing. A more modern equivalent is: ```javascript parent.addEventListener("click", handler, { capture: true }); ``` --- # 7. Target Phase The event reaches the clicked element. Example: ```text button ``` Its listeners execute. --- # 8. Bubbling Phase Now the event travels back upward. ```text button ↓ div ↓ body ↓ html ↓ document ``` This is the **default** behavior. Most listeners you write participate in bubbling. --- # Example ```javascript parent.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Parent"); }); child.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Child"); }); ``` Click the button. Output: ```text Child Parent ``` Why? The child handles the event first at the target phase. Then the event bubbles upward. --- # Visual ```text Click ↓ button ↓ Child Listener ↓ Bubble Up ↓ Parent Listener ``` --- # 9. `event.target` One of the most common interview questions. Suppose: ```html
``` Click the button. ```javascript parent.addEventListener("click", function(event) { console.log(event.target); }); ``` Output: ```text ``` Click the button. Inside the parent's listener: ```text target ↓ button ---------------- currentTarget ↓ div ``` --- # 11. `preventDefault()` Some HTML elements have built-in browser behavior. Example: ```html Home ``` Clicking navigates. Sometimes you want to stop that. ```javascript link.addEventListener("click", function(event) { event.preventDefault(); }); ``` Now the browser does **not** navigate. --- # Other Examples Forms: ```html
``` Normally: ```text Submit ↓ Reload Page ``` Prevent it: ```javascript form.addEventListener("submit", function(event){ event.preventDefault(); }); ``` Useful for React, Vue, Angular, and AJAX forms. --- # 12. `stopPropagation()` Suppose: ```javascript parent.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Parent"); }); child.addEventListener("click", function(event){ event.stopPropagation(); console.log("Child"); }); ``` Click child. Output: ```text Child ``` The event stops. It never reaches the parent. --- # Visual Without: ```text Child ↓ Parent ``` With `stopPropagation()`: ```text Child ↓ STOP ``` --- # 13. Event Delegation One of the most frequently asked frontend interview topics. Suppose you have: ```html
    1000 list items
``` Option 1: ```javascript items.forEach(item => { item.addEventListener(...); }); ``` 1000 listeners. Not ideal. Instead: Attach one listener to the parent. ```javascript list.addEventListener("click", function(event){ console.log(event.target); }); ``` Because events bubble. --- # Visual Without Delegation ```text LI Listener LI Listener LI Listener ... ``` 1000 listeners. --- With Delegation ```text UL ↓ One Listener ↓ Detect Clicked LI ↓ Done ``` --- # Real Example ```html
  • Home
  • Products
  • Contact
``` ```javascript const menu = document.getElementById("menu"); menu.addEventListener("click", function(event){ if(event.target.tagName === "LI"){ console.log(event.target.textContent); } }); ``` One listener handles every current and future `
  • `. --- # Why Event Delegation? Advantages: - Less memory usage. - Better performance. - Handles dynamically added elements automatically. - Cleaner code. --- # React Connection React doesn't attach an `onClick` listener to every DOM node. Instead (historically, and still conceptually), React uses **event delegation** internally. It listens at a higher level and dispatches events to components. React also wraps native events in a **SyntheticEvent** object (though React 17+ changed where delegation is attached). Interviewers may ask this to see if you understand the underlying browser model. --- # Common Mistakes ## Mistake 1 Using: ```javascript event.target ``` when you actually meant: ```javascript event.currentTarget ``` Know the difference. --- ## Mistake 2 Calling: ```javascript stopPropagation() ``` without understanding its impact. It can break parent components relying on bubbling. --- ## Mistake 3 Adding listeners to hundreds of elements instead of using delegation. --- # Under the Hood When a user clicks: ```text Mouse Click ↓ Browser Detects Click ↓ Creates Event Object ↓ Capturing Phase ↓ Target Phase ↓ Bubbling Phase ↓ Remove Event Object ``` The browser handles this entire lifecycle automatically. --- # Interview Perspective Common questions: ### What is event bubbling? > The process where an event propagates upward from the target element through its ancestors. --- ### What is event capturing? > The phase where the event travels from the document down to the target before reaching it. --- ### Difference between `target` and `currentTarget`? > `target` is the element that initiated the event. `currentTarget` is the element whose event listener is currently executing. --- ### Why use event delegation? > To reduce the number of event listeners, improve performance, and automatically handle dynamically added elements. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Attach a click listener to a button that changes its text. --- ## Medium Build a `
      ` where clicking any `
    • ` logs its text using **one** event listener. --- ## Hard Implement a simple todo list: - Add tasks dynamically. - Remove a task when its delete button is clicked. - Use **event delegation** for delete actions. --- # Time Complexity | Operation | Complexity | |-----------|------------| | Adding one event listener | O(1) | | Adding listeners to `n` elements | O(n) | | Event delegation | O(1) listener setup, event handling depends on the logic | --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. What is an event? 2. What is an event listener? 3. Name the three phases of event propagation. 4. What is event bubbling? 5. What is event capturing? 6. What is the difference between `event.target` and `event.currentTarget`? 7. What does `preventDefault()` do? 8. What does `stopPropagation()` do? 9. Why is event delegation useful? 10. How does event delegation help with dynamically added elements? --- ## Coding 11. Add a click listener to a button that changes its background color. 12. Prevent a form from reloading the page when submitted. 13. Create a list where clicking any item logs its text using one parent listener. 14. Build a navigation menu that highlights the clicked item using event delegation. 15. Add and remove tasks from a todo list while keeping only one listener on the list container. --- ## Debugging 16. Why is the parent's click handler firing when you click the child? 17. Why does `event.target` return a `` instead of the ` ``` And the JavaScript: ```javascript document .getElementById("container") .addEventListener("click", function (event) { console.log("target:", event.target.tagName); console.log("currentTarget:", event.currentTarget.tagName); }); ``` If the user clicks directly on the **``**: 1. What is printed for `event.target.tagName`? 2. What is printed for `event.currentTarget.tagName`? 3. Explain the full event propagation path. 4. Would `stopPropagation()` inside the button's click handler prevent the container's listener from running? Why? --- ## Coming Next Reply **Next** for **Lesson 6.3 — Web Storage (`localStorage`, `sessionStorage`)**, where you'll learn: - The differences between `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and cookies. - Storage limits. - Persisting user preferences. - JSON serialization (`JSON.stringify` / `JSON.parse`). - Common interview questions about client-side storage. - Security considerations and best practices.

questions.questionText: What phase of event propagation occurs first?
questions.explanation: Event propagation goes: Capturing (outermost to target), Target, then Bubbling (target back to outermost).

questions.questionText: Which event methods stop default behavior or halt event propagation? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: `preventDefault()` stops browser default. `stopPropagation()` stops bubble/capture. `stopImmediatePropagation()` stops both and halts other listeners on same node.

questions.questionText: What method registers an event handler on a DOM element?
questions.explanation: `addEventListener()` binds callback handlers for specific events on target elements.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.3
lessons.objective: Master client-side persistence APIs: localStorage vs sessionStorage operations.
lessons.content:
# Module 6 — Browser APIs

# Lesson 6.3 — Web Storage (`localStorage`, `sessionStorage`)

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Intermediate)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Very High)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

One of the most common interview misconceptions is:

> **"`localStorage` is a database."**

❌ **False.**

Another misconception:

> **"`localStorage` is secure because users can't see it."**

❌ **Also false.**

Everything stored in Web Storage is **accessible to JavaScript running on the page**, which means you should **never store sensitive information** such as passwords or long-lived authentication tokens there.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what Web Storage is.
- Differentiate `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`.
- Store, retrieve, update, and remove data.
- Store objects and arrays using JSON.
- Understand storage limits.
- Understand common interview questions.
- Know security best practices.

---

# 1. What is Web Storage?

Web Storage is a browser feature that lets websites save **small amounts of data** in the user's browser.

Think of it as a simple **key-value store**.

Example:

```text
Key           Value

theme         dark

language      en

username      John
```

---

# Why Was It Introduced?

Before Web Storage, developers mainly used cookies to store client-side data.

Cookies have limitations:

- Small storage size.
- Sent with every HTTP request.
- Primarily intended for server communication.

Web Storage was introduced to store client-side data **without sending it to the server on every request**.

---

# Visual Model

```text
Browser

│

├── Cookies

├── localStorage

└── sessionStorage
```

---

# 2. `localStorage`

`localStorage` stores data that **persists** even after:

- Closing the browser.
- Restarting the computer.
- Reopening the website.

The data remains until it is explicitly removed or the user clears site data.

---

## Example

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
```

Now:

```text
theme

↓

dark
```

Close the browser.

Reopen it.

The value is still there.

---

# 3. `sessionStorage`

`sessionStorage` stores data **only for the current browser tab/session**.

When that tab or window is closed:

```text
Data

↓

Deleted
```

---

Example:

```javascript
sessionStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
```

Close the tab.

Reopen the site.

The data is gone.

---

# Comparison

| Feature | `localStorage` | `sessionStorage` |
|----------|----------------|------------------|
| Survives page reload | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| Survives closing browser/tab | ✅ Yes (until cleared) | ❌ No |
| Shared across tabs of the same origin | ✅ Generally yes | ❌ No (each tab has its own session) |
| Sent to server automatically | ❌ No | ❌ No |

---

# Visual Timeline

## `localStorage`

```text
Open Website

↓

Save Data

↓

Close Browser

↓

Open Tomorrow

↓

Data Still Exists
```

---

## `sessionStorage`

```text
Open Website

↓

Save Data

↓

Close Tab

↓

Open Again

↓

Data Gone
```

---

# 4. Storing Data

Use:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem(key, value);
```

Example:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("username", "Alice");
```

---

### Syntax Breakdown

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("username", "Alice");
```

Breakdown:

```text
localStorage

↓

Browser Storage Object

----------------------

.

↓

Access Method

----------------------

setItem

↓

Store Data

----------------------

(

Start Arguments

----------------------

"username"

↓

Key

----------------------

"Alice"

↓

Value

----------------------

)

End Arguments
```

---

# 5. Retrieving Data

```javascript
const name = localStorage.getItem("username");

console.log(name);
```

Output:

```text
Alice
```

If the key doesn't exist:

```javascript
console.log(localStorage.getItem("age"));
```

Output:

```text
null
```

---

# 6. Updating Data

Calling `setItem()` again with the same key overwrites the old value.

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("theme", "light");
```

Then:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
```

Result:

```text
theme

↓

dark
```

---

# 7. Removing Data

Remove one item:

```javascript
localStorage.removeItem("theme");
```

Remove everything for that origin:

```javascript
localStorage.clear();
```

Be careful with `clear()` because it deletes **all** keys stored by your site.

---

# 8. Storing Objects

This is where beginners often make mistakes.

Suppose:

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "Alice",
    age: 25
};
```

Doing this:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("user", user);
```

Results in:

```text
[object Object]
```

Why?

Because Web Storage stores **strings only**.

---

# Correct Approach

Convert the object to JSON.

```javascript
localStorage.setItem(
    "user",
    JSON.stringify(user)
);
```

Now the stored value is:

```json
{"name":"Alice","age":25}
```

---

# Reading It Back

```javascript
const stored =
    localStorage.getItem("user");
```

Currently:

```text
{"name":"Alice","age":25}
```

Still a string.

Convert it back:

```javascript
const user =
    JSON.parse(stored);

console.log(user.name);
```

Output:

```text
Alice
```

---

# Visual Flow

```text
JavaScript Object

↓

JSON.stringify()

↓

String

↓

localStorage

↓

getItem()

↓

String

↓

JSON.parse()

↓

Object
```

---

# Arrays

Same idea.

```javascript
const skills = [
    "JavaScript",
    "React",
    "TypeScript"
];

localStorage.setItem(
    "skills",
    JSON.stringify(skills)
);
```

Retrieve:

```javascript
const skills =
    JSON.parse(
        localStorage.getItem("skills")
    );
```

---

# 9. Storage Limits

Storage is **not unlimited**.

Typical browser limits are around **5–10 MB per origin**, though the exact amount depends on the browser and platform.

Web Storage is designed for **small amounts of data** such as:

- User preferences.
- UI settings.
- Draft text.
- Recently viewed items.

It is **not** suitable for:

- Videos.
- Images.
- Large databases.
- Large file uploads.

---

# 10. Real-World Examples

## Dark Mode

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
```

On page load:

```javascript
const theme =
    localStorage.getItem("theme");

if (theme === "dark") {
    document.body.classList.add("dark");
}
```

The user's preference persists between visits.

---

## Shopping Cart

Store cart items:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem(
    "cart",
    JSON.stringify(cart)
);
```

When the user comes back tomorrow:

```text
Cart Restored
```

---

## Form Draft

Imagine typing a long message.

Every few seconds:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem(
    "draft",
    textarea.value
);
```

If the page accidentally reloads:

```text
Draft Restored
```

---

# 11. Security Considerations

Many beginners store JWTs or sensitive data in `localStorage` without understanding the risks.

Important points:

- Any JavaScript running on your page can read Web Storage.
- If your site has an **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** vulnerability, an attacker may be able to access stored data.

Never store:

- Passwords.
- Credit card numbers.
- Sensitive personal information.

Authentication tokens require careful design. Many applications prefer secure, `HttpOnly` cookies for session management because JavaScript cannot read them.

---

# 12. Cookies vs Web Storage

| Feature | Cookies | Web Storage |
|----------|----------|-------------|
| Sent with HTTP requests | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Accessible from JavaScript | Usually yes (unless `HttpOnly`) | ✅ Yes |
| Typical storage size | ~4 KB | ~5–10 MB |
| Primary purpose | Server/client session management | Client-side persistence |

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Storing objects directly.

Bad:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("user", user);
```

Good:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem(
    "user",
    JSON.stringify(user)
);
```

---

## Mistake 2

Forgetting `JSON.parse()`.

Bad:

```javascript
const user =
    localStorage.getItem("user");

console.log(user.name);
```

`user` is a string, so `user.name` is `undefined`.

---

## Mistake 3

Using `localStorage` for secrets.

Never assume client-side storage is private.

---

# Under the Hood

When you call:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
```

Conceptually:

```text
JavaScript

↓

Browser Storage Engine

↓

Write Key

↓

Persist on Disk

↓

Available Next Visit
```

---

# Interview Perspective

Common questions:

### What is the difference between `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`?

> `localStorage` persists until removed. `sessionStorage` lasts only for the lifetime of the current browser tab or window.

---

### Can `localStorage` store objects?

> Not directly. It stores strings, so objects must be serialized with `JSON.stringify()` and parsed back with `JSON.parse()`.

---

### Why shouldn't you store passwords in `localStorage`?

> Because any JavaScript running on the page can read it, making it vulnerable if the application suffers from XSS.

---

### Is `localStorage` sent to the server?

> No. Unlike cookies, Web Storage data is not automatically included in HTTP requests.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Save the user's preferred language in `localStorage`.

---

## Medium

Store an array of todo items and display them after refreshing the page.

---

## Hard

Implement a shopping cart that:

- Saves items to `localStorage`.
- Restores them when the page reloads.
- Removes items when the user clicks "Delete".
- Keeps the UI synchronized with storage.

---

# Time Complexity

Browser implementations vary, but for practical purposes:

| Operation | Complexity |
|-----------|------------|
| `setItem()` | O(1) average |
| `getItem()` | O(1) average |
| `removeItem()` | O(1) average |
| `clear()` | O(n), where `n` is the number of stored keys |

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is Web Storage?
2. What is the difference between `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`?
3. Does `localStorage` survive a browser restart?
4. Why are values stored as strings?
5. Why do we use `JSON.stringify()`?
6. Why do we use `JSON.parse()`?
7. Is `localStorage` automatically sent to the server?
8. Why shouldn't you store sensitive data in Web Storage?
9. When would `sessionStorage` be a better choice than `localStorage`?
10. What happens if you call `getItem()` for a missing key?

---

## Coding

11. Save a user's name in `localStorage` and display it on page load.
12. Save an object representing a logged-in user.
13. Save and restore a list of favorite books.
14. Build a "Remember Me" toggle using `localStorage`.
15. Build a page that remembers whether dark mode is enabled.

---

## Debugging

16. Why does this store `[object Object]`?

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("user", {
  name: "Alice"
});
```

17. Why does this fail?

```javascript
const user = localStorage.getItem("user");

console.log(user.name);
```

18. Explain why clearing browser site data removes values stored in `localStorage`.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Web Storage
│
├── localStorage
│   ├── Persistent
│   ├── Shared Across Tabs (same origin)
│   └── Manual Removal
│
└── sessionStorage
    ├── Current Tab Only
    ├── Cleared When Tab Closes
    └── Not Shared Across Tabs

-------------------------

Store Object

Object
│
▼
JSON.stringify()
│
▼
String
│
▼
localStorage

-------------------------

Retrieve Object

localStorage
│
▼
String
│
▼
JSON.parse()
│
▼
Object

-------------------------

Security

Never Store

❌ Passwords

❌ Sensitive Secrets

-------------------------

Best Uses

✔ Theme

✔ Language

✔ Cart

✔ Draft

✔ Preferences
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain the purpose of Web Storage.
- ✅ Distinguish `localStorage` from `sessionStorage`.
- ✅ Store and retrieve primitive values.
- ✅ Correctly serialize and deserialize objects using JSON.
- ✅ Explain why Web Storage only stores strings.
- ✅ Describe when Web Storage is appropriate and when it is not.
- ✅ Explain the security implications of storing data on the client.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Build a simple **Theme Preference Manager**.

Requirements:

1. Create a button labeled **"Toggle Theme"**.
2. Clicking it should switch between `"light"` and `"dark"` themes.
3. Save the current theme in `localStorage`.
4. When the page reloads, restore the saved theme automatically.
5. Explain:
   - Why `localStorage` is a better choice than `sessionStorage` for this feature.
   - What would happen if the user cleared site data.
   - Whether the theme preference is sent to the server automatically.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 6.4 — Fetch API**, where you'll learn:

- How `fetch()` works under the hood.
- Request and response objects.
- HTTP methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`).
- Headers and request bodies.
- Handling JSON responses.
- Error handling with `fetch()`.
- `AbortController` for request cancellation.
- Common frontend interview questions and live coding exercises involving APIs.

questions.questionText: What is the key difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
options: sessionStorage data is cleared when the tab/session ends; localStorage persists
localStorage can store objects directly without serialization
sessionStorage is stored on the server side
questions.explanation: `sessionStorage` survives page reloads but is destroyed when tab/browser is closed. `localStorage` persists indefinitely.

questions.questionText: Which are valid Web Storage API methods? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: All four methods are standard parts of the Storage interface.

questions.questionText: What built-in JSON method must you call to convert objects into strings before saving them to localStorage?
questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify(obj)` is used to serialize objects because Web Storage only stores strings.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.4
lessons.objective: Master the Fetch API for network requests, response status validation, and error handles.
lessons.content:
# Module 6 — Browser APIs

# Lesson 6.4 — Fetch API

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the Most Frequently Asked Frontend Topics)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

Many developers think:

> **"`fetch()` gets data from the server."**

This is only partially true.

`fetch()` does **not** return the data.

It returns a **Promise** that eventually resolves to a **Response object**.

Understanding this distinction is one of the most common interview topics.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what the Fetch API is.
- Understand the request-response lifecycle.
- Use `fetch()` with different HTTP methods.
- Send headers and request bodies.
- Parse JSON responses.
- Handle errors correctly.
- Cancel requests with `AbortController`.
- Explain common interview questions.

---

# 1. What is the Fetch API?

The **Fetch API** is a browser API for making **HTTP requests**.

It allows JavaScript to communicate with servers without reloading the page.

Examples:

- Login
- Load products
- Search users
- Submit forms
- Upload files
- Delete records

---

# Real-World Example

Suppose you're building an e-commerce website.

When the user opens the products page:

```text
User Opens Products

↓

Browser Requests Products

↓

Server Returns JSON

↓

JavaScript Updates DOM

↓

Products Appear
```

The page never reloads.

---

# 2. The Request–Response Lifecycle

Whenever `fetch()` is called:

```javascript
fetch("/users");
```

The following happens:

```text
JavaScript

↓

Create Request

↓

Browser Networking Layer

↓

Internet

↓

Server

↓

Server Processes Request

↓

Server Sends Response

↓

Browser Receives Response

↓

Promise Resolves

↓

JavaScript Continues
```

---

# 3. Basic Syntax

```javascript
fetch(url);
```

Example:

```javascript
fetch("/users");
```

This returns:

```javascript
Promise<Response>
```

Not:

```javascript
Array

Object

JSON
```

---

# Syntax Breakdown

```javascript
fetch("/users");
```

Breakdown:

```text
fetch

↓

Browser Function

----------------

(

Start Argument

----------------

"/users"

↓

URL

----------------

)

Call Function
```

---

# 4. Using `await`

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/users");
```

Question:

What is inside `response`?

Not:

```text
Users
```

Instead:

```text
Response Object
```

---

# Response Object

The Response object contains information such as:

```text
status

statusText

headers

ok

body

json()

text()

blob()
```

Think of it as an envelope.

```text
Envelope

↓

Status

↓

Headers

↓

Body
```

You still need to open the envelope.

---

# 5. Reading JSON

Suppose the server returns:

```json
[
    {
        "id": 1,
        "name": "John"
    }
]
```

Your code:

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/users");

const data = await response.json();

console.log(data);
```

Output:

```javascript
[
    {
        id: 1,
        name: "John"
    }
]
```

Notice:

There are **two awaits**.

```javascript
await fetch()

↓

Response

↓

await response.json()

↓

JavaScript Object
```

---

# Why Two Awaits?

Interview favorite.

Step 1:

```javascript
await fetch()
```

Waits for the HTTP response.

Step 2:

```javascript
await response.json()
```

Reads the response body and parses the JSON.

The body is consumed asynchronously because it may still be streaming from the network.

---

# Visual

```text
fetch()

↓

Response

↓

json()

↓

JavaScript Object
```

---

# 6. Checking for Errors

Many developers write:

```javascript
const response =
    await fetch("/users");

const data =
    await response.json();
```

Looks fine.

But what if:

```text
404

500

401
```

The Promise **usually still resolves**.

Why?

Because the network request succeeded.

The server simply responded with an error status.

---

# Correct Way

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/users");

if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error("Request failed");
}

const data = await response.json();
```

`response.ok` is:

```text
true

↓

200–299

false

↓

Everything Else
```

---

# 7. Handling Errors

Use `try...catch`.

```javascript
try {

    const response =
        await fetch("/users");

    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error("Failed");
    }

    const users =
        await response.json();

    console.log(users);

} catch(error) {

    console.error(error);

}
```

This catches:

- Network failures.
- Errors you throw yourself.
- JSON parsing errors.

---

# 8. HTTP Methods

By default:

```javascript
fetch("/users");
```

is:

```text
GET
```

---

## GET

Retrieve data.

```javascript
fetch("/products");
```

---

## POST

Create data.

```javascript
fetch("/users", {

    method: "POST"

});
```

---

## PUT

Replace an entire resource.

```javascript
method: "PUT"
```

Example:

```text
Old User

↓

Replace Everything

↓

New User
```

---

## PATCH

Update part of a resource.

Example:

```text
Change Name Only
```

---

## DELETE

Delete a resource.

```javascript
method: "DELETE"
```

---

# HTTP Method Comparison

| Method | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| GET | Read data |
| POST | Create |
| PUT | Replace |
| PATCH | Partial update |
| DELETE | Remove |

---

# 9. Sending JSON

Suppose:

```javascript
const user = {

    name: "Alice"

};
```

Request:

```javascript
await fetch("/users", {

    method: "POST",

    headers: {

        "Content-Type":
            "application/json"

    },

    body: JSON.stringify(user)

});
```

---

# Why `JSON.stringify()`?

The request body must be sent as text.

Objects must be converted into JSON strings.

---

# 10. Headers

Headers provide metadata about the request or response.

Example:

```javascript
headers: {

    "Content-Type":
        "application/json"

}
```

This tells the server:

```text
"I'm sending JSON."
```

Other common headers:

```text
Authorization

Accept

Content-Type

Cache-Control
```

---

# 11. AbortController

Suppose a user searches:

```text
a

ab

abc

abcd
```

You don't want all four requests to finish.

Cancel the older ones.

```javascript
const controller =
    new AbortController();

fetch("/users", {

    signal:
        controller.signal

});
```

Later:

```javascript
controller.abort();
```

The request is canceled.

---

# Visual

```text
Request Started

↓

User Navigates Away

↓

AbortController

↓

Request Cancelled
```

This is especially useful in search boxes, autocomplete, and React components that unmount before a request completes.

---

# 12. Real-World Example

Login.

```javascript
const response =
    await fetch("/login", {

        method: "POST",

        headers: {

            "Content-Type":
                "application/json"

        },

        body:
            JSON.stringify(credentials)

    });
```

Server:

```text
Checks Password

↓

Returns Token

↓

Frontend Stores Session

↓

Navigate Dashboard
```

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Forgetting:

```javascript
await response.json();
```

Instead:

```javascript
console.log(response);
```

This logs the Response object, not the parsed data.

---

## Mistake 2

Assuming `fetch()` rejects on `404`.

It usually does **not**.

You must check:

```javascript
response.ok
```

---

## Mistake 3

Sending objects directly.

Bad:

```javascript
body: user
```

Good:

```javascript
body:
JSON.stringify(user)
```

---

## Mistake 4

Missing the `Content-Type` header.

Many APIs expect:

```text
application/json
```

Without it, the server may not parse your request correctly.

---

# Under the Hood

When you write:

```javascript
await fetch("/users");
```

Conceptually:

```text
JavaScript

↓

Create Request

↓

Browser Network Layer

↓

TCP / HTTPS Connection

↓

Server

↓

HTTP Response

↓

Response Object

↓

json()

↓

JavaScript Object
```

---

# Interview Perspective

Common questions:

### Does `fetch()` return JSON?

> No. It returns a Promise that resolves to a `Response` object.

---

### Why do we call `response.json()`?

> Because the response body is separate from the Response metadata. `json()` reads the body and parses it into a JavaScript value.

---

### Does `fetch()` reject on HTTP 404?

> Usually no. It resolves with a Response whose `ok` property is `false`.

---

### Why use `AbortController`?

> To cancel unnecessary requests, improve performance, avoid race conditions, and prevent updates from requests that are no longer relevant.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Fetch a list of users and print their names.

---

## Medium

Create a form that sends a POST request with JSON data and handles success and failure.

---

## Hard

Build a search input that:

- Sends a request on each keystroke.
- Cancels the previous request using `AbortController`.
- Displays only the latest results.

---

# Time Complexity

The `fetch()` call itself is O(1) from the JavaScript perspective. The actual response time depends on network latency and server processing.

JSON parsing with `response.json()` is generally O(n), where `n` is the size of the response body.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What does `fetch()` return?
2. Why are there often two `await`s when using `fetch()`?
3. What is the purpose of the `Response` object?
4. What does `response.ok` indicate?
5. Does `fetch()` reject on a 404 response?
6. What is the difference between `PUT` and `PATCH`?
7. Why do we use `JSON.stringify()` for request bodies?
8. Why is the `Content-Type` header important?
9. What is `AbortController` used for?
10. When would request cancellation improve the user experience?

---

## Coding

11. Fetch a list of products and render them in the DOM.
12. Submit a new user using a `POST` request.
13. Update a user's email using `PATCH`.
14. Delete a todo item using `DELETE`.
15. Implement a search box that cancels previous requests as the user types.

---

## Debugging

16. Why does this code log a `Response` object instead of user data?

```javascript
const users = await fetch("/users");
console.log(users);
```

17. Explain why this request fails on many APIs:

```javascript
fetch("/users", {
  method: "POST",
  body: { name: "Alice" }
});
```

18. Explain why the following code enters the `if` block when the server returns a 500 response:

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/users");

if (!response.ok) {
  console.log("Error");
}
```

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
fetch()
│
▼
Promise<Response>
│
▼
await
│
▼
Response
│
├── status
├── headers
├── ok
└── body
     │
     ▼
response.json()
│
▼
JavaScript Object

-------------------------

HTTP Methods

GET    → Read

POST   → Create

PUT    → Replace

PATCH  → Partial Update

DELETE → Remove

-------------------------

Error Handling

fetch()

↓

Response

↓

Check response.ok

↓

Throw if Needed

↓

try...catch

-------------------------

AbortController

Start Request

↓

User No Longer Needs It

↓

abort()

↓

Request Cancelled
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain the complete request-response lifecycle.
- ✅ Describe what `fetch()` returns.
- ✅ Parse JSON responses correctly.
- ✅ Handle HTTP errors using `response.ok`.
- ✅ Use different HTTP methods appropriately.
- ✅ Send JSON request bodies with the correct headers.
- ✅ Explain when and why to use `AbortController`.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Implement a **User Management API Client**.

Requirements:

1. Fetch and display a list of users.
2. Add a new user with a `POST` request.
3. Update a user's email with a `PATCH` request.
4. Delete a user with a `DELETE` request.
5. Handle loading and error states.
6. Cancel an in-progress fetch if the user navigates away or starts a new search.

Then explain:

- Why `fetch()` requires `response.json()`.
- Why checking `response.ok` is necessary.
- How `AbortController` prevents outdated responses from affecting the UI.

---

# 🎉 Module 6 Complete!

You have now covered the core Browser APIs that every frontend engineer should know:

- ✅ DOM
- ✅ Event handling and propagation
- ✅ Event delegation
- ✅ Web Storage
- ✅ Fetch API

These topics appear regularly in frontend interviews because they demonstrate your understanding of how JavaScript interacts with the browser.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** to begin **Module 7 — Advanced JavaScript**, starting with:

**Lesson 7.1 — `this` Keyword**

We'll cover:

- What `this` really is.
- How `this` is determined at runtime.
- Default, implicit, explicit, and constructor binding.
- `this` in arrow functions vs regular functions.
- Common interview traps and live coding questions involving `this`.

questions.questionText: How does `fetch()` handle HTTP error statuses like 404 or 500?
options: It resolves the promise normally with response.ok set to false.
questions.explanation: `fetch()` only rejects on network failures. HTTP errors resolve normally, and you must check `response.ok` or `response.status`.

questions.questionText: Which scenarios cause the `fetch()` promise to reject? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Network errors and CORS blocks reject the promise. Server error statuses resolve successfully.

questions.questionText: What boolean property on the fetch Response object indicates a status code in the 200-299 range?
questions.explanation: `response.ok` is a boolean representing successful status code range.

lessons.title: Lesson 7.1
lessons.objective: Master this keyword binding rules: default, implicit, explicit, and new bindings.
lessons.content:
# Module 7 — Advanced JavaScript

# Lesson 7.1 — The `this` Keyword

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the Most Asked JavaScript Topics)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

This is one of the most misunderstood concepts in JavaScript.

Many developers think:

> **"`this` refers to the function."**

❌ Incorrect.

Others think:

> **"`this` refers to where the function was written."**

❌ Also incorrect.

The single most important rule to remember is:

> **`this` is determined by *how a function is called*, not where it is defined.**

There is **one major exception** to this rule:

> **Arrow functions do not have their own `this`.** They inherit (`lexically capture`) `this` from the surrounding scope.

If you truly understand this lesson, you'll solve about **90% of `this` interview questions**.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what `this` is.
- Explain how JavaScript determines `this`.
- Understand the four binding rules.
- Explain `this` in arrow functions.
- Explain `this` inside classes.
- Explain `this` in event listeners.
- Predict the output of tricky interview questions.

---

# 1. What is `this`?

`this` is a **special keyword**.

It refers to an object determined **when the function is called** (except for arrow functions, which inherit `this`).

Think of `this` as:

> "Who is calling me?"

---

# Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a phone.

Different people call you.

```text
Alice Calls

↓

Who called?

↓

Alice

----------------

Bob Calls

↓

Who called?

↓

Bob
```

You are the same person.

Only the caller changes.

Functions work similarly.

The function is the same.

The caller determines `this`.

---

# 2. `this` is NOT Fixed

Consider:

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this);
}
```

Nothing about this function tells us what `this` is.

Why?

Because JavaScript waits until the function is called.

---

# Visual

```text
Function Created

↓

No this Yet

↓

Function Called

↓

JavaScript Determines this

↓

Execute Function
```

---

# 3. The Four Binding Rules

JavaScript determines `this` using four primary rules (ignoring arrows for the moment):

1. Default Binding
2. Implicit Binding
3. Explicit Binding
4. Constructor (`new`) Binding

We'll learn them one at a time.

---

# Rule 1 — Default Binding

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this);
}

greet();
```

Question:

What is `this`?

Answer depends on **strict mode**.

---

## Non-Strict Mode

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this);
}

greet();
```

Output (in browsers):

```text
Window
```

Why?

Because there is no object before the function call.

```text
greet()

↓

No Owner

↓

Default Object

↓

Window (browser, non-strict mode)
```

---

## Strict Mode

```javascript
"use strict";

function greet() {
    console.log(this);
}

greet();
```

Output:

```text
undefined
```

Strict mode prevents the automatic fallback to the global object.

---

# Interview Tip

Modern JavaScript (ES modules and class bodies) runs in strict mode by default.

Many bundlers and frameworks also emit strict-mode code.

Don't assume you'll get `window`.

---

# Rule 2 — Implicit Binding

Suppose:

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John",

    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

user.greet();
```

Output:

```text
John
```

Why?

Because:

```text
user.greet()

↓

Object Before Dot

↓

user

↓

this = user
```

---

# Visual

```text
user

│

└── greet()

↓

this

↓

user
```

---

# Another Example

```javascript
const person = {
    age: 30,

    showAge() {
        console.log(this.age);
    }
};

person.showAge();
```

Output:

```text
30
```

---

# Interview Rule

When you see:

```javascript
object.method()
```

Ask:

> "What object is immediately before the dot?"

That object is usually the value of `this`.

---

# Rule 3 — Explicit Binding

Sometimes you choose `this` yourself.

JavaScript provides:

```javascript
call()

apply()

bind()
```

We'll cover these deeply in the next lessons.

Example:

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this.name);
}

const user = {
    name: "Alice"
};

greet.call(user);
```

Output:

```text
Alice
```

You explicitly told JavaScript:

```text
Use user as this.
```

---

# Rule 4 — Constructor Binding

Suppose:

```javascript
function User(name) {
    this.name = name;
}

const john = new User("John");
```

Question:

What is `this`?

When you use `new`:

JavaScript creates a new object.

```text
{}

↓

this

↓

{}

↓

Add Properties

↓

Return Object
```

After execution:

```javascript
john
```

becomes:

```javascript
{
    name: "John"
}
```

---

# Under the Hood of `new`

```javascript
const john = new User("John");
```

Conceptually, JavaScript does something like:

```javascript
const obj = {};

Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, User.prototype);

User.call(obj, "John");

return obj;
```

This is a simplified mental model, but it's useful for interviews.

---

# 4. Arrow Functions

This is the biggest interview topic involving `this`.

Arrow functions **do not have their own `this`.**

Instead:

They inherit `this` from the surrounding scope.

---

Example:

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "Alice",

    greet() {
        const arrow = () => {
            console.log(this.name);
        };

        arrow();
    }
};

user.greet();
```

Output:

```text
Alice
```

Why?

The arrow inherits:

```text
greet()

↓

this = user

↓

Arrow

↓

Uses Same this
```

---

# Compare with Regular Function

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "Alice",

    greet() {

        function test() {
            console.log(this.name);
        }

        test();
    }
};

user.greet();
```

In strict mode:

```text
TypeError (because this is undefined)
```

or in sloppy mode:

```text
undefined
```

because `this` is the global object, which typically has no `name` property.

The inner regular function has its **own** `this`.

---

# Visual Comparison

Regular Function

```text
Function

↓

Gets New this
```

Arrow Function

```text
Arrow

↓

Looks Up

↓

Uses Parent this
```

---

# 5. `this` in Event Listeners

Example:

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", function () {
    console.log(this);
});
```

Output:

```text
<button>
```

The browser calls the listener with `this` set to the element the listener is attached to.

Equivalent conceptually:

```javascript
listener.call(button, event);
```

---

Now use an arrow:

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log(this);
});
```

Now `this` comes from the surrounding scope, **not** the button.

This is a common interview trap.

---

# 6. `this` Inside Classes

```javascript
class User {

    constructor(name) {

        this.name = name;

    }

    greet() {

        console.log(this.name);

    }

}
```

```javascript
const john =
    new User("John");

john.greet();
```

Output:

```text
John
```

Why?

Because:

```text
john.greet()

↓

this = john
```

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Thinking:

```javascript
this
```

means:

```text
Current Function
```

Wrong.

---

## Mistake 2

Believing arrow functions behave exactly like regular functions.

They do not.

They don't create their own `this`.

---

## Mistake 3

Extracting methods without preserving `this`.

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "Alice",
    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

const sayHi = user.greet;

sayHi();
```

Output (strict mode):

```text
TypeError / undefined
```

Why?

The function is no longer called as `user.greet()`.

It's just `sayHi()`.

Default binding applies.

---

# Under the Hood

When JavaScript encounters:

```javascript
user.greet();
```

Conceptually:

```text
Locate Function

↓

Who Called It?

↓

user

↓

Set this = user

↓

Execute
```

For arrows:

```text
Arrow Function

↓

No this

↓

Look Outside

↓

Use Parent this
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What determines `this`?

> How a function is called (except arrow functions).

---

### Do arrow functions have `this`?

> No. They inherit `this` from their enclosing scope.

---

### What does `this` refer to in a method call?

> The object immediately before the dot.

---

### What does `this` refer to in a constructor?

> The newly created object.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Predict the output:

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "Jane",
    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

user.greet();
```

---

## Medium

Explain why this prints `undefined` (or throws in strict mode):

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "Jane",
    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

const fn = user.greet;

fn();
```

---

## Hard

Given:

```javascript
class Counter {
    count = 0;

    increment() {
        this.count++;
    }
}

const counter = new Counter();

setTimeout(counter.increment, 1000);
```

Why doesn't `count` increase?

How would you fix it?

(Hint: we'll cover `bind()` in the next lesson.)

---

# Time Complexity

`this` binding itself is determined during function invocation and is effectively **O(1)**.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is `this`?
2. Is `this` determined when the function is defined or called?
3. Name the four primary binding rules.
4. What is default binding?
5. What is implicit binding?
6. What is explicit binding?
7. What is constructor binding?
8. Do arrow functions have their own `this`?
9. Why does extracting a method often lose `this`?
10. Why does `new` change the value of `this`?

---

## Coding

11. Create an object with a method that logs its own properties using `this`.
12. Write a constructor function that stores a person's name.
13. Convert a regular callback inside a method to an arrow function so it retains `this`.
14. Create a class with two methods and verify that `this` refers to the instance.
15. Demonstrate the difference between calling a function directly and as an object method.

---

## Debugging

16. Why does this fail?

```javascript
const obj = {
  value: 10,
  show() {
    console.log(this.value);
  }
};

const fn = obj.show;
fn();
```

17. Explain why an arrow function used as an object method may not behave as expected:

```javascript
const obj = {
  value: 10,
  show: () => {
    console.log(this.value);
  }
};

obj.show();
```

18. Explain why using a regular function inside an event listener callback gives a different `this` than using an arrow function.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
this
│
▼
Determined at Call Time
(except arrows)

-------------------------

1. Default Binding

greet()

↓

undefined (strict mode)

or

window (non-strict browser)

-------------------------

2. Implicit Binding

user.greet()

↓

this = user

-------------------------

3. Explicit Binding

greet.call(user)

↓

this = user

-------------------------

4. Constructor Binding

new User()

↓

this = New Object

-------------------------

Arrow Function

↓

No Own this

↓

Uses Parent this
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain what `this` is.
- ✅ State that `this` is determined by the call site (except for arrow functions).
- ✅ Describe the four primary binding rules.
- ✅ Explain how arrow functions handle `this`.
- ✅ Predict `this` in object methods, constructors, and event listeners.
- ✅ Recognize common pitfalls when methods are detached from their objects.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Without running the code, predict the output and explain **why**:

```javascript
"use strict";

const user = {
  name: "Alice",

  greet() {
    console.log(this.name);

    function inner() {
      console.log(this);
    }

    const arrow = () => {
      console.log(this.name);
    };

    inner();
    arrow();
  }
};

user.greet();
```

Questions:

1. What does the first `console.log()` print?
2. What does `inner()` log?
3. What does `arrow()` log?
4. Why do `inner()` and `arrow()` behave differently?

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 7.2 — `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`**, where you'll learn:

- How explicit binding works.
- The differences between `call`, `apply`, and `bind`.
- Borrowing methods between objects.
- Fixing lost `this` in callbacks.
- Common interview questions and live coding exercises involving these three methods.

options: Dynamically based on how the function is invoked
Always points to the global object
Always points to undefined in strict mode

lessons.content:
# Module 7 — Advanced JavaScript

# Lesson 7.2 — `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely High)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

This lesson builds directly on **Lesson 7.1 (`this`)**.

If you remember only one thing from the previous lesson, remember this:

> **`this` is determined by how a function is called.**

Now we're going to learn how to **control** what `this` is.

Many interviewers will ask:

> **"What's the difference between `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`?"**

A lot of candidates answer:

> "They're all the same."

❌ They're related, but **not** the same.

The easiest way to remember them is:

| Method | Calls Function Immediately? | Returns a New Function? | How Are Arguments Passed? |
|---------|-----------------------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| `call()` | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | Individually |
| `apply()` | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | As an array (or array-like) |
| `bind()` | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | Individually (when binding), remaining arguments when called |

If you understand **why `bind()` exists**, you'll solve most interview questions involving callbacks.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain why `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()` exist.
- Borrow methods between objects.
- Fix lost `this`.
- Understand partial application using `bind()`.
- Explain common interview questions.

---

# 1. Why Do We Need `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`?

Let's revisit a problem from the last lesson.

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "Alice",

    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

const sayHi = user.greet;

sayHi();
```

Output (strict mode):

```text
TypeError / undefined
```

Why?

Because:

```text
user.greet()

↓

Works

------------------

sayHi()

↓

No Owner

↓

Default Binding
```

We've lost the object.

What if we could tell JavaScript:

> "Pretend this function belongs to another object."

That's exactly what these methods let us do.

---

# 2. Understanding Function Objects

Functions in JavaScript are **objects**.

That means they have methods.

Example:

```javascript
function greet() {}

console.log(typeof greet);
```

Output:

```text
function
```

But internally, functions are also objects, so they have methods like:

```javascript
greet.call()

greet.apply()

greet.bind()
```

---

# Visual

```text
Function

│

├── call()

├── apply()

└── bind()
```

---

# 3. `call()`

`call()` invokes a function immediately and lets you specify what `this` should be.

---

## Syntax

```javascript
function.call(thisArg, arg1, arg2, arg3);
```

---

# Example

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this.name);
}

const user = {
    name: "Alice"
};

greet.call(user);
```

Output:

```text
Alice
```

---

# Under the Hood

Conceptually:

```text
greet.call(user)

↓

Use user as this

↓

Execute greet()
```

Equivalent mental model:

```javascript
this = user;

greet();
```

(Not actual JavaScript code, just a conceptual model.)

---

# Passing Arguments

```javascript
function introduce(age, city) {

    console.log(
        this.name,
        age,
        city
    );

}

const user = {
    name: "Alice"
};

introduce.call(
    user,
    25,
    "London"
);
```

Output:

```text
Alice 25 London
```

Arguments are passed one by one.

---

# Syntax Breakdown

```javascript
introduce.call(user, 25, "London");
```

```text
introduce

↓

Function

-------------------

.

↓

Access Method

-------------------

call

↓

Immediately Invoke

-------------------

user

↓

this

-------------------

25

↓

Argument 1

-------------------

"London"

↓

Argument 2
```

---

# 4. `apply()`

`apply()` is almost identical to `call()`.

The only difference is **how arguments are supplied**.

---

## Syntax

```javascript
function.apply(thisArg, [args]);
```

---

Example:

```javascript
introduce.apply(
    user,
    [25, "London"]
);
```

Output:

```text
Alice 25 London
```

Notice:

`call`

```javascript
call(user, 25, "London");
```

`apply`

```javascript
apply(user, [25, "London"]);
```

---

# Visual Comparison

```text
call()

↓

Arguments Individually

---------------------

apply()

↓

Arguments Inside Array
```

---

# Why Did `apply()` Exist?

Before the spread operator (`...`) became common, `apply()` was the easiest way to pass an array of arguments.

Example:

```javascript
Math.max.apply(null, [2, 8, 5]);
```

Today, you'd usually write:

```javascript
Math.max(...[2, 8, 5]);
```

`apply()` still appears in interviews and legacy code, so it's worth knowing.

---

# 5. `bind()`

This is the most important one.

Unlike `call()` and `apply()`:

**`bind()` does NOT execute the function.**

Instead:

It returns a **new function**.

---

Example:

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this.name);
}

const user = {
    name: "Alice"
};

const bound =
    greet.bind(user);

bound();
```

Output:

```text
Alice
```

Notice:

```text
bind()

↓

New Function

↓

Later...

↓

Execute
```

---

# Visual

```text
Original Function

↓

bind(user)

↓

New Function

↓

Call Later
```

---

# Why Does `bind()` Exist?

Remember this problem:

```javascript
const sayHi =
    user.greet;

sayHi();
```

Lost `this`.

Solution:

```javascript
const sayHi =
    user.greet.bind(user);

sayHi();
```

Now `this` is permanently bound to `user`.

---

# Real-World Example

```javascript
class Counter {

    constructor() {

        this.count = 0;

    }

    increment() {

        this.count++;

        console.log(this.count);

    }

}

const counter =
    new Counter();

setTimeout(
    counter.increment,
    1000
);
```

Output:

```text
TypeError / undefined
```

Because `setTimeout` calls the function without the original object.

Fix:

```javascript
setTimeout(
    counter.increment.bind(counter),
    1000
);
```

Now:

```text
1
```

---

# 6. Method Borrowing

Suppose:

```javascript
const person1 = {
    name: "John"
};

const person2 = {
    name: "Alice"
};

function greet() {
    console.log(
        `Hello ${this.name}`
    );
}
```

Instead of duplicating `greet`:

```javascript
greet.call(person1);

greet.call(person2);
```

Output:

```text
Hello John

Hello Alice
```

The same function is reused with different objects.

---

# 7. Partial Application with `bind()`

`bind()` can also preset arguments.

```javascript
function multiply(a, b) {
    return a * b;
}

const double =
    multiply.bind(null, 2);

console.log(double(5));
```

Output:

```text
10
```

What happened?

```text
multiply(2, 5)
```

The first argument was fixed at bind time.

This is called **partial application**.

---

# Visual

```text
multiply(a, b)

↓

bind(null, 2)

↓

double(b)

↓

multiply(2, b)
```

---

# 8. `call()` vs `apply()` vs `bind()`

| Feature | `call()` | `apply()` | `bind()` |
|----------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| Executes immediately | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Returns a function | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Accepts array of arguments | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ (but can preset individual arguments) |
| Sets `this` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Expecting `bind()` to execute immediately.

```javascript
const fn = greet.bind(user);
```

Nothing happens until:

```javascript
fn();
```

---

## Mistake 2

Using `apply()` when you mean `call()`.

If you already have separate arguments:

```javascript
greet.call(user, a, b);
```

is clearer.

---

## Mistake 3

Forgetting that arrow functions ignore `bind()`, `call()`, and `apply()` for changing `this`.

Example:

```javascript
const obj = {
  value: 1
};

const arrow = () => {
  console.log(this);
};

arrow.call(obj);
```

`this` **does not become `obj`** because arrow functions don't have their own `this`.

---

# Under the Hood

When you write:

```javascript
greet.call(user);
```

Conceptually:

```text
Set this = user

↓

Execute greet

↓

Done
```

When you write:

```javascript
greet.bind(user);
```

Conceptually:

```text
Create Wrapper Function

↓

Store user

↓

Return Wrapper

↓

Later...

↓

Wrapper Executes greet with this = user
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What's the difference between `call()` and `apply()`?

> Both invoke the function immediately and set `this`. The difference is that `call()` accepts arguments individually, while `apply()` accepts them as an array (or array-like object).

---

### What's the difference between `call()` and `bind()`?

> `call()` invokes immediately. `bind()` returns a new function that can be called later with `this` already fixed.

---

### When should you use `bind()`?

> When passing methods as callbacks (e.g., to `setTimeout`, event handlers, or other APIs) and you need to preserve `this`.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Use `call()` to invoke a function with a different object.

---

## Medium

Borrow a method from one object and use it with another using `call()`.

---

## Hard

Fix the following code so that `count` increments correctly:

```javascript
class Counter {
  constructor() {
    this.count = 0;
  }

  increment() {
    this.count++;
    console.log(this.count);
  }

  start() {
    setInterval(this.increment, 1000);
  }
}
```

Can you solve it using:

1. `bind()`?
2. An arrow function?

---

# Time Complexity

All three methods perform constant-time binding operations from the JavaScript perspective:

| Method | Complexity |
|----------|------------|
| `call()` | O(1) |
| `apply()` | O(1) (excluding any cost to create the arguments array) |
| `bind()` | O(1) to create the bound function |

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. Why do `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()` exist?
2. Which method returns a new function?
3. Which methods execute immediately?
4. How does `apply()` receive arguments?
5. Why is `bind()` useful with callbacks?
6. Can `bind()` preset arguments?
7. Does `bind()` change the original function?
8. Why doesn't `bind()` change `this` for arrow functions?
9. What is method borrowing?
10. Which modern JavaScript feature often replaces `apply()` for spreading arrays?

---

## Coding

11. Borrow a method from one object and use it on another.
12. Use `apply()` to find the largest number in an array (then rewrite it using the spread operator).
13. Create a `triple` function using `bind()` and partial application.
14. Fix a lost `this` problem with `setTimeout()`.
15. Rewrite the same solution using an arrow function instead of `bind()`.

---

## Debugging

16. Why does this log `undefined`?

```javascript
const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  greet() {
    console.log(this.name);
  }
};

setTimeout(user.greet, 1000);
```

17. Why doesn't this change `this`?

```javascript
const arrow = () => console.log(this);

arrow.call({ name: "Bob" });
```

18. Explain why this works:

```javascript
const bound = user.greet.bind(user);

bound();
```

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Function
│
├── call(thisArg, arg1, arg2)
│      │
│      └── Executes Immediately
│
├── apply(thisArg, [args])
│      │
│      └── Executes Immediately
│
└── bind(thisArg, arg1...)
       │
       └── Returns New Function

-------------------------

call()

↓

Immediate

Individual Arguments

-------------------------

apply()

↓

Immediate

Array Arguments

-------------------------

bind()

↓

Later

Returns Function

-------------------------

Common Use

Lost this

↓

bind()

↓

Callback Works
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain why explicit binding exists.
- ✅ Distinguish `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`.
- ✅ Preserve `this` in callbacks using `bind()`.
- ✅ Borrow methods between objects.
- ✅ Use `bind()` for partial application.
- ✅ Explain why arrow functions ignore `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()` for `this`.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Predict the output **without running the code**:

```javascript
const person = {
  name: "Alice"
};

function introduce(city, country) {
  console.log(`${this.name} lives in ${city}, ${country}`);
}

const bound = introduce.bind(person, "Lagos");

introduce.call(person, "Abuja", "Nigeria");
introduce.apply(person, ["Ibadan", "Nigeria"]);
bound("Nigeria");
```

Questions:

1. What does each line print?
2. Why does `bound("Nigeria")` still use `"Lagos"`?
3. If you wrote `bound.call({ name: "Bob" }, "Canada")`, would `this` become `{ name: "Bob" }`? Why or why not?

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 7.3 — Prototypes and the Prototype Chain**, one of the deepest JavaScript topics. You'll learn:

- What prototypes really are.
- How inheritance works in JavaScript.
- `__proto__` vs `prototype`.
- The prototype chain lookup algorithm.
- How `class` is built on top of prototypes.
- Common interview questions on inheritance and object creation.

questions.questionText: What is the key difference between call() and apply()?
options: call() takes arguments individually; apply() takes them as an array
call() creates a new bound function; apply() invokes it immediately
questions.explanation: `fn.call(thisArg, arg1, arg2)` vs `fn.apply(thisArg, [arg1, arg2])`.

questions.questionText: Which methods invoke the function immediately? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: `call()` and `apply()` invoke immediately. `bind()` returns a new function bound to the context for later execution.

questions.questionText: Which function method returns a bound function instance instead of calling it immediately?
questions.explanation: `bind()` creates a new function copy with its `this` value permanently locked to the provided argument.
