lessons.content:
# Module 9 — Advanced TypeScript

# Lesson 9.3 — `keyof`, `typeof`, Indexed Access Types & Lookup Types

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely Common)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

This lesson covers one of the biggest transitions from **using TypeScript** to **thinking in TypeScript**.

A beginner often writes the same information twice:

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}
```

Later:

```ts
type UserKeys =
    | "id"
    | "name"
    | "email";
```

This is duplication.

If someone later adds:

```ts
age: number
```

to `User`, they also have to remember to update `UserKeys`.

This is error-prone.

TypeScript gives us tools to **derive types from existing types**, avoiding duplication.

These tools are:

- `keyof`
- `typeof`
- Indexed Access Types
- Lookup Types

These appear everywhere in modern React, Redux, API wrappers, utility libraries, and component libraries.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Use `keyof` to extract property names.
- Use `typeof` in TypeScript (not JavaScript).
- Extract property types with indexed access types.
- Combine `keyof` and generics.
- Build reusable helper functions.
- Understand why these features reduce maintenance and improve type safety.

---

# 1. What is `keyof`?

`keyof` extracts the **property names** of an object type and produces a **union of string (or number/symbol) literal keys**.

Example:

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}
```

Now:

```ts
type UserKeys = keyof User;
```

Result:

```ts
"id" | "name" | "email"
```

---

## Visual

```text
User

│

├── id

├── name

└── email

↓

keyof

↓

"id"

|

"name"

|

"email"
```

---

# Why is this useful?

Instead of manually writing:

```ts
type UserKey =
    | "id"
    | "name"
    | "email";
```

you simply write:

```ts
type UserKey = keyof User;
```

If you later add:

```ts
age: number;
```

Then:

```ts
keyof User
```

automatically becomes:

```ts
"id" | "name" | "email" | "age"
```

No extra work.

---

# 2. Real-World Example

Imagine a reusable sorting function.

Instead of:

```ts
sort(users, "name");
```

where `"name"` is just a string, you can type the parameter:

```ts
function sortUsers(
    key: keyof User
) {}
```

Now only valid property names are accepted.

---

Valid:

```ts
sortUsers("email");
```

---

Invalid:

```ts
sortUsers("salary");
```

Compiler error.

---

# 3. `typeof` in TypeScript

You've already seen JavaScript's `typeof`:

```js
typeof "Hello"
```

returns:

```text
"string"
```

That's a **runtime operator**.

---

TypeScript also has:

```ts
typeof
```

used in **type positions**.

Example:

```ts
const user = {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice"
};
```

Now:

```ts
type UserType = typeof user;
```

Result:

```ts
{
    id: number;
    name: string;
}
```

No interface needed.

---

# Visual

```text
Value

↓

typeof

↓

Type
```

---

# Why is this useful?

Suppose you already have:

```ts
const config = {
    apiUrl: "...",
    timeout: 5000,
    retries: 3
};
```

Instead of rewriting:

```ts
interface Config {
    apiUrl: string;
    timeout: number;
    retries: number;
}
```

you can write:

```ts
type Config = typeof config;
```

One source of truth.

---

# 4. `keyof typeof`

These operators are often combined.

Example:

```ts
const colors = {
    primary: "#000",
    secondary: "#fff",
    danger: "#f00"
};
```

Now:

```ts
type Color =
    keyof typeof colors;
```

Result:

```ts
"primary"
|
"secondary"
|
"danger"
```

---

## Visual

```text
Object

↓

typeof

↓

Object Type

↓

keyof

↓

Keys
```

---

# Real-World React Example

Theme systems often use this pattern.

```ts
const theme = {
    primary: "#1976d2",
    secondary: "#9c27b0"
};

type ThemeColor =
    keyof typeof theme;
```

Now your components only accept valid theme keys.

---

# 5. Indexed Access Types

Suppose:

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}
```

You want only the type of `name`.

Instead of writing:

```ts
string
```

you can derive it.

```ts
type UserName =
    User["name"];
```

Result:

```ts
string
```

---

# Visual

```text
User

↓

["name"]

↓

string
```

---

Another example:

```ts
type UserId =
    User["id"];
```

Result:

```ts
number
```

---

# Multiple Properties

You can extract multiple types at once.

```ts
type BasicInfo =
    User["id" | "name"];
```

Result:

```ts
number | string
```

Notice this produces a **union of the property value types**, not an object.

---

# 6. Combining `keyof` and Indexed Access

Suppose:

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}
```

Then:

```ts
type AllValues =
    User[keyof User];
```

Let's evaluate it step by step.

First:

```ts
keyof User
```

becomes:

```ts
"id"
|
"name"
|
"email"
```

Now:

```ts
User[
    "id" |
    "name" |
    "email"
]
```

becomes:

```ts
number
|
string
```

The duplicate `string` values are collapsed into one.

---

# Visual

```text
keyof User

↓

"id"

"name"

"email"

↓

User[...]

↓

number

|

string
```

---

# 7. Generic Property Access

One of the most common interview questions.

Write a function that safely retrieves a property.

```ts
function getProperty<
    T,
    K extends keyof T
>(
    obj: T,
    key: K
): T[K] {
    return obj[key];
}
```

---

## Let's Break It Down

```ts
T
```

The object type.

---

```ts
K extends keyof T
```

The key must be one of the object's keys.

---

```ts
T[K]
```

The return type is the type of the selected property.

---

Usage:

```ts
const user = {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice"
};

const value =
    getProperty(user, "name");
```

Type:

```text
string
```

---

Another example:

```ts
const id =
    getProperty(user, "id");
```

Type:

```text
number
```

---

Invalid:

```ts
getProperty(
    user,
    "salary"
);
```

Compiler error.

---

# Why is This Powerful?

Without Generics:

```ts
function getProperty(
    obj: any,
    key: string
)
```

Everything becomes `any`.

With Generics:

- Valid keys only.
- Exact return type.
- Full IntelliSense.
- Refactoring safety.

---

# 8. Real-World React Example

Imagine a reusable table component.

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}
```

Props:

```ts
interface Column<T> {
    key: keyof T;
    label: string;
}
```

Usage:

```ts
const columns: Column<User>[] = [
    {
        key: "name",
        label: "Name"
    },
    {
        key: "email",
        label: "Email"
    }
];
```

Trying:

```ts
key: "salary"
```

results in a compile-time error.

This is how many UI libraries achieve strong typing.

---

# 9. Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Confusing JavaScript `typeof` with TypeScript `typeof`.

JavaScript:

```js
typeof 10
```

returns the string:

```text
"number"
```

TypeScript:

```ts
type T = typeof value;
```

produces a type, not a runtime value.

---

## Mistake 2

Writing duplicated unions.

Instead of:

```ts
type Keys =
    | "id"
    | "name"
    | "email";
```

prefer:

```ts
keyof User
```

---

## Mistake 3

Using `string` instead of `keyof`.

Wrong:

```ts
function get(
    key: string
)
```

Better:

```ts
function get(
    key: keyof User
)
```

---

## Mistake 4

Forgetting generic constraints.

```ts
K extends keyof T
```

ensures only valid keys are accepted.

---

# Under the Hood

```text
Object Type

↓

keyof

↓

Keys

↓

Indexed Access

↓

Property Type

↓

Generic Function

↓

Fully Type Safe
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What does `keyof` do?

> It creates a union of the property names of an object type.

---

### What does `typeof` do in TypeScript?

> It extracts the type of an existing value so you can reuse it in type annotations.

---

### What is an indexed access type?

> A way to retrieve the type of a property using bracket notation, such as `User["name"]`.

---

### Why combine `keyof` with Generics?

> It lets you write reusable functions that only accept valid property names and automatically infer the correct return type.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Create:

```ts
type UserKeys =
    keyof User;
```

---

## Medium

Write:

```ts
type Name =
    User["name"];
```

---

## Hard

Implement:

```ts
getProperty()
```

using:

- `keyof`
- Generics
- Indexed access types

---

# Time Complexity

These features exist only during compilation and have no runtime performance cost.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What does `keyof` return?
2. What is the difference between JavaScript `typeof` and TypeScript `typeof`?
3. What is an indexed access type?
4. What does `User[keyof User]` evaluate to?
5. Why is `keyof` useful?
6. Why combine `keyof` with Generics?
7. What does `T[K]` mean?
8. Why is `K extends keyof T` important?
9. When would you use `keyof typeof`?
10. How do these features reduce duplication?

---

## Coding

11. Create `type ProductKeys = keyof Product`.
12. Extract `Product["price"]`.
13. Write a generic `getProperty()` helper.
14. Create a `theme` object and derive its valid keys using `keyof typeof`.
15. Build a generic `Column<T>` interface where `key` is `keyof T`.

---

## Debugging

16. Why does this fail?

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
}

function get(
    key: keyof User
) {}

get("salary");
```

17. Why does this work?

```ts
const user = {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice"
};

type UserType =
    typeof user;
```

18. What is the type of:

```ts
type Values =
    User[keyof User];
```

and why?

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
keyof

↓

Property Names

-------------------------

typeof

↓

Type of Existing Value

-------------------------

keyof typeof

↓

Keys of an Object Value

-------------------------

User["name"]

↓

Property Type

-------------------------

User[keyof User]

↓

Union of All Property Value Types

-------------------------

T[K]

↓

Type of Property K on Object T
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain `keyof`.
- ✅ Explain the difference between JavaScript `typeof` and TypeScript `typeof`.
- ✅ Extract property types with indexed access types.
- ✅ Use `keyof typeof` to derive keys from existing objects.
- ✅ Write a generic `getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>()` helper.
- ✅ Explain why these features reduce duplication and improve maintainability.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Consider the following code:

```ts
const settings = {
    theme: "dark",
    language: "en",
    notifications: true
};

type Settings = typeof settings;

type SettingKey = keyof Settings;

function getSetting<
    T,
    K extends keyof T
>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
    return obj[key];
}

const value1 = getSetting(settings, "theme");
const value2 = getSetting(settings, "notifications");
// const value3 = getSetting(settings, "timezone");
```

Answer the following:

1. What is the type of `Settings`?
2. What is the type of `SettingKey`?
3. What is the inferred type of `value1`?
4. What is the inferred type of `value2`?
5. Why does `value3` fail to compile?
6. Explain what `T[K]` represents in `getSetting`.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 9.4 — Mapped Types & Conditional Types**, where you'll learn the advanced mechanisms behind many built-in utility types such as `Partial`, `Pick`, and `Readonly`, and how to build your own custom utility types—a topic that frequently appears in senior frontend interviews.

questions.questionText: What does the `keyof` operator return?
options: A union of string/numeric literal types representing the keys of an object type
An array of object keys at runtime
A boolean checking if a key exists
questions.explanation: `keyof T` yields the union of public keys of `T` (e.g. `keyof { id: number }` yields `'id'`).

questions.questionText: Which are true regarding the `typeof` operator in TypeScript? (Select all that apply)
options: It can extract the static type of a variable/object in type space.
It behaves like standard JavaScript typeof at runtime.
It converts arrays to tuples at compile time.
It can only be used on string variables.
questions.explanation: `typeof` can refer to a variable's static type in TS type space, or execute at runtime as standard JS `typeof`.

questions.questionText: What syntax lookup accessor is used to retrieve the type of a specific property 'id' from type 'User'? (Format: User[...])
questions.explanation: Indexed access types use bracket notation, e.g. `User['id']`.

lessons.title: Lesson 9.4
lessons.objective: Understand mapped types, conditional type structures, and type inference keywords.
lessons.content:
# Module 9 — Advanced TypeScript

# Lesson 9.4 — Mapped Types & Conditional Types

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Senior-Level & Frequently Asked)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

So far, you've used utility types like:

```ts
Partial<User>
Readonly<User>
Pick<User, "id">
Omit<User, "id">
```

Have you ever wondered:

> **"How does TypeScript actually create these new types?"**

The answer is:

- **Mapped Types**
- **Conditional Types**

These are the building blocks behind most of TypeScript's built-in utility types.

Once you understand these, you'll stop memorizing utility types and start creating your own.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what a mapped type is.
- Build your own `Partial<T>`.
- Build your own `Readonly<T>`.
- Understand conditional types.
- Use the `extends` keyword in conditional types.
- Understand the `infer` keyword.
- Explain how built-in utility types work internally.
- Answer advanced TypeScript interview questions confidently.

---

# 1. What is a Mapped Type?

Imagine you have:

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}
```

Instead of manually writing:

```ts
type OptionalUser = {
    id?: number;
    name?: string;
    email?: string;
}
```

TypeScript can **loop through every property**.

This is called a **Mapped Type**.

---

## Mental Model

Think of it like JavaScript's `.map()`.

JavaScript:

```ts
const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

const doubled = numbers.map(n => n * 2);
```

Visual:

```text
1 → 2
2 → 4
3 → 6
```

Mapped Types do the same thing...

But with **properties instead of array elements**.

---

Visual

```text
User

↓

id

↓

name

↓

email

↓

Transform Each Property

↓

New Type
```

---

# 2. Basic Mapped Type Syntax

```ts
type Copy<T> = {
    [K in keyof T]: T[K];
};
```

This may look intimidating, but it's actually straightforward.

Let's break it down.

---

# Syntax Breakdown

```ts
[K in keyof T]
```

Character by character.

---

### `K`

A variable representing one property key.

Example:

```text
K

↓

"id"

↓

"name"

↓

"email"
```

---

### `in`

Just like JavaScript:

```js
for (const key in obj)
```

TypeScript uses:

```ts
[K in keyof T]
```

to iterate through each key.

---

### `keyof T`

Gets all keys.

```text
"id"

"name"

"email"
```

---

### `T[K]`

Gets the type of that property.

Example:

```text
K = "name"

↓

T["name"]

↓

string
```

---

Complete picture:

```ts
type Copy<T> = {
    [K in keyof T]: T[K];
};
```

Visual:

```text
id

↓

number

--------------

name

↓

string

--------------

email

↓

string
```

It recreates the original type.

---

# 3. Build Your Own `Partial<T>`

Let's make every property optional.

```ts
type MyPartial<T> = {
    [K in keyof T]?: T[K];
};
```

Notice the only difference:

```ts
?
```

after the property.

---

Example:

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
}

type UpdateUser = MyPartial<User>;
```

Result:

```ts
{
    id?: number;
    name?: string;
}
```

Exactly how `Partial<T>` works internally.

---

# 4. Build Your Own `Readonly<T>`

```ts
type MyReadonly<T> = {
    readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K];
};
```

Result:

```ts
{
    readonly id: number;
    readonly name: string;
}
```

Again, just one keyword changes the behavior.

---

# 5. Modifying Property Types

Suppose every property should become a boolean.

```ts
type BooleanFields<T> = {
    [K in keyof T]: boolean;
};
```

Example:

```ts
interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
}

type Flags = BooleanFields<User>;
```

Result:

```ts
{
    id: boolean;
    name: boolean;
}
```

---

## Real-World Example

Permission flags.

```ts
interface Permissions {
    read: boolean;
    write: boolean;
    delete: boolean;
}
```

Instead of writing them manually from another interface, a mapped type can generate them.

---

# 6. What is a Conditional Type?

Sometimes you want different types depending on a condition.

Example:

```ts
type IsString<T> =
    T extends string
        ? true
        : false;
```

---

Visual

```text
Is T a string?

↓

Yes

↓

true

------------

No

↓

false
```

---

Examples:

```ts
type A = IsString<string>;
```

Result:

```ts
true
```

---

```ts
type B = IsString<number>;
```

Result:

```ts
false
```

---

# Syntax Breakdown

```ts
T extends string
    ? true
    : false
```

Looks just like JavaScript's ternary operator.

JavaScript:

```js
condition
    ? value1
    : value2
```

TypeScript:

```ts
TypeCondition
    ? TypeA
    : TypeB
```

The only difference is you're choosing **types**, not values.

---

# 7. Another Example

```ts
type ToArray<T> =
    T extends any
        ? T[]
        : never;
```

Now:

```ts
ToArray<number>
```

becomes:

```ts
number[]
```

---

```ts
ToArray<string>
```

becomes:

```ts
string[]
```

---

# 8. The `never` Type

You've seen `never` before.

It represents:

> **A value that should never exist.**

In conditional types, it's often used to filter types.

Example:

```ts
type RemoveString<T> =
    T extends string
        ? never
        : T;
```

Now:

```ts
RemoveString<
    string | number | boolean
>
```

Result:

```ts
number | boolean
```

The `string` part becomes `never`, and `never` disappears from the union.

---

# 9. Distributive Conditional Types

Conditional types automatically distribute over union types.

Example:

```ts
type IsString<T> =
    T extends string
        ? true
        : false;
```

Now evaluate:

```ts
IsString<
    string | number
>
```

TypeScript does this internally:

```text
IsString<string>

↓

true

OR

IsString<number>

↓

false
```

Result:

```ts
true | false
```

This behavior is called **distributive conditional types**.

---

# 10. The `infer` Keyword

One of the most advanced TypeScript features.

Suppose:

```ts
type GetReturnType<T> =
    T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R
        ? R
        : never;
```

---

What is happening?

```text
Function

↓

Can You Infer

↓

Return Type?

↓

Yes

↓

Store It

↓

R
```

---

Example:

```ts
function greet() {
    return "Hello";
}
```

Now:

```ts
type Result =
    GetReturnType<
        typeof greet
    >;
```

Result:

```ts
string
```

---

This is essentially how the built-in `ReturnType<T>` utility works.

---

# 11. How Utility Types Are Built

Here are simplified versions of real utility types.

### `Partial`

```ts
type MyPartial<T> = {
    [K in keyof T]?: T[K];
};
```

---

### `Readonly`

```ts
type MyReadonly<T> = {
    readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K];
};
```

---

### `Pick`

```ts
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = {
    [P in K]: T[P];
};
```

---

These patterns appear repeatedly throughout advanced TypeScript.

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Thinking mapped types loop over values.

They loop over **property keys**.

---

## Mistake 2

Confusing runtime loops with type-level loops.

```ts
[K in keyof T]
```

exists only at compile time.

No JavaScript loop is generated.

---

## Mistake 3

Confusing `extends` in Generics with `extends` in Conditional Types.

### Generic Constraint

```ts
function f<T extends object>() {}
```

Means:

> T must satisfy this requirement.

---

### Conditional Type

```ts
T extends string
    ? A
    : B
```

Means:

> If T is assignable to `string`, choose `A`; otherwise choose `B`.

Same keyword, different purpose depending on context.

---

## Mistake 4

Using `infer` before you're comfortable with Generics and Conditional Types.

Treat `infer` as a tool for extracting a type from another type.

---

# Under the Hood

```text
Original Type

↓

Mapped Type

↓

New Object Type

-------------------------

Conditional Type

↓

Check Condition

↓

Choose Type

-------------------------

infer

↓

Extract Type Information
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What is a mapped type?

> A mapped type iterates over the keys of an existing type and creates a new type by transforming each property.

---

### What is a conditional type?

> A conditional type chooses one type or another based on whether a type satisfies a condition.

---

### What does `infer` do?

> It introduces a temporary type variable that lets TypeScript extract part of another type, such as the return type of a function.

---

### How is `Partial<T>` implemented?

A simplified version:

```ts
type MyPartial<T> = {
    [K in keyof T]?: T[K];
};
```

---

### How is `Pick<T, K>` implemented?

A simplified version:

```ts
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = {
    [P in K]: T[P];
};
```

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Implement your own:

```ts
MyReadonly<T>
```

---

## Medium

Implement:

```ts
MyPartial<T>
```

---

## Hard

Implement:

```ts
MyPick<T, K>
```

using mapped types and generic constraints.

---

# Time Complexity

Mapped types and conditional types exist only during compilation. They have no runtime execution cost.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is a mapped type?
2. What is a conditional type?
3. What does `[K in keyof T]` mean?
4. What does `T[K]` represent?
5. Why are mapped types useful?
6. What is `infer`?
7. What is `never` used for in conditional types?
8. What are distributive conditional types?
9. How does `Partial<T>` work internally?
10. How does `Pick<T, K>` work internally?

---

## Coding

11. Build `MyReadonly<T>`.
12. Build `MyPartial<T>`.
13. Build `MyPick<T, K>`.
14. Create a mapped type that converts every property into a `string`.
15. Write a conditional type that returns `"Array"` if the type is an array and `"NotArray"` otherwise.

---

## Debugging

16. Why does this produce booleans instead of the original property types?

```ts
type Flags<T> = {
    [K in keyof T]: boolean;
};
```

17. What does this evaluate to?

```ts
type Test<T> =
    T extends number
        ? "Yes"
        : "No";

type Result = Test<string | number>;
```

18. Why does `infer` make `ReturnType<T>` possible?

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Mapped Type

↓

[K in keyof T]

↓

Transform Every Property

-------------------------

Conditional Type

↓

T extends U

?

A

:

B

-------------------------

infer

↓

Extract Type Information

-------------------------

never

↓

Impossible Type

↓

Useful for Filtering Unions

-------------------------

Built From These

↓

Partial

Readonly

Pick

Omit

ReturnType
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain mapped types.
- ✅ Explain conditional types.
- ✅ Build a custom `Partial<T>`.
- ✅ Build a custom `Readonly<T>`.
- ✅ Explain `infer`.
- ✅ Explain how many built-in utility types are implemented internally.
- ✅ Distinguish `extends` as a generic constraint from `extends` in a conditional type.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Without using the built-in utilities, implement the following:

1. `MyRequired<T>` — make every property required.
2. `MyMutable<T>` — remove `readonly` from every property.
3. `MyValueTypes<T>` — create a union of all property value types (hint: think about `T[keyof T]`).
4. Explain why the following works:

```ts
type MyPartial<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]?: T[K];
};
```

5. Explain why this conditional type returns different results for unions:

```ts
type IsNumber<T> = T extends number ? true : false;

type Result = IsNumber<number | string>;
```

Walk through the evaluation step by step.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 9.5 — Type Guards, Narrowing, Assertion Functions, and the `satisfies` Operator**, where you'll learn how TypeScript progressively narrows types at runtime using checks like `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, custom type guards, assertion functions, and the modern `satisfies` operator. These concepts are heavily used in React, API handling, and senior-level TypeScript interviews.

# Module 9 — Advanced TypeScript

# Lesson 9.5 — Type Guards, Narrowing, Assertion Functions & the `satisfies` Operator

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Very Common)

---

# 🚨 Before We Start

One of the biggest misconceptions about TypeScript is:

> **"TypeScript automatically knows the exact type of every variable."**

It doesn't.

Consider this:

```ts
function print(value: string | number) {
    console.log(value);
}
```

Inside the function, what is `value`?

```text
string ?

number ?

Both?
```

The answer is:

```text
string | number
```

TypeScript only knows it could be **either**.

So if you try:

```ts
function print(value: string | number) {
    console.log(value.toUpperCase());
}
```

You'll get an error.

Why?

Because `number` doesn't have `toUpperCase()`.

TypeScript needs **proof** that the value is a string before it allows string-specific operations.

That process is called **narrowing**, and the checks you use are called **type guards**.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain what narrowing is.
- Use all built-in type guards (`typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`).
- Write custom type guards.
- Write assertion functions.
- Understand the `satisfies` operator.
- Explain these concepts in interviews.

---

# 1. What is Narrowing?

Narrowing means reducing a broad type into a more specific one.

Example:

```ts
string | number
```

↓

After checking:

```ts
typeof value === "string"
```

↓

TypeScript now knows:

```text
string
```

---

## Visual

```text
Before

string | number

↓

typeof value === "string"

↓

After

string
```

---

# 2. `typeof` Type Guard

This is the most common one.

```ts
function print(value: string | number) {
    if (typeof value === "string") {
        console.log(value.toUpperCase());
    } else {
        console.log(value.toFixed(2));
    }
}
```

---

## What happens?

Initially:

```text
value

↓

string | number
```

Inside the `if` block:

```text
value

↓

string
```

Inside the `else` block:

```text
value

↓

number
```

TypeScript automatically narrows the type.

---

## Syntax Breakdown

```ts
typeof value === "string"
```

- `typeof` → JavaScript runtime operator.
- `value` → Variable being checked.
- `===` → Strict equality comparison.
- `"string"` → One of JavaScript's valid `typeof` results.

---

## Valid `typeof` Results

```text
"string"
"number"
"boolean"
"bigint"
"symbol"
"undefined"
"object"
"function"
```

---

# 3. `instanceof` Type Guard

Used with classes and constructor functions.

```ts
class Dog {
    bark() {}
}

class Cat {
    meow() {}
}

function speak(animal: Dog | Cat) {
    if (animal instanceof Dog) {
        animal.bark();
    } else {
        animal.meow();
    }
}
```

---

## Visual

```text
Dog Instance

↓

instanceof Dog

↓

true

↓

Dog
```

---

### When to use

- Class instances.
- Built-in classes like `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, and `Error`.

Example:

```ts
if (value instanceof Date) {
    console.log(value.getFullYear());
}
```

---

# 4. `in` Type Guard

Checks whether an object contains a property.

```ts
interface User {
    name: string;
}

interface Product {
    price: number;
}

function display(item: User | Product) {
    if ("name" in item) {
        console.log(item.name);
    } else {
        console.log(item.price);
    }
}
```

---

## Visual

```text
Object

↓

Has "name"?

↓

Yes

↓

User

------------

No

↓

Product
```

---

# 5. Equality Narrowing

Literal values can also narrow types.

```ts
type Status =
    | "loading"
    | "success"
    | "error";

function handle(status: Status) {
    if (status === "loading") {
        // status is "loading"
    }
}
```

---

## Why?

The comparison proves the exact value.

---

# 6. Truthiness Narrowing

Example:

```ts
function greet(name?: string) {
    if (name) {
        console.log(name.toUpperCase());
    }
}
```

Initially:

```text
string | undefined
```

Inside the `if` block:

```text
string
```

Because `undefined` is falsy.

> **Note:** Be careful with truthiness checks. Values like `0`, `false`, and `""` (empty string) are also falsy. If those are valid values, an explicit comparison (e.g. `value !== undefined`) is often safer.

---

# 7. Custom Type Guards

Sometimes built-in guards aren't enough.

Example:

```ts
interface Admin {
    role: "admin";
    permissions: string[];
}

interface Customer {
    role: "customer";
    points: number;
}
```

Create a custom guard:

```ts
function isAdmin(
    user: Admin | Customer
): user is Admin {
    return user.role === "admin";
}
```

---

## Syntax Breakdown

```ts
user is Admin
```

This is called a **type predicate**.

It tells TypeScript:

> "If this function returns `true`, treat `user` as an `Admin`."

---

Usage:

```ts
if (isAdmin(user)) {
    console.log(user.permissions);
}
```

TypeScript now knows `user` is an `Admin`.

---

## Visual

```text
User

↓

isAdmin()

↓

true

↓

Admin
```

---

# 8. Assertion Functions

Sometimes you want to stop execution if a condition isn't met.

```ts
function assertDefined<T>(
    value: T
): asserts value is NonNullable<T> {
    if (value == null) {
        throw new Error("Value is missing");
    }
}
```

Usage:

```ts
const user: User | null = getUser();

assertDefined(user);

// From here onward,
// user is treated as User
console.log(user.name);
```

If `assertDefined` returns normally, TypeScript assumes the assertion succeeded and narrows the type.

---

# 9. Discriminated Unions

A very common interview topic.

```ts
type Shape =
    | {
          kind: "circle";
          radius: number;
      }
    | {
          kind: "square";
          side: number;
      };
```

Now:

```ts
function area(shape: Shape) {
    switch (shape.kind) {
        case "circle":
            return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;

        case "square":
            return shape.side * shape.side;
    }
}
```

The `kind` property is called the **discriminant** (or **tag**).

It allows TypeScript to narrow each branch automatically.

---

## Visual

```text
Shape

↓

kind

↓

circle

↓

Circle Type

------------

square

↓

Square Type
```

---

# 10. Exhaustive Checking with `never`

A useful pattern to ensure all union members are handled.

```ts
function area(shape: Shape) {
    switch (shape.kind) {
        case "circle":
            return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;

        case "square":
            return shape.side * shape.side;

        default: {
            const _exhaustive: never = shape;
            return _exhaustive;
        }
    }
}
```

If you later add a `"triangle"` variant and forget to handle it, TypeScript will report an error in the `default` branch.

---

# 11. The `satisfies` Operator

Introduced to validate a value against a type **without changing the inferred type**.

Example:

```ts
type Theme = {
    primary: string;
    secondary: string;
};

const theme = {
    primary: "#1976d2",
    secondary: "#9c27b0"
} satisfies Theme;
```

This checks that `theme` satisfies the `Theme` type.

Unlike a type annotation, `satisfies` preserves the most specific inferred types for the object's properties where possible.

---

## Why use `satisfies`?

Consider:

```ts
type Colors = "red" | "blue";

const palette = {
    primary: "red",
    secondary: "blue"
} satisfies Record<string, Colors>;
```

You get:

- Validation that values are `"red"` or `"blue"`.
- Better inference than using a broad type annotation in many scenarios.

This is especially useful for configuration objects.

---

# Common Mistakes

## Mistake 1

Using `typeof` for arrays.

```ts
typeof []
```

returns:

```text
"object"
```

Use:

```ts
Array.isArray(value)
```

instead.

---

## Mistake 2

Using `instanceof` with interfaces.

Interfaces do **not** exist at runtime.

This is invalid:

```ts
interface User {}

value instanceof User // ❌
```

Use a property check (`in`) or a custom type guard instead.

---

## Mistake 3

Forgetting that type guards only narrow within their scope.

Once you leave the guarded block, the original broader type may apply again.

---

## Mistake 4

Confusing `as` with narrowing.

```ts
const user = value as User;
```

This **does not prove** the value is a `User`.

It simply tells TypeScript to trust you.

Prefer real runtime checks when possible.

---

# Under the Hood

```text
Union Type

↓

Runtime Check

↓

Type Guard

↓

Narrowed Type

↓

Safe Property Access
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What is narrowing?

> Narrowing is the process of reducing a broader type to a more specific type using runtime checks that TypeScript understands.

---

### Name three built-in type guards.

- `typeof`
- `instanceof`
- `in`

(You can also mention equality checks and truthiness narrowing.)

---

### What is a custom type guard?

> A function that returns a type predicate (e.g. `user is Admin`) so TypeScript can narrow the type when the function returns `true`.

---

### What is an assertion function?

> A function whose return type uses `asserts` to tell TypeScript that a condition must be true if the function completes successfully.

---

### What does the `satisfies` operator do?

> It checks that a value conforms to a type while preserving more specific inferred types than a normal type annotation often would.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Write a function that accepts `string | number` and prints:

- uppercase if it's a string.
- fixed decimal if it's a number.

---

## Medium

Create a custom type guard:

```ts
isAdmin(user)
```

that narrows `Admin | Customer` to `Admin`.

---

## Hard

Implement an exhaustive `switch` over a discriminated union and use `never` to ensure every case is handled.

---

# Time Complexity

Type guards are runtime checks. Most have constant-time complexity (`O(1)`), though it depends on the check you perform.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is narrowing?
2. What is a type guard?
3. When should you use `typeof`?
4. When should you use `instanceof`?
5. When should you use the `in` operator?
6. What is a custom type guard?
7. What is a type predicate?
8. What is an assertion function?
9. What is a discriminated union?
10. What is the purpose of the `satisfies` operator?

---

## Coding

11. Write a function using `typeof` to narrow `string | number`.
12. Create `Admin` and `Customer` interfaces and write an `isAdmin` guard.
13. Write an assertion function that ensures a value is not `null` or `undefined`.
14. Create a discriminated union for `Circle`, `Square`, and `Triangle`, then compute the area with an exhaustive `switch`.
15. Create a configuration object that uses the `satisfies` operator with `Record<string, "light" | "dark">`.

---

## Debugging

16. Why doesn't `value instanceof User` work when `User` is an interface?
17. Why is `Array.isArray(value)` preferred over `typeof value === "object"` for arrays?
18. Why is `value as User` different from using a custom type guard?

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Narrowing
    ↓
More Specific Type

-------------------------

typeof
    ↓
Primitive Types

-------------------------

instanceof
    ↓
Classes

-------------------------

in
    ↓
Object Properties

-------------------------

Type Predicate
    ↓
user is Admin

-------------------------

asserts
    ↓
Assertion Function

-------------------------

Discriminated Union
    ↓
Tagged Union
    ↓
Safe switch

-------------------------

satisfies
    ↓
Validate Shape
+
Preserve Inference
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain what narrowing is.
- ✅ Use `typeof`, `instanceof`, and `in` appropriately.
- ✅ Write a custom type guard.
- ✅ Explain what a type predicate is.
- ✅ Write a simple assertion function.
- ✅ Explain discriminated unions and exhaustive checking.
- ✅ Describe when and why to use the `satisfies` operator.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

Given:

```ts
type ApiResult =
    | { status: "success"; data: { id: number; name: string } }
    | { status: "error"; message: string }
    | { status: "loading" };

function handleResult(result: ApiResult) {
    // Implement this
}
```

Your tasks:

1. Use a `switch` on `result.status`.
2. Handle all three cases.
3. Use an exhaustive `never` check in the `default` branch.
4. Explain why TypeScript knows `result.data` only exists in the `"success"` case.
5. Explain why this pattern is preferred over checking arbitrary properties like `"data" in result` for tagged unions.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Module 10 — React Interview Mastery**, starting with **Lesson 10.1 — JSX, React Elements, Rendering, and the Virtual DOM**, where we'll transition from advanced TypeScript into React concepts that are commonly tested in frontend interviews.

questions.questionText: What is the return signature of a user-defined type guard function checking if `val` is a `User`?
questions.explanation: Type guards use type predicates in return positions, e.g. `function isUser(val: any): val is User`.

questions.questionText: Which JavaScript operators trigger static type narrowing in TypeScript? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: TypeScript compiles control flow, narrowing types inside branches that check types via `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, and strict equality `===`.

questions.questionText: What TypeScript operator verifies that an expression matches a type, without widening or changing the expression's inferred type?

lessons.objective: Master JSX structures, React elements, rendering loop, and virtual DOM diffing algorithms.
lessons.content:
# Module 10 — React Interview Mastery # Lesson 10.1 — JSX, React Elements, Rendering & the Virtual DOM > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (Intermediate) > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Asked in Almost Every React Interview) --- # 🚨 Before We Start One of the biggest misconceptions about React is: > **"JSX is HTML."** It isn't. Another common misconception is: > **"React updates the DOM every time state changes."** It doesn't. Understanding what JSX actually is, what React Elements are, how React renders, and how the Virtual DOM works is the foundation of React. These concepts are frequently tested because they reveal whether you understand React beyond just writing components. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Explain what JSX is. - Explain what a React Element is. - Describe how JSX is transformed. - Understand the React rendering process. - Explain the Virtual DOM and reconciliation. - Distinguish between React Elements, Components, and DOM Elements. - Answer common React interview questions on rendering. --- # 1. What is JSX? JSX stands for: ```text JavaScript XML ``` JSX is a **syntax extension for JavaScript** that lets you write UI using a syntax that resembles HTML. Example: ```jsx const element =

Hello, World!

; ``` Many beginners think this is HTML. It isn't. It's JavaScript syntax that is transformed into function calls during compilation. --- ## Why Does JSX Exist? Without JSX: ```jsx const element = React.createElement( "h1", null, "Hello, World!" ); ``` With JSX: ```jsx const element =

Hello, World!

; ``` Both produce the same React Element, but JSX is much easier to read and write. --- # Visual ```text JSX ↓ Compiler (Babel / SWC / TypeScript) ↓ React.createElement(...) (or the newer JSX runtime) ↓ React Element ↓ Rendered UI ``` > **Modern React Note:** Since React 17, most projects use the **new JSX Transform**, so you no longer need to manually write `import React from "react"` just to use JSX. The compiler transforms JSX using helper functions automatically. --- # 2. JSX Syntax Deep Dive Example: ```jsx const title =

Hello

; ``` Let's break it down. ```jsx const ``` Declares a constant variable. --- ```jsx title ``` Variable name. --- ```jsx = ``` Assignment operator. --- ```jsx

``` JSX opening tag. Represents an HTML element **or** a custom React component. --- ```jsx Hello ``` Child content. --- ```jsx

``` Closing tag. --- Internally, React sees something conceptually like: ```jsx React.createElement( "h1", null, "Hello" ); ``` --- # 3. JSX Is an Expression Since JSX is just JavaScript, it can appear anywhere an expression is valid. Example: ```jsx const name = "Alice"; const element =

Hello {name}

; ``` Result: ```html

Hello Alice

``` --- ## What Are the Curly Braces `{}`? Curly braces let you switch from JSX back into JavaScript. Example: ```jsx const age = 30;

Age: {age}

``` --- You can place expressions inside: ```jsx
{2 + 2}
``` Output: ```text 4 ``` --- You can call functions: ```jsx
{getFullName()}
``` --- You can use ternary operators: ```jsx
{isLoggedIn ? "Welcome" : "Login"}
``` --- You **cannot** place statements like `if`, `for`, or `while` directly inside JSX because they are statements, not expressions. ❌ Invalid: ```jsx
{if (loggedIn) {}}
``` Instead, use a ternary, logical `&&`, or compute the value before the `return`. --- # 4. Rules of JSX ### One Parent Element This is invalid: ```jsx return (

Hello

World

); ``` React components must return a **single root element**. Correct: ```jsx return (

Hello

World

); ``` Or use a Fragment: ```jsx return ( <>

Hello

World

); ``` --- ### Self-Closing Tags HTML: ```html ``` JSX: ```jsx ``` Also: ```jsx
``` --- ### `class` Becomes `className` HTML: ```html
``` JSX: ```jsx
``` Because `class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript. --- ### `for` Becomes `htmlFor` ```jsx ``` This maps to the HTML `for` attribute. --- # 5. What is a React Element? A React Element is a **plain JavaScript object** describing what should appear on the screen. Example: ```jsx const element =

Hello

; ``` Conceptually, React creates something like: ```js { type: "h1", props: { children: "Hello" } } ``` A React Element is **not**: - A DOM node. - A component instance. It is simply a description of the UI. --- # Visual ```text JSX ↓ React Element (Object) ↓ Virtual DOM ↓ Real DOM ``` --- # 6. React Elements vs Components vs DOM Elements This is a common interview question. ### React Element ```jsx

Hello

``` A JavaScript object describing the UI. --- ### React Component ```jsx function Header() { return

Hello

; } ``` A function (or class) that returns React Elements. --- ### DOM Element ```html

Hello

``` The actual node created by the browser. --- ## Visual ```text Component ↓ Returns ↓ React Element ↓ React Renders ↓ DOM Element ``` --- # 7. Rendering Rendering means React calls your component to determine what UI it should produce. Example: ```jsx function Greeting() { return

Hello

; } ``` When React renders: ```text Call Greeting() ↓ Returns React Element ↓ Compare with Previous Render ↓ Update DOM if Needed ``` Rendering **does not necessarily mean** updating the browser's DOM. A render can occur without any DOM changes if React determines the output hasn't changed. --- # 8. What Triggers a Render? Common triggers include: - State updates (`setState`, `useState` setter). - Parent component re-rendering. - Context value changes. - New props. - Initial mount. --- Example: ```jsx const [count, setCount] = useState(0); setCount(1); ``` This schedules another render of the component. --- # 9. The Virtual DOM The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of your UI. Think of it as a lightweight tree of React Elements. Example UI: ```jsx

Hello

``` Virtual DOM Tree (conceptually): ```text div ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── button └── "Click" ``` When state changes, React creates a **new** Virtual DOM tree for the updated UI. --- # 10. Reconciliation Reconciliation is the process React uses to compare the previous Virtual DOM tree with the new one. ```text Old Virtual DOM ↓ Compare ↓ New Virtual DOM ↓ Find Differences ↓ Update Real DOM Minimally ``` This comparison is often called **diffing**. --- ## Example Initial render: ```jsx

Hello

``` After state change: ```jsx

Hello, Alice

``` React notices that only the text changed. It updates only that text node instead of recreating the entire page. --- # 11. Keys and Reconciliation When rendering lists: ```jsx users.map(user => (
  • {user.name}
    • )); ``` The `key` helps React identify which items were added, removed, or moved. Avoid using the array index as a key when items can be reordered, inserted, or removed, because it can lead to incorrect state being preserved across list items. --- # 12. Common Mistakes ## Mistake 1 Thinking JSX is HTML. It is JavaScript syntax that compiles to React element creation. --- ## Mistake 2 Thinking React updates the entire DOM on every render. React compares the previous and new Virtual DOM trees and updates only what's necessary. --- ## Mistake 3 Using unstable keys. ```jsx
  • ``` This creates a different key every render, preventing React from matching elements efficiently. Prefer stable, unique IDs from your data. --- ## Mistake 4 Returning multiple root elements without a wrapper or Fragment. --- # Under the Hood ```text JSX ↓ Compiler ↓ React Element Objects ↓ Component Render ↓ Virtual DOM Tree ↓ Reconciliation (Diff) ↓ Minimal DOM Updates ``` --- # Interview Perspective ### What is JSX? > JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension that makes it easier to describe UI. It is compiled into React element creation code. --- ### What is a React Element? > A React Element is an immutable JavaScript object describing what should be rendered. --- ### What is the Virtual DOM? > The Virtual DOM is React's in-memory representation of the UI used to compare renders and determine the minimal set of DOM updates. --- ### What is reconciliation? > Reconciliation is React's algorithm for comparing the previous and current Virtual DOM trees and updating the real DOM efficiently. --- ### Does every render update the DOM? > No. Every update may trigger a render, but React only updates the real DOM if the rendered output has changed. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Explain the difference between: ```jsx

    Hello

    ``` and ```jsx React.createElement(...) ``` --- ## Medium Create a component that renders a list of users using proper `key` values. --- ## Hard Explain, step by step, what happens after calling: ```jsx setCount(count + 1); ``` Include: - State update scheduling. - Component rendering. - Virtual DOM creation. - Reconciliation. - Real DOM updates. --- # Time Complexity React's reconciliation algorithm is optimized for common UI update patterns and avoids comparing every node with every other node. In practice, updates are typically efficient, though performance also depends on component structure and key usage. --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. What is JSX? 2. Is JSX HTML? 3. What does JSX compile into? 4. What is a React Element? 5. What is the difference between a React Element and a DOM Element? 6. What triggers a render? 7. What is the Virtual DOM? 8. What is reconciliation? 9. Why are `key` props important? 10. Why doesn't every render cause a DOM update? --- ## Coding 11. Write a component that displays a greeting using JSX. 12. Use curly braces to display a computed value. 13. Render a list of products with stable `key` values. 14. Use a Fragment instead of a wrapping `div`. 15. Conditionally render a message using a ternary expression. --- ## Debugging 16. Why is this invalid? ```jsx return (

    Hello

    World

    ); ``` 17. Why shouldn't you use `Math.random()` for keys? 18. Why can't you write an `if` statement directly inside JSX? --- # Interview Cheatsheet ```text JSX ↓ Syntax Extension ↓ Compiled ↓ React Elements (Objects) ↓ Rendered by Components ↓ Virtual DOM ↓ Reconciliation (Diff) ↓ Minimal DOM Updates ------------------------- Component ↓ Returns React Elements ------------------------- React Element ↓ Description of UI ------------------------- DOM Element ↓ Actual Browser Node ``` --- # Mastery Checklist Before moving on, make sure you can: - ✅ Explain what JSX is and how it's transformed. - ✅ Distinguish React Elements, Components, and DOM Elements. - ✅ Explain the React rendering process. - ✅ Describe the Virtual DOM. - ✅ Explain reconciliation and why it improves performance. - ✅ Explain the importance of stable `key` props. --- # Mini Interview Challenge Given: ```jsx function App() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( <>

    {count}

    ); } ``` Walk through **everything** that happens after the button is clicked: 1. What does the click event trigger? 2. What does `setCount` do? 3. Does React update the DOM immediately? 4. When is the component rendered again? 5. What is created during the new render? 6. How does React decide whether to update the `

    `? 7. Why isn't the entire page recreated? --- ## Coming Next Reply **Next** for **Lesson 10.2 — Functional Components, Props, Component Composition, and Rendering Patterns**, where you'll learn how React components communicate, how to design reusable components, and the composition patterns that are commonly evaluated in React interviews.

JSX elements must always close their tags.

# Module 10 — React Interview Mastery # Lesson 10.2 — Functional Components, Props, Component Composition & Rendering Patterns > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Intermediate) > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely Common) --- # 🚨 Before We Start If there is one concept that separates a beginner React developer from an experienced one, it's **component thinking**. Many beginners think: > "A React app is just a collection of pages." Experienced React developers think: > "A React app is a tree of reusable components." For example, when you open a shopping website, you don't see one huge page. Instead, you see a hierarchy of reusable pieces: ```text App │ ├── Header │ ├── Logo │ ├── SearchBar │ └── UserMenu │ ├── Sidebar │ ├── CategoryList │ └── Filters │ ├── ProductGrid │ ├── ProductCard │ ├── ProductCard │ └── ProductCard │ └── Footer ``` Each box is a React component. Learning to design these reusable building blocks is one of the most common interview topics. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Explain what a React component is. - Understand functional components. - Pass and receive props. - Use destructuring with props. - Compose components together. - Understand one-way data flow. - Learn common rendering patterns. - Answer React interview questions about component architecture. --- # 1. What is a Component? A component is simply a JavaScript function that returns React Elements. Example: ```jsx function Welcome() { return

Hello

; } ``` Think of a component as a **recipe**. The recipe itself isn't the cake. Every time React renders the component, it follows the recipe to produce UI. --- ## Visual ```text Component ↓ Function Executes ↓ Returns React Elements ↓ React Renders UI ``` --- # Why Components Exist Imagine writing this repeatedly: ```jsx

iPhone

$999

``` Ten times. Instead: ```jsx ``` Now React can reuse the same component. Benefits: - Reusability - Maintainability - Separation of concerns - Easier testing --- # 2. Functional Components Modern React uses function components. Example: ```jsx function Button() { return ; } ``` Or: ```jsx const Button = () => { return ; }; ``` Both are valid. --- ## Under the Hood When React sees: ```jsx ; } ``` Usage: ```jsx ); } ``` The child doesn't modify the parent. It simply **calls the function** the parent provided. --- # Visual ```text Parent State ↓ Props ↓ Child ↓ Callback ↓ Parent Updates State ``` --- # 9. Benefits: - Easier maintenance - Better reusability - Smaller responsibilities - Easier testing --- # 10. The `children` Prop Every React component automatically receives a special prop named `children` when elements are nested inside it. Example: ```jsx

{children}
); } ``` Output: ```jsx

``` --- ## Visual ```text ↓ Children ↓
