lessons.content:
# Module 11 — Frontend System Design # Lesson 11.1 — Component Architecture: Smart vs Presentational Components, Composition Patterns, Folder Structure & Scalable React Applications > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced) > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Very Common for Mid-Level and Senior Frontend Interviews) --- # 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters At junior interviews, you'll mostly be asked: > "Can you build this component?" At mid-level interviews: > "How would you organize this feature?" At senior interviews: > "How would you architect this application so that it's maintainable for a team of 20 developers over the next 5 years?" This lesson is about writing code that **scales**, not just code that works. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Design reusable components. - Separate business logic from UI. - Use composition instead of inheritance. - Structure large React applications. - Build scalable folder structures. - Explain architectural decisions in interviews. --- # 1. What is Component Architecture? Component architecture is the process of deciding: - How components are divided. - Where state should live. - How components communicate. - How logic is shared. - How files are organized. - How the application can grow without becoming difficult to maintain. Think of building a house. ```text House ↓ Rooms ↓ Furniture ↓ Decorations ``` You wouldn't pour all the concrete into one giant room. Similarly, you shouldn't build one giant React component containing every piece of functionality. --- # 2. The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) One of the most important software engineering principles. > **A component should have one primary responsibility.** Bad example: ```jsx Dashboard.jsx ``` Contains: - API calls - Filtering - Sorting - Pagination - Modal logic - Authentication checks - Form validation - Rendering That's far too much. Better: ```text Dashboard │ ├── UserTable ├── SearchBar ├── Pagination ├── Filters └── AddUserModal ``` Each component focuses on one concern. --- # 3. Smart vs Presentational Components This pattern is also called: - Container vs Presentational - Logic vs UI Components Although modern React often mixes these responsibilities when appropriate (especially with hooks), understanding the distinction is valuable. --- ## Smart (Container) Components Responsible for: - Fetching data. - Managing state. - Business logic. - Calling APIs. - Handling side effects. Example: ```jsx function UserPage() { const { data, loading } = useUsers(); return ( ); } ``` Notice: `UserPage` doesn't render each user itself. It manages the logic. --- ## Presentational Components Responsible for: - Rendering UI. - Receiving props. - Displaying information. - Triggering callbacks. Example: ```jsx function UserList({ users }) { return (
    {users.map(user => (
  • {user.name}
    • ))}
); } ``` No API calls. No business logic. Just UI. --- ## Visual ```text UserPage (Logic) ↓ UserList (UI) ↓ UserCard (UI) ↓ Avatar (UI) ``` --- # 4. Why Separate Logic and UI? Suppose you're building a dashboard. Without separation: ```text Dashboard ↓ Everything ``` With separation: ```text Dashboard ↓ useUsers() ↓ UserList ↓ UserCard ↓ Avatar ``` Benefits: - Easier testing. - Easier reuse. - Smaller components. - Easier debugging. - Better readability. --- # 5. Component Composition React encourages **composition over inheritance**. Instead of creating giant configurable components: ```jsx ``` ```jsx ``` ```jsx ``` Compose smaller building blocks. Example: ```jsx ``` Each part has a clear responsibility. --- ## Children Prop Composition often relies on the special `children` prop. Example: ```jsx function Card({ children }) { return (
{children}
); } ``` Usage: ```jsx

Revenue

$12,000

 ``` The `Card` component doesn't know what content it will render—it simply provides structure and styling. --- # 6. Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components ## Controlled React owns the value. ```jsx const [name, setName] = useState(""); setName(e.target.value)} /> ``` Advantages: - Easy validation. - Easy synchronization. - Predictable state. --- ## Uncontrolled The DOM owns the value. ```jsx const inputRef = useRef(null); ``` You read the value only when needed. Useful for: - Simple forms. - File inputs. - Integrating with non-React libraries. --- # 7. Lifting State Up Imagine: ```text Parent ↓ Search ↓ Results ``` Both components need access to the search term. Instead of each managing its own copy: ```text Search ↓ Own State ------------------- Results ↓ Own State ``` Lift the state to the nearest common parent. ```jsx function SearchPage() { const [query, setQuery] = useState(""); return ( <> ); } ``` --- # 8. Folder Structure There isn't one universally correct structure, but consistency is crucial. ### Small Project ```text src/ │ ├── components/ ├── pages/ ├── hooks/ ├── services/ ├── utils/ └── App.jsx ``` --- ### Large Feature-Based Project ```text src/ │ ├── features/ │ ├── auth/ │ ├── users/ │ ├── dashboard/ │ └── notifications/ │ ├── shared/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── hooks/ │ ├── utils/ │ └── types/ │ ├── services/ ├── routes/ └── app/ ``` Feature-based organization scales better because everything related to a feature lives together. --- # 9. Colocation A common React principle is **colocation**. Keep code close to where it's used. Instead of: ```text components/ ``` containing hundreds of unrelated files, organize by feature: ```text users/ │ ├── UserCard.jsx ├── UserTable.jsx ├── UserFilters.jsx └── user.api.js ``` Developers working on the users feature know exactly where to look. --- # 10. Avoid "God Components" A "God Component" tries to do everything. Example: ```jsx Dashboard.jsx ``` 1,500+ lines long. Contains: - API requests. - Authentication. - Charts. - Forms. - Modals. - Tables. - Validation. - Notifications. This becomes difficult to understand and maintain. A good rule of thumb: if a component is becoming difficult to read or has multiple unrelated responsibilities, consider extracting smaller components or hooks. --- # 11. Real-World Example Imagine you're building an e-commerce application. Instead of: ```text ProductPage ``` doing everything: Organize it like this: ```text ProductPage ↓ useProduct() ↓ ProductGallery ↓ ProductInfo ↓ Reviews ↓ RelatedProducts ↓ AddToCartButton ``` Each piece is reusable and easier to test. --- # 12. Common Mistakes ### Mistake 1 Passing props through many layers (prop drilling) when Context or composition would be more appropriate. --- ### Mistake 2 Putting API calls inside every small component. Centralize business logic where it makes sense. --- ### Mistake 3 Creating components that are too generic. Example: ```jsx ``` that tries to handle every possible use case. Over-abstraction can make code harder to understand. --- ### Mistake 4 Creating components that are too specific. Example: ```jsx ``` These are rarely reusable. Aim for components that are reusable within a reasonable domain. --- # Under the Hood ```text Page ↓ Business Logic ↓ Reusable Components ↓ Small UI Components ↓ DOM ``` A common layered approach: ```text Feature ↓ Custom Hook ↓ Container Component ↓ Presentational Components ↓ Reusable UI Components ``` --- # Interview Perspective ### What is the Single Responsibility Principle? > A component should have one primary reason to change. It should focus on one concern. --- ### Why use composition instead of inheritance? > Composition is more flexible, easier to reuse, and aligns with React's design philosophy. --- ### When should state be lifted? > When multiple sibling components need access to the same data, lift it to their nearest common parent. --- ### What makes a component reusable? > A clear API, minimal assumptions, focused responsibility, and the ability to receive behavior and data through props. --- ### Feature-based or type-based folder structure? > For larger applications, feature-based organization usually scales better because related files stay together. Smaller projects may do well with a simpler type-based structure. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Split this large `UserCard` component into smaller reusable components. --- ## Medium Design a reusable `Modal` component using composition: ```jsx ``` Discuss how you would manage its open/closed state. --- ## Hard You're asked to build a dashboard with: - User profile. - Notifications. - Analytics charts. - Search. - Filters. - Data table. - Pagination. - Export button. Explain: 1. Which components you would create. 2. Where state would live. 3. Which logic belongs in Custom Hooks. 4. Which data belongs in Context. 5. How you would organize the folders. --- # Time Complexity Component architecture doesn't change algorithmic complexity directly. Its impact is on maintainability, readability, testability, and how efficiently React can render and update your UI. --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. What is component architecture? 2. Explain the Single Responsibility Principle. 3. What's the difference between smart and presentational components? 4. Why is composition preferred over inheritance in React? 5. What is the `children` prop used for? 6. What is lifting state up? 7. What is colocation? 8. What is a "God Component"? 9. What are the benefits of a feature-based folder structure? 10. What makes a component reusable? --- ## Coding 11. Refactor a large component into smaller ones. 12. Build a reusable `Card` component using `children`. 13. Build a compound `Modal` component. 14. Move duplicated business logic into a Custom Hook. 15. Design a feature-based folder structure for a blog application. --- ## Debugging 16. Why is passing a `user` prop through six components a code smell? 17. A component has grown to 2,000 lines. What refactoring steps would you take? 18. A reusable component now has 40 props to support every scenario. What architectural issue does this suggest? --- # Interview Cheatsheet ```text Single Responsibility ↓ One Component = One Primary Concern ------------------------------------- Smart Component ↓ Business Logic Data Fetching State Side Effects ------------------------------------- Presentational Component ↓ UI Props Rendering ------------------------------------- Composition ↓ Build Small Pieces Combine Together ------------------------------------- Lifting State ↓ Move Shared State To Common Parent ------------------------------------- Folder Structure ↓ Prefer Feature-Based For Large Projects ``` --- # Mastery Checklist Before moving on, make sure you can: - ✅ Explain smart vs presentational components. - ✅ Design components with a single responsibility. - ✅ Use composition effectively. - ✅ Know when to lift state. - ✅ Organize a scalable React project. - ✅ Avoid "God Components." - ✅ Justify architectural decisions in an interview. --- # Mini Interview Challenge You're building **VentureMatch**, a startup-investor marketplace (similar to the project you've been designing). Requirements: - Public landing page. - Authentication. - Investor dashboard. - Founder dashboard. - Startup profile. - Messaging. - Notifications. - Search and filtering. - Settings. Answer the following: 1. How would you divide the application into features? 2. Which components would be shared across features? 3. Which state would remain local, which would use Context, and which would use a server-state solution? 4. Where would you place API logic? 5. Sketch a folder structure that would still be maintainable after the project grows to hundreds of components and multiple developers. --- ## Coming Next Reply **Next** for **Lesson 11.2 — State Management Architecture: Local State vs Context vs Redux vs Zustand vs Server State**, where we'll cover one of the most common system design topics in React interviews: choosing the right place for different kinds of state and avoiding unnecessary complexity.

lessons.title: Lesson 11.2
lessons.objective: Learn local, global (Context/Zustand/Redux), and server (React Query) state management layouts.
lessons.content:
# Module 11 — Frontend System Design

# Lesson 11.2 — State Management Architecture: Local State vs Context vs Redux vs Zustand vs Server State

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the Most Frequently Asked React System Design Topics)

---

# 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters

One of the most common architecture questions is:

> **"Where would you store this piece of state?"**

This is a trickier question than it sounds.

Many developers immediately answer:

> "Redux."

Or:

> "Context."

Experienced frontend engineers first ask:

> **"What kind of state is this?"**

The choice of state management depends on **ownership, scope, update frequency, and the source of truth**.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Classify different types of state.
- Choose between local state, Context, Redux, Zustand, and server-state libraries.
- Explain your decisions in interviews.
- Avoid common state management mistakes.
- Design scalable state architecture.

---

# 1. What is State?

**State** is data that can change over time and influences what your UI displays or how it behaves.

Examples:

```text
Login Status

Shopping Cart

Theme

Search Query

Notifications

Selected Product

Current Page

Loading State

Error State
```

Not all state is the same.

Understanding the categories is the key to choosing the right tool.

---

# 2. The Five Major Types of State

Think of application state as falling into five broad categories.

```text
Application State
│
├── Local UI State
├── Shared Client State
├── Server State
├── URL State
└── Form State
```

We'll examine each one.

---

# 3. Local UI State

This is state used **only within a single component or a small group of closely related components**.

Examples:

- Is a modal open?
- Current tab.
- Dropdown visibility.
- Accordion expansion.
- Input value before submission.

```jsx
const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);
```

Visual:

```text
Modal

↓

isOpen

↓

Only Modal Uses It
```

### Best Tool

- `useState`
- `useReducer` (when logic becomes more complex)

---

### Interview Rule

> **Keep state as close as possible to where it is used.**

Don't move local state to a global store without a good reason.

---

# 4. Shared Client State

Sometimes multiple unrelated components need the same data.

Examples:

- Logged-in user.
- Theme.
- Language.
- Notification preferences.

Visual:

```text
Navbar

↓

User

↑

Sidebar

↑

Dashboard
```

This is shared client state.

Possible tools:

- Context API.
- Zustand.
- Redux Toolkit.

The best choice depends on complexity and update frequency.

---

# 5. Server State

Server state comes from an external source.

Examples:

```text
Products

Orders

Users

Messages

Comments

Invoices
```

Key characteristics:

- Fetched from an API.
- Can become stale.
- May need caching.
- Can be refetched.
- Can fail.
- Can be shared across screens.

Example:

```jsx
const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["products"],
    queryFn: fetchProducts
});
```

> This example uses **TanStack Query (formerly React Query)**.

---

### Why Server State is Different

Unlike local state:

```jsx
const [products, setProducts] = useState([]);
```

the **server** is the source of truth.

Your application only keeps a temporary copy.

---

### Best Tools

- **TanStack Query**
- **SWR**
- Framework-specific data fetching (depending on the framework)

Avoid storing large amounts of server state in Redux or Context unless you have a specific need.

---

# 6. URL State

Some state belongs in the URL.

Examples:

```text
?page=2

?sort=price

?search=laptop

?tab=reviews
```

Benefits:

- Shareable links.
- Browser back/forward works naturally.
- Refreshing the page preserves state.

Example:

```text
/products?page=3&category=phones
```

Instead of:

```jsx
const [page, setPage] = useState(3);
```

consider synchronizing it with the URL when appropriate.

---

# 7. Form State

Forms deserve their own category.

Examples:

- Name.
- Email.
- Password.
- Validation errors.
- Touched fields.
- Dirty state.

Large forms can become difficult to manage with many `useState` calls.

Popular libraries:

- React Hook Form.
- Formik.

These provide features such as validation, field registration, and better performance for complex forms.

---

# 8. Local State vs Context

Imagine:

```text
Search Input

↓

Search Results
```

Only these two components need the query.

Keep it local:

```jsx
const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
```

Now imagine:

```text
Navbar

Sidebar

Profile

Settings
```

All need the logged-in user.

Context becomes a good fit.

---

# 9. Context vs Redux Toolkit

## Context

Good for:

- Theme.
- Auth.
- Locale.
- Feature flags.

Not ideal for:

- Very frequently changing global state.
- Large, complex update logic.

---

## Redux Toolkit

Good for:

- Large applications.
- Predictable state transitions.
- Complex business rules.
- Time-travel debugging (with Redux DevTools).
- Rich middleware ecosystem.

Redux Toolkit reduces much of the boilerplate that older Redux versions required.

---

# 10. Context vs Zustand

Zustand is a lightweight state management library.

Example:

```jsx
const count = useStore(state => state.count);
```

Advantages:

- Minimal boilerplate.
- Fine-grained subscriptions.
- Easy to learn.
- Great for many medium-sized applications.

Many modern React teams choose Zustand when they want something simpler than Redux Toolkit.

---

# 11. Decision Tree

Ask these questions:

```text
Does only one component need it?

↓

Yes

↓

useState

---------------------

No

↓

Does it come from the server?

↓

Yes

↓

TanStack Query / SWR

---------------------

No

↓

Is it app-wide configuration?

↓

Yes

↓

Context

---------------------

No

↓

Complex shared business state?

↓

Redux Toolkit / Zustand
```

This isn't a rigid rule, but it's a useful starting point.

---

# 12. Common Mistakes

### Mistake 1

Putting everything in Redux.

Not every value needs global state.

---

### Mistake 2

Using Context for constantly changing data.

This can lead to unnecessary re-renders.

---

### Mistake 3

Duplicating server state.

Fetching products into TanStack Query and then copying them into Redux without a clear reason creates multiple sources of truth.

---

### Mistake 4

Making local state global.

Example:

```text
Dropdown Open

↓

Redux
```

This adds unnecessary complexity.

---

### Mistake 5

Using one giant Context.

```jsx
<AppContext>
```

containing theme, user, notifications, cart, filters, chat messages, etc.

Split concerns into focused contexts or stores.

---

# 13. Real-World Example

Imagine you're building an online marketplace.

State includes:

```text
Theme

Logged-in User

Shopping Cart

Product Catalog

Wishlist

Notifications

Search Query

Checkout Form

Current Page
```

A possible architecture:

| State | Recommended Tool | Why |
|--------|------------------|-----|
| Theme | Context | Shared, infrequently changes |
| Logged-in user | Context (or auth provider) | App-wide session |
| Product catalog | TanStack Query | Server is the source of truth |
| Wishlist | Zustand or Redux Toolkit | Shared client state with updates |
| Search query | Local state or URL | Depends on whether it should be shareable |
| Checkout form | React Hook Form | Complex form management |
| Notifications | Zustand/Redux or Context (depending on complexity) | Shared UI state |
| Current page | URL | Bookmarkable and shareable |

---

# Under the Hood

```text
User Clicks Button

↓

State Updates

↓

React Schedules Render

↓

Affected Components Re-render

↓

DOM Updates
```

The architecture determines **where** the state lives and **which components** need to react to changes.

---

# Interview Perspective

### What's the difference between client state and server state?

> Client state originates within the application (such as theme or modal state). Server state comes from an external system and requires fetching, caching, synchronization, and error handling.

---

### Why not store API responses in Redux?

> Modern server-state libraries already solve caching, deduplication, background refetching, retries, and stale data management. Duplicating that state often adds unnecessary complexity.

---

### When should you use Context?

> For app-wide values that don't change extremely frequently, such as authentication, theme, locale, or feature flags.

---

### When would you choose Zustand?

> When you need shared client state with a simple API and fine-grained subscriptions without the ceremony of Redux Toolkit.

---

### When would you choose Redux Toolkit?

> For large applications with complex business logic, predictable state transitions, middleware requirements, or teams already standardized on Redux.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

A modal's open/closed state is only used within one page.

Where should it live, and why?

---

## Medium

Design the state architecture for a blog application with:

- User authentication.
- Theme.
- Articles.
- Comments.
- Search.
- Pagination.

Explain your choices.

---

## Hard

You're building a fintech dashboard.

Requirements:

- Live account balances.
- Transactions.
- Authentication.
- User preferences.
- Notifications.
- Real-time stock prices.
- Multi-step transfer form.

For each piece of state:

1. Identify its type.
2. Choose the appropriate management solution.
3. Explain why.

---

# Time Complexity

State management choices don't inherently change algorithmic complexity. Their impact is on rendering behavior, synchronization, maintainability, and developer experience.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is local UI state?
2. What is shared client state?
3. What is server state?
4. What is URL state?
5. Why is form state often managed separately?
6. When is Context appropriate?
7. When is Redux Toolkit appropriate?
8. When is Zustand appropriate?
9. Why shouldn't you duplicate server state?
10. What does "keep state close to where it's used" mean?

---

## Coding

11. Refactor a global modal state into local component state.
12. Move theme management into Context.
13. Fetch products using TanStack Query.
14. Synchronize a search query with the URL.
15. Build a form using React Hook Form.

---

## Debugging

16. A developer stores every API response in Redux after fetching it with TanStack Query. What problems can this create?
17. A `ThemeContext` also stores chat messages that update every second. What performance concerns arise?
18. A component receives a `searchQuery` prop through five intermediate components. How would you redesign it?

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Local UI State
        ↓
useState
useReducer

-------------------------------------

Shared Client State
        ↓
Context
Zustand
Redux Toolkit

-------------------------------------

Server State
        ↓
TanStack Query
SWR

-------------------------------------

URL State
        ↓
Search Params
Route Params

-------------------------------------

Form State
        ↓
React Hook Form
Formik

-------------------------------------

Golden Rule
        ↓
Choose the Simplest Tool
That Solves the Problem
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Classify different types of state.
- ✅ Choose the right state management solution.
- ✅ Explain why server state is different from client state.
- ✅ Avoid making local state global unnecessarily.
- ✅ Justify your architectural decisions in an interview.
- ✅ Design scalable state management for a real application.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

You're designing **VentureMatch**, the startup-investor marketplace.

The application includes:

- Authentication.
- Founder profiles.
- Investor profiles.
- Startup listings.
- Search and filters.
- Saved startups.
- Messaging.
- Notifications.
- Theme.
- Multi-step startup application form.
- Analytics dashboard.

For each feature:

1. Classify the state (local, shared client, server, URL, or form).
2. Choose the most appropriate management solution.
3. Explain why.
4. Identify where you would avoid global state.
5. Sketch a high-level state architecture showing how these pieces fit together.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 11.3 — API Layer Design, Data Fetching Architecture, Error Handling, Caching, and Request Management**, where you'll learn how senior frontend engineers structure API communication, organize services, handle retries and errors, and design maintainable data-fetching layers for large applications.

options: Client state is local UI state (e.g. open/closed); server state resides on the database and needs fetching.
Server state is stored in client cookies.
Client state has no memory footprint.
Server state is faster to update.
questions.explanation: Client state covers ephemeral local UI values. Server state represents remote data owned by databases, requiring async fetch, sync, and cache strategies.

questions.questionText: Which are valid state management libraries or tools? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Redux Toolkit, Zustand, Context, and React Query are all widely used state management solutions in modern React.

questions.questionText: What is the term for lifting state up to the closest common ancestor so multiple sibling components can share it?
questions.explanation: Lifting state up hoists variables to share data between siblings.

lessons.objective: Master network API layers isolation, fetch instances setup, centralized error handles, and request deduplication.
lessons.content:
# Module 11 — Frontend System Design

# Lesson 11.3 — API Layer Design, Data Fetching Architecture, Error Handling, Caching & Request Management

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced)
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely Common for Mid-Level & Senior Frontend Interviews)

---

# 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters

Junior developers often write API calls like this:

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
    fetch("/api/users")
        .then(res => res.json())
        .then(data => setUsers(data));
}, []);
```

It works.

But imagine your application has:

- 200 API endpoints.
- Authentication.
- Token refresh.
- File uploads.
- Pagination.
- Retries.
- Offline support.
- Request cancellation.
- Caching.
- Error handling.

Copying `fetch()` everywhere quickly becomes difficult to maintain.

Senior frontend engineers design an **API layer**, not just API calls.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Design a scalable API layer.
- Separate UI from networking.
- Organize services.
- Handle authentication.
- Manage errors consistently.
- Cancel requests.
- Implement caching strategies.
- Explain data-fetching architecture in interviews.

---

# 1. The Problem

Imagine this code appears in 30 components:

```jsx
fetch("/api/users")
```

Then the backend changes:

```
/api/v2/users
```

Now you must update 30 files.

This is a maintenance problem.

---

# Better Architecture

Instead of:

```text
Component

↓

fetch()

↓

API
```

Use:

```text
Component

↓

Hook

↓

Service

↓

HTTP Client

↓

API
```

Each layer has a responsibility.

---

# 2. Layers Explained

```text
UI

↓

Custom Hook

↓

Service

↓

HTTP Client

↓

Backend
```

---

## UI Layer

Responsible for:

- Rendering.
- User interaction.
- Displaying loading and errors.

Example:

```jsx
function UsersPage() {
    const { users } = useUsers();
}
```

No networking logic here.

---

## Custom Hook

Responsible for:

- Calling the service.
- Managing loading.
- Managing errors.
- Returning state.

Example:

```jsx
const { users, loading } = useUsers();
```

---

## Service Layer

Responsible for business-specific API operations.

Example:

```jsx
userService.getUsers();
```

or

```jsx
userService.updateProfile();
```

The service knows which endpoint to call.

---

## HTTP Client

Responsible for:

- Base URL.
- Authentication headers.
- Interceptors or middleware.
- Request configuration.
- Response normalization.

Often built using `fetch` wrappers or libraries like **Axios**.

---

# Visual

```text
UsersPage

↓

useUsers()

↓

userService.getUsers()

↓

apiClient.get()

↓

Backend
```

---

# 3. Example Folder Structure

```text
src/
│
├── api/
│   ├── client.js
│   ├── endpoints.js
│   └── interceptors.js
│
├── services/
│   ├── user.service.js
│   ├── auth.service.js
│   └── startup.service.js
│
├── hooks/
│   ├── useUsers.js
│   └── useProfile.js
│
└── features/
```

This scales much better than scattering `fetch()` calls throughout the application.

---

# 4. HTTP Client

Instead of:

```jsx
fetch(...)
```

everywhere,

create one client.

Example:

```jsx
const apiClient = axios.create({
    baseURL: "/api"
});
```

Benefits:

- One place for configuration.
- One place for headers.
- One place for authentication.
- One place for interceptors.
- One place for logging.

---

# 5. Service Layer

Example:

```jsx
export async function getUsers() {
    return apiClient.get("/users");
}
```

Instead of:

```jsx
fetch("/users")
```

inside components.

Benefits:

- Easier testing.
- Easier reuse.
- Cleaner UI.

---

# 6. Custom Hook Layer

Example:

```jsx
function useUsers() {
    return useQuery({
        queryKey: ["users"],
        queryFn: getUsers
    });
}
```

Now components only use:

```jsx
const { data } = useUsers();
```

The component doesn't need to know how data is fetched.

---

# 7. Authentication

Most APIs require a token.

Bad:

```jsx
fetch("/users", {
    headers: {
        Authorization:
            "Bearer " + token
    }
});
```

Repeated everywhere.

Better:

```text
HTTP Client

↓

Automatically Adds Token
```

Every request gets the token without repeating code.

---

# 8. Token Refresh

Imagine:

```text
Request

↓

401 Unauthorized
```

Instead of logging the user out immediately:

```text
401

↓

Refresh Token

↓

Retry Original Request
```

This logic belongs in the HTTP client, not in every component.

---

# 9. Error Handling

Bad:

```jsx
try {
    ...
}
catch {
}
```

Repeated in every component.

Better:

```text
HTTP Client

↓

Normalizes Errors

↓

Components Display Friendly Messages
```

For example:

```text
Network Error

↓

"No internet connection."
```

or

```text
500

↓

"Something went wrong."
```

---

# 10. Request Cancellation

Suppose the user types:

```text
a

↓

Request
```

Before it finishes:

```text
ab

↓

Request
```

Then:

```text
abc

↓

Request
```

Without cancellation:

All three requests may complete, and an older response could overwrite a newer one.

Modern `fetch` supports `AbortController`:

```jsx
const controller = new AbortController();

fetch(url, {
    signal: controller.signal
});
```

Cleanup:

```jsx
controller.abort();
```

Libraries like TanStack Query also support request cancellation patterns.

---

# 11. Loading States

Never do this:

```jsx
users && users.map(...)
```

without handling loading.

Instead:

```text
Loading

↓

Spinner

↓

Success

↓

Render Data

↓

Error

↓

Error UI
```

Always consider:

- Loading.
- Success.
- Error.
- Empty state.

---

# 12. Empty States

Example:

```text
No Products Found
```

is better than a blank page.

Design explicitly for:

- No search results.
- Empty cart.
- No notifications.

---

# 13. Caching

Without caching:

```text
Open Page

↓

GET /users

↓

Back

↓

Open Again

↓

GET /users
```

Many unnecessary requests.

With caching:

```text
GET /users

↓

Cache

↓

Reuse Cached Data
```

Server-state libraries make this straightforward.

---

# 14. Retry Strategy

Network requests fail.

Good libraries allow automatic retries.

Example:

```text
Request

↓

Fail

↓

Retry

↓

Success
```

Be careful not to retry requests that are unlikely to succeed, such as certain client errors (for example, many `4xx` responses).

---

# 15. Optimistic Updates

Example:

User likes a post.

Instead of:

```text
Click

↓

Wait

↓

Server Responds

↓

Update UI
```

Use:

```text
Click

↓

Update UI Immediately

↓

Send Request

↓

Success ✓
```

If it fails:

```text
Rollback
```

This makes applications feel much faster.

---

# 16. Pagination

Avoid:

```text
GET /products
```

returning 1 million records.

Use:

```text
GET /products?page=1&limit=20
```

or cursor-based pagination for large datasets.

---

# 17. Infinite Scroll

Pattern:

```text
Page 1

↓

Page 2

↓

Page 3

↓

Load More
```

Many server-state libraries provide utilities for infinite queries.

---

# 18. Common Mistakes

### Mistake 1

Calling `fetch()` directly in every component.

---

### Mistake 2

Duplicating API endpoints across the application.

---

### Mistake 3

Mixing rendering and networking logic.

---

### Mistake 4

Ignoring loading states.

---

### Mistake 5

Ignoring error states.

---

### Mistake 6

Not cancelling outdated requests when appropriate.

---

# Under the Hood

```text
User Clicks

↓

Custom Hook

↓

Service

↓

HTTP Client

↓

Backend

↓

Response

↓

Cache

↓

Component Re-renders
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### Why use a service layer?

> It centralizes API operations, avoids duplication, improves testability, and keeps components focused on rendering.

---

### Why create an HTTP client?

> To configure shared behavior such as base URLs, authentication, headers, logging, retries, and interceptors in one place.

---

### Why use Custom Hooks for data fetching?

> They encapsulate fetching logic, loading, errors, and caching behind a reusable API.

---

### What is optimistic updating?

> Updating the UI before the server confirms the change, then rolling back if the request fails.

---

### Why cancel requests?

> To avoid race conditions, unnecessary work, and updating the UI with stale responses.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Create a reusable `userService.getUsers()` function and use it from a component.

---

## Medium

Build a `useUsers()` hook that returns:

- `data`
- `loading`
- `error`

using a service function.

---

## Hard

Design the API layer for **VentureMatch**.

Requirements:

- Authentication.
- Startup CRUD.
- Investor search.
- Messaging.
- Notifications.
- File uploads.
- Analytics.

Explain:

1. Folder structure.
2. Services.
3. Hooks.
4. HTTP client responsibilities.
5. Error handling strategy.
6. Caching approach.
7. Authentication flow.

---

# Time Complexity

Most API operations are dominated by **network latency**, not CPU complexity. Architectural decisions improve maintainability, reduce redundant requests, and provide a better user experience rather than changing Big-O complexity.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is an API layer?
2. Why shouldn't components call `fetch()` directly everywhere?
3. What belongs in a service layer?
4. What belongs in an HTTP client?
5. Why use Custom Hooks for fetching?
6. Why centralize authentication?
7. What is optimistic updating?
8. Why cache server data?
9. Why cancel requests?
10. Why design loading and empty states?

---

## Coding

11. Build a reusable HTTP client.
12. Create a `userService`.
13. Create a `useUsers` hook.
14. Handle loading, error, success, and empty states.
15. Add request cancellation to a search feature.

---

## Debugging

16. Why is repeating `fetch("/users")` across many components a maintenance problem?
17. Why can search results appear out of order if previous requests aren't cancelled?
18. Why shouldn't authentication headers be manually added in every API request?

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
UI
    ↓
Custom Hook
    ↓
Service
    ↓
HTTP Client
    ↓
Backend

-------------------------

HTTP Client
    ↓
Base URL
Headers
Auth
Interceptors
Retries

-------------------------

Service
    ↓
Business API Functions

-------------------------

Custom Hook
    ↓
Loading
Error
Caching
Data

-------------------------

Best Practices
    ↓
Cancel Requests
Handle Errors
Cache Data
Optimistic Updates
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Design a layered API architecture.
- ✅ Explain the responsibilities of the UI, Custom Hooks, Services, and HTTP Client.
- ✅ Centralize authentication and error handling.
- ✅ Handle loading, empty, and error states gracefully.
- ✅ Explain request cancellation and optimistic updates.
- ✅ Design an API layer that scales to a large application.

---

# Mini Interview Challenge

You're building **VentureMatch**, a platform where founders connect with investors.

Features:

- Login and token refresh.
- Startup profiles.
- Investor search.
- Messaging.
- Notifications.
- Document uploads.
- Dashboard analytics.
- Saved startups.

Design an API architecture by answering:

1. How would you organize the `api/`, `services/`, and `hooks/` folders?
2. Which responsibilities belong in the HTTP client?
3. Which data would you cache, and for how long?
4. Which operations would benefit from optimistic updates?
5. How would you prevent duplicate API calls and stale search results?

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 11.4 — Frontend Performance Architecture: Rendering Performance, Code Splitting, Lazy Loading, Virtualization, Bundle Optimization & Real-World Performance Strategies**, where you'll learn how senior engineers optimize large React applications for speed and scalability.

questions.questionText: Why isolate the API layer from UI components?
options: To separate networking logic, enable easy mocking, and make code modular
To run requests on server threads
questions.explanation: Separating the API layer from views keeps components clean, makes network logic reusable, and facilitates testing with mocks.

questions.questionText: Which are best practices in API layer design? (Select all that apply)
options: Axios or fetch instances with baseURL set
Fetching directly inside components using raw URLs
questions.explanation: Centralized configs, interceptors, and mock adapters are best practices. Writing raw URLs inside views causes duplication and is hard to test.

questions.questionText: What term describes merging multiple separate network requests into a single request, or limiting duplicate requests?
questions.explanation: Deduplication prevents sending duplicate requests for the same resource concurrently.

lessons.objective: Learn frontend rendering optimizations: code splitting, lazy loading, Suspense, and viewport virtualization.
lessons.content:
# Module 11 — Frontend System Design # Lesson 11.4 — Frontend Performance Architecture: Rendering Performance, Code Splitting, Lazy Loading, Virtualization, Bundle Optimization & Real-World Performance Strategies > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced) > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely Common for Mid-Level & Senior Frontend Interviews) --- # 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters One of the most common senior frontend interview questions is: > **"Your React application has become slow. How would you investigate and improve its performance?"** Interviewers are **not** looking for you to immediately answer: > "Use `useMemo`." Instead, they want to know if you can: - Identify the bottleneck. - Measure before optimizing. - Apply the right optimization technique. - Avoid premature optimization. Performance is about **systematic problem-solving**, not memorizing hooks. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Understand why React apps become slow. - Optimize rendering. - Reduce unnecessary re-renders. - Split bundles. - Lazy load components. - Virtualize large lists. - Optimize assets. - Measure performance with the right tools. - Explain performance strategies in interviews. --- # 1. What Makes a React App Slow? Performance problems usually come from one (or more) of these areas: ```text Slow App │ ├── Too many re-renders ├── Large JavaScript bundle ├── Expensive calculations ├── Too many API requests ├── Large DOM trees ├── Large images ├── Inefficient rendering ├── Memory leaks └── Unnecessary network requests ``` The first step is identifying **which** one is causing the issue. --- # 2. Measure Before You Optimize A common mistake is optimizing without evidence. Use tools like: - **React DevTools Profiler** (to see which components re-render and how long they take). - Browser Performance panel. - Lighthouse. - Web Vitals. > **Interview Tip:** A strong answer starts with "I would profile the application first." --- # 3. Understanding Re-renders Whenever state or props change, React re-renders components that depend on them. Example: ```jsx function App() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( <>
); } ``` When `count` changes: ```text App │ ├── Counter ✅ └── Footer (may also re-render because App rendered) ``` Even if `Footer` doesn't use `count`, it may still render because its parent rendered. --- # 4. Preventing Unnecessary Re-renders React provides several tools: - `React.memo` - `useMemo` - `useCallback` ### `React.memo` ```jsx const Footer = React.memo(function Footer() { return
Footer
; }); ``` If its props don't change, React can skip re-rendering it. --- ### `useMemo` Memoizes expensive computed values. ```jsx const sortedUsers = useMemo(() => { return users.sort(compareUsers); }, [users]); ``` --- ### `useCallback` Memoizes function references. ```jsx const handleClick = useCallback(() => { saveUser(); }, []); ``` Useful when passing callbacks to memoized child components. --- # ⚠️ Important Don't wrap **everything** in `useMemo` or `useCallback`. These hooks have their own cost. Use them **only when profiling shows a benefit** or when stabilizing references for memoized children. --- # 5. Code Splitting Without code splitting: ```text App Loads ↓ 2 MB JavaScript ↓ User Waits ``` The browser downloads everything before the app becomes interactive. --- ### With Code Splitting ```text Home Page ↓ Downloads Home Code ↓ User Opens Dashboard ↓ Downloads Dashboard Code ``` Users only download what they need. --- ### Using `React.lazy` ```jsx const Dashboard = React.lazy(() => import("./Dashboard")); ``` Wrap it with `Suspense`: ```jsx }> ``` --- # 6. Route-Based Code Splitting Large applications often split code by route. ```text / ↓ Home Bundle ---------------- /dashboard ↓ Dashboard Bundle ---------------- /settings ↓ Settings Bundle ``` This keeps the initial download much smaller. --- # 7. Lazy Loading Images Don't load every image immediately. Use browser-native lazy loading: ```html ``` Images load only when they are close to entering the viewport. --- # 8. Virtualization Imagine rendering: ```text 100,000 Products ``` Rendering every row is expensive. Instead, render only what's visible. ```text Viewport │ ├── Row 50 ├── Row 51 ├── Row 52 ├── Row 53 └── Row 54 ``` As the user scrolls: ```text Rows Removed ↓ New Rows Added ``` Libraries such as **react-window** and **react-virtualized** implement this pattern. --- # 9. Bundle Optimization Large bundles increase load time. Common ways to reduce bundle size: - Remove unused dependencies. - Prefer tree-shakeable libraries. - Use dynamic imports. - Compress assets (Gzip/Brotli on the server). - Avoid importing entire utility libraries when only one function is needed. Example: Instead of importing an entire library, import only what you need (when the library supports it). --- # 10. Optimize API Requests Avoid: ```text Page Loads ↓ 10 Duplicate Requests ``` Better: - Cache responses. - Deduplicate requests. - Debounce search. - Batch requests where appropriate. --- # 11. Debouncing Search Without debounce: ```text a ↓ Request ab ↓ Request abc ↓ Request ``` With debounce: ```text Typing... ↓ Pause ↓ One Request ``` Fewer requests, better UX, less server load. --- # 12. Infinite Scroll vs Pagination ### Pagination ```text Page 1 ↓ Page 2 ↓ Page 3 ``` Better for: - Search engines. - Predictable navigation. - Jumping to specific pages. --- ### Infinite Scroll ```text Scroll ↓ Load More ↓ Scroll ↓ Load More ``` Better for: - Social media feeds. - Content discovery. Choose based on the user experience, not because one is always "better." --- # 13. Memory Leaks A common cause: ```jsx useEffect(() => { window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize); }, []); ``` The listener is never removed. Correct: ```jsx useEffect(() => { window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize); return () => { window.removeEventListener("resize", handleResize); }; }, []); ``` Always clean up subscriptions, timers, and listeners. --- # 14. Performance Checklist When a page is slow, ask: 1. Is the component re-rendering too often? 2. Is there an expensive calculation? 3. Is the bundle too large? 4. Are images optimized? 5. Are too many DOM nodes rendered? 6. Are there unnecessary API requests? 7. Is virtualization needed? 8. Are event listeners cleaned up? 9. Are there memory leaks? 10. Have I measured the issue? --- # 15. Real-World Example Imagine you're building **VentureMatch**. Dashboard: - Charts. - Notifications. - Startup list. - Investor list. - Analytics. - Messages. Performance improvements: - Lazy load charts. - Virtualize long lists. - Cache API responses. - Split bundles by route. - Memoize expensive chart calculations. - Debounce search. - Optimize images. --- # Common Mistakes ### Mistake 1 Using `useMemo` everywhere. --- ### Mistake 2 Rendering thousands of DOM nodes at once. --- ### Mistake 3 Ignoring bundle size. --- ### Mistake 4 Loading every route on startup. --- ### Mistake 5 Ignoring memory leaks. --- ### Mistake 6 Optimizing without measuring. --- # Under the Hood ```text User Action ↓ State Changes ↓ React Schedules Update ↓ Reconciliation ↓ Diffing ↓ DOM Updates ↓ Browser Paint ``` Performance optimization focuses on reducing unnecessary work at each stage. --- # Interview Perspective ### How do you investigate a slow React app? > I start by profiling the application with React DevTools Profiler and browser performance tools to identify the bottleneck before making optimizations. --- ### When should you use `React.memo`? > When a component re-renders frequently with unchanged props and profiling shows it's worth memoizing. --- ### What is code splitting? > Splitting JavaScript into smaller bundles so users download only the code they need. --- ### Why virtualize lists? > Rendering only visible items dramatically reduces DOM size and rendering work for large datasets. --- ### Why is premature optimization harmful? > It adds complexity and can even hurt performance without solving a real problem. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Implement route-based lazy loading using `React.lazy` and `Suspense`. --- ## Medium Build a searchable list with a debounced search input. --- ## Hard A dashboard becomes sluggish when displaying 50,000 transactions. Explain: 1. How you would diagnose the issue. 2. Which optimizations you would apply. 3. Which tools you would use. 4. Whether virtualization is appropriate. 5. Whether memoization would help. --- # Time Complexity | Technique | Effect | |-----------|--------| | Virtualization | Reduces rendering work from thousands of visible DOM nodes to only those in the viewport | | Memoization | Avoids repeating expensive computations when dependencies haven't changed | | Code Splitting | Reduces initial download size (not algorithmic complexity) | | Debouncing | Reduces the number of function calls and network requests | --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. What causes unnecessary re-renders? 2. Why should you measure before optimizing? 3. What is `React.memo`? 4. When should `useMemo` be used? 5. When should `useCallback` be used? 6. What is code splitting? 7. What is virtualization? 8. Why debounce search? 9. What causes memory leaks? 10. Why is bundle size important? --- ## Coding 11. Lazy load a dashboard page. 12. Build a virtualized product list. 13. Implement a debounced search input. 14. Memoize an expensive calculation. 15. Clean up an event listener inside `useEffect`. --- ## Debugging 16. A component re-renders hundreds of times. How would you investigate? 17. A page displays 100,000 table rows and freezes the browser. What architectural changes would you make? 18. The application downloads every route on the first page load. How would you improve it? --- # Interview Cheatsheet ```text Performance Strategy ↓ Measure First ------------------------------------- Rendering ↓ React.memo useMemo useCallback ------------------------------------- Bundle ↓ Code Splitting Lazy Loading ------------------------------------- Large Lists ↓ Virtualization ------------------------------------- Networking ↓ Caching Debounce Request Deduplication ------------------------------------- Always ↓ Profile Before Optimizing ``` --- # Mastery Checklist Before moving on, make sure you can: - ✅ Explain common React performance bottlenecks. - ✅ Use `React.memo`, `useMemo`, and `useCallback` appropriately. - ✅ Implement route-based code splitting. - ✅ Explain virtualization. - ✅ Optimize bundles and API requests. - ✅ Diagnose performance problems using profiling tools. - ✅ Avoid premature optimization. --- # Mini Interview Challenge You're optimizing the **VentureMatch** dashboard. Problems: - Initial load takes 8 seconds. - The startup table contains 80,000 rows. - Search sends a request on every keypress. - Charts are slow to render. - Users report memory usage increases after long sessions. - Every route is bundled into the first page load. For each issue: 1. Identify the likely bottleneck. 2. Explain how you would verify it. 3. Choose the most appropriate optimization. 4. Explain the trade-offs. 5. Describe how you would confirm that your optimization actually improved performance. --- ## Coming Next Reply **Next** for **Lesson 11.5 — Frontend Security & Accessibility: XSS, CSRF, Authentication, Secure Storage, OWASP Principles, ARIA, Keyboard Navigation, and Building Accessible React Applications**, the final lesson of Module 11 and another area frequently covered in senior frontend interviews.

questions.questionText: What does virtualization do for large list rendering?
options: Renders only the elements currently visible in the viewport
Runs list sorting on background threads
questions.explanation: Virtualization keeps the DOM small and fast by only rendering elements in or near the viewport, swapping others out dynamically.

questions.questionText: Which of the following optimize bundle size? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Code splitting, tree shaking, and compression optimize bundle and asset size. Virtualization optimizes rendering performance, not bundle size.

questions.questionText: What component does React use along with `React.lazy` to show a fallback loader while a component loads dynamically?
questions.explanation: `<Suspense fallback={...}>` holds dynamic components while they load.

lessons.title: Lesson 11.5
lessons.objective: Understand security guidelines (XSS, CSRF) and accessibility ARIA standards inside React.
lessons.content:
# Module 11 — Frontend System Design # Lesson 11.5 — Frontend Security & Accessibility: XSS, CSRF, Authentication, Secure Storage, OWASP Principles, ARIA, Keyboard Navigation & Building Accessible React Applications > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Advanced) > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Very Common for Mid-Level & Senior Frontend Interviews) --- # 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters Many frontend developers believe: > **"Security is the backend developer's responsibility."** Or: > **"Accessibility is just adding `alt` text."** Neither is true. Frontend developers are responsible for: - Preventing common client-side attacks. - Handling authentication safely. - Protecting sensitive user data. - Building interfaces that everyone can use, including people using assistive technologies. Senior interviews often include questions on both security and accessibility because they directly impact real users. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Understand common frontend security threats. - Explain XSS and CSRF. - Handle authentication securely. - Store tokens appropriately. - Understand basic OWASP principles. - Build accessible React applications. - Use semantic HTML and ARIA correctly. - Explain accessibility decisions in interviews. --- # 1. What is Frontend Security? Frontend security focuses on protecting users and reducing the risk of attacks that target the browser. Common threats include: ```text XSS CSRF Clickjacking Sensitive Data Exposure Insecure Authentication Unsafe Third-Party Scripts ``` Frontend security is about reducing risk—not replacing backend security. --- # 2. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) XSS happens when an attacker injects malicious JavaScript that runs in another user's browser. Example: A comment field accepts: ```html ``` If your application renders that as HTML, the script executes. --- ## React's Protection React escapes values by default. ```jsx

{userComment}

``` If `userComment` contains HTML, React renders it as text rather than executing it. --- ## Dangerous API ```jsx
``` This bypasses React's escaping. Only use it with **trusted or sanitized** HTML. --- # 3. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Imagine: 1. User logs into your banking site. 2. Their browser stores a session cookie. 3. They visit a malicious website. 4. That site submits a request to your bank. If protections aren't in place, the browser may automatically send the session cookie. --- ## Common Defenses - CSRF tokens. - SameSite cookies. - Server-side origin validation. These protections are primarily implemented on the server, but frontend developers should understand how they work. --- # 4. Authentication Typical flow: ```text User Logs In ↓ Server Validates Credentials ↓ Server Returns Token or Session ↓ Frontend Stores It ↓ Authenticated Requests ``` The frontend is responsible for handling authentication data carefully. --- # 5. Where Should Tokens Be Stored? ### Option 1: Memory Pros: - Harder for injected scripts to persistently steal after refresh. - Cleared when the page reloads. Cons: - User must authenticate again after a refresh unless another mechanism restores the session. --- ### Option 2: `localStorage` Pros: - Persists across page reloads. Cons: - If an XSS vulnerability exists, JavaScript can read it. --- ### Option 3: `sessionStorage` Pros: - Cleared when the browser tab closes. Cons: - Also accessible to JavaScript if XSS occurs. --- ### Option 4: HTTP-only Cookies Pros: - JavaScript cannot read them. - Often preferred for session cookies. Cons: - Require CSRF protections when applicable. There is no one-size-fits-all answer. The best approach depends on your application's architecture and security requirements. --- # 6. Never Trust User Input Never assume user input is safe. Validate: - On the frontend (for user experience). - On the backend (for security). The backend remains the ultimate source of truth. --- # 7. Sensitive Data Never expose: - API secrets. - Database passwords. - Private keys. Environment variables bundled into frontend code are visible to users if included in the client bundle. Only expose values intended for the client. --- # 8. HTTPS Always use HTTPS in production. Benefits: - Encrypts traffic. - Protects credentials in transit. - Helps prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. --- # 9. Content Security Policy (CSP) A **Content Security Policy** restricts which resources the browser is allowed to load and execute. It can help reduce the impact of XSS by limiting inline scripts and untrusted sources. This is usually configured by the server. --- # 10. OWASP Top Risks (High Level) Some common web security risks include: - Broken access control. - Cryptographic failures. - Injection attacks. - Security misconfiguration. - Vulnerable components. You don't need to memorize the full list for most frontend interviews, but you should recognize these categories. --- # 11. What is Accessibility (a11y)? Accessibility means building applications that can be used by people with: - Visual impairments. - Hearing impairments. - Motor impairments. - Cognitive impairments. Accessibility also improves usability for everyone. --- # 12. Semantic HTML Prefer semantic elements. Good: ```html ``` Instead of: ```html
Save
``` Native elements provide keyboard support and accessibility features by default. --- # 13. Images Decorative images may use an empty `alt=""`. Informative images should have meaningful `alt` text. Example: ```html ``` --- # 14. Labels Every form control should have an associated label. ```jsx ``` This improves usability and screen-reader support. --- # 15. Keyboard Navigation Users should be able to navigate using: - Tab. - Shift + Tab. - Enter. - Space. - Arrow keys (where appropriate). Avoid building interfaces that only work with a mouse. --- # 16. Focus Management When opening a modal: - Move focus into the modal. - Keep keyboard focus inside while it's open (focus trap). - Return focus to the triggering element when it closes. Proper focus management improves accessibility. --- # 17. ARIA **ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)** provides additional information to assistive technologies when native HTML is insufficient. Example: ```html ``` Use ARIA to enhance accessibility—not to replace semantic HTML. --- # 18. Color Contrast Avoid combinations like: ```text Light Gray Text On White Background ``` Ensure sufficient contrast so text remains readable for users with low vision. --- # 19. Error Messages Instead of: ```text Invalid. ``` Use: ```text Email address is required. ``` Helpful, specific error messages improve both accessibility and usability. --- # 20. Screen Readers Screen readers interpret the accessibility tree—not the visual layout. A page with proper headings, labels, landmarks, and semantic elements is much easier to navigate. --- # 21. Common Mistakes ### Mistake 1 Using `
` for buttons. --- ### Mistake 2 Relying on color alone to convey meaning. Example: ```text Red = Error Green = Success ``` Also include text or icons. --- ### Mistake 3 Missing form labels. --- ### Mistake 4 Using `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with untrusted content. --- ### Mistake 5 Storing secrets in frontend code. --- ### Mistake 6 Ignoring keyboard users. --- # Under the Hood ```text User ↓ Browser ↓ React ↓ DOM ↓ Accessibility Tree ↓ Screen Reader ``` Security and accessibility influence how the browser interprets and exposes your application. --- # Interview Perspective ### What is XSS? > An attack where malicious JavaScript is injected into a webpage and executed in another user's browser. --- ### How does React help prevent XSS? > React escapes rendered values by default, preventing injected HTML from being interpreted as executable code. --- ### What is CSRF? > An attack that tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended requests to a trusted site. --- ### Why use semantic HTML? > It provides built-in accessibility, better keyboard support, and clearer meaning for browsers and assistive technologies. --- ### What is ARIA? > A set of attributes that improve accessibility when native HTML alone isn't sufficient. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Create an accessible login form with proper labels and validation messages. --- ## Medium Build a modal that: - Traps keyboard focus. - Closes with the Escape key. - Restores focus when closed. --- ## Hard You're reviewing a React application that has the following issues: - Tokens stored in `localStorage`. - User-generated HTML rendered with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. - Every button is a clickable `
`. - Forms have placeholders but no labels. - The app cannot be used with a keyboard. Identify: 1. The security risks. 2. The accessibility issues. 3. How you would fix each one. 4. Any trade-offs involved. --- # Time Complexity Security and accessibility practices generally do not affect algorithmic complexity. Their impact is on safety, usability, maintainability, and compliance. --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. What is XSS? 2. How does React reduce XSS risk? 3. What is CSRF? 4. Why is `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` risky? 5. Why shouldn't secrets be stored in frontend code? 6. Why use semantic HTML? 7. What is ARIA? 8. Why are labels important? 9. Why is keyboard navigation necessary? 10. Why is HTTPS important? --- ## Coding 11. Build an accessible form. 12. Create a keyboard-accessible dropdown. 13. Implement a modal with focus management. 14. Sanitize trusted HTML before rendering it. 15. Replace non-semantic clickable elements with proper HTML elements. --- ## Debugging 16. Why is rendering unsanitized HTML dangerous? 17. Why can't some users interact with an application built entirely from clickable `
` elements? 18. Why is relying only on placeholder text a poor replacement for labels? --- # Interview Cheatsheet ```text Security ↓ XSS CSRF HTTPS CSP Safe Authentication ------------------------------------- React ↓ Escapes Values By Default ------------------------------------- Accessibility ↓ Semantic HTML Labels Keyboard Navigation Focus Management ARIA ------------------------------------- Golden Rule ↓ Build Secure, Accessible, Usable Interfaces ``` --- # Mastery Checklist Before moving on, make sure you can: - ✅ Explain XSS and how React helps mitigate it. - ✅ Explain CSRF at a high level. - ✅ Compare common client-side token storage options. - ✅ Build accessible forms and interactive components. - ✅ Use semantic HTML before reaching for ARIA. - ✅ Design applications that work with keyboard navigation and assistive technologies. - ✅ Recognize common frontend security and accessibility mistakes. --- # 🎉 Module 11 Complete! You've now completed **Frontend System Design**, including: - ✅ Component Architecture - ✅ State Management Architecture - ✅ API Layer Design - ✅ Performance Architecture - ✅ Frontend Security & Accessibility These are the topics that distinguish **mid-level and senior frontend engineers** in technical interviews. --- # Coming Next Reply **Next** to begin **Module 12 — JavaScript & React Interview Challenges**, where you'll solve progressively harder real-world interview questions, live coding problems, debugging exercises, and complete system design scenarios that combine everything you've learned so far. This module is designed to simulate actual technical interviews from companies ranging from startups to large tech organizations.

lessons.content:
# Module 12 — JavaScript & React Interview Challenges

# Lesson 12.1 — JavaScript Interview Challenge I: Variables, Scope, Hoisting, Closures & Execution Context

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Asked in almost every JavaScript interview)

---

# 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters

By now, you know the theory behind:

- Variables
- Scope
- Hoisting
- Closures
- Execution Context
- `this`
- Functions

But interviews rarely ask:

> "What is hoisting?"

Instead, they show you code and ask:

> **"What will this print?"**

or

> **"Why does this happen?"**

This lesson simulates those interview questions.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Trace JavaScript execution.
- Predict outputs without running code.
- Explain hoisting confidently.
- Understand closure behavior.
- Identify scope issues.
- Answer common interview questions.

---

# Challenge 1 — Hoisting

What is the output?

```javascript
console.log(a);

var a = 10;
```

### Think First...

⬇️

### Answer

```text
undefined
```

### Why?

During the creation phase:

```javascript
var a = undefined;
```

Execution phase:

```javascript
console.log(a); // undefined

a = 10;
```

---

# Challenge 2 — `let`

```javascript
console.log(age);

let age = 25;
```

### Output

```text
ReferenceError
```

### Why?

`let` is hoisted but remains in the **Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)** until initialization.

---

# Challenge 3 — Function Declaration

```javascript
greet();

function greet() {
    console.log("Hello");
}
```

### Output

```text
Hello
```

### Why?

Function declarations are fully hoisted with their implementation.

---

# Challenge 4 — Function Expression

```javascript
greet();

var greet = function () {
    console.log("Hello");
};
```

### Output

```text
TypeError: greet is not a function
```

### Why?

Creation phase:

```javascript
var greet = undefined;
```

Execution:

```javascript
greet();
```

becomes:

```javascript
undefined();
```

which throws a `TypeError`.

---

# Challenge 5 — Scope

```javascript
let x = 5;

function test() {
    let x = 10;
    console.log(x);
}

test();

console.log(x);
```

### Output

```text
10
5
```

### Why?

The inner `x` shadows the outer `x`.

---

# Challenge 6 — Closures

```javascript
function outer() {
    let count = 0;

    return function () {
        count++;
        console.log(count);
    };
}

const counter = outer();

counter();
counter();
counter();
```

### Output

```text
1
2
3
```

### Why?

The inner function closes over `count`, preserving it between calls.

---

# Challenge 7 — Loop with `var`

```javascript
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => {
        console.log(i);
    }, 100);
}
```

### Output

```text
3
3
3
```

### Why?

`var` is function-scoped. By the time the callbacks execute, the loop has finished and `i` equals `3`.

---

# Challenge 8 — Loop with `let`

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => {
        console.log(i);
    }, 100);
}
```

### Output

```text
0
1
2
```

### Why?

`let` creates a new binding for `i` on each iteration.

---

# Challenge 9 — Nested Scope

```javascript
let a = 1;

function one() {
    let b = 2;

    function two() {
        let c = 3;
        console.log(a, b, c);
    }

    two();
}

one();
```

### Output

```text
1 2 3
```

### Why?

The scope chain allows `two()` to access variables from its own scope and all outer lexical scopes.

---

# Challenge 10 — Shadowing

```javascript
let name = "John";

function greet() {
    let name = "Jane";
    console.log(name);
}

greet();

console.log(name);
```

### Output

```text
Jane
John
```

### Why?

The inner variable shadows the outer variable.

---

# Challenge 11 — Block Scope

```javascript
{
    let x = 10;
}

console.log(x);
```

### Output

```text
ReferenceError
```

### Why?

`let` is block-scoped, so `x` only exists inside the block.

---

# Challenge 12 — `var` Block Scope

```javascript
{
    var x = 10;
}

console.log(x);
```

### Output

```text
10
```

### Why?

`var` is **not** block-scoped; it is function-scoped (or global if declared outside a function).

---

# Challenge 13 — Function Scope

```javascript
function test() {
    var a = 1;
}

console.log(a);
```

### Output

```text
ReferenceError
```

### Why?

`a` only exists within the function.

---

# Challenge 14 — Hoisting Order

```javascript
var a = 1;

function test() {
    console.log(a);

    var a = 2;
}

test();
```

### Output

```text
undefined
```

### Why?

Inside `test()`, JavaScript treats it as:

```javascript
function test() {
    var a;

    console.log(a);

    a = 2;
}
```

The local `a` shadows the global `a`.

---

# Challenge 15 — Closure in Action

```javascript
function makeAdder(x) {
    return function (y) {
        return x + y;
    };
}

const add5 = makeAdder(5);

console.log(add5(3));
```

### Output

```text
8
```

### Why?

The returned function remembers `x` even after `makeAdder()` has finished executing.

---

# Common Interview Mistakes

### Mistake 1

Thinking hoisting moves code.

> Hoisting is about how JavaScript sets up bindings during the creation phase—not physically moving code.

---

### Mistake 2

Believing `let` isn't hoisted.

> `let` **is** hoisted, but it's inaccessible until initialized because of the TDZ.

---

### Mistake 3

Confusing `undefined` with `ReferenceError`.

- `var` before initialization → `undefined`
- `let`/`const` before initialization → `ReferenceError`

---

### Mistake 4

Assuming closures copy variables.

Closures keep a **reference** to variables, not a copy.

---

# Under the Hood

For this code:

```javascript
var a = 10;

function test() {
    console.log(a);
}

test();
```

Creation Phase:

```text
Global Execution Context

a → undefined

test → function
```

Execution Phase:

```text
a = 10

↓

test()

↓

Function Execution Context

↓

console.log(a)

↓

Looks in local scope ❌

↓

Looks in global scope ✅

↓

10
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What is hoisting?

> Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of creating bindings for variables and functions before execution begins.

---

### Why does `var` print `undefined`?

> Because it's initialized to `undefined` during the creation phase.

---

### Why does `let` throw a `ReferenceError`?

> Because it's in the Temporal Dead Zone until initialization.

---

### What is a closure?

> A closure is a function that remembers and can access variables from the lexical scope where it was created, even after that outer function has finished executing.

---

### Why does `var` in a loop print the same value?

> Because all callbacks share the same function-scoped variable.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Explain the output:

```javascript
console.log(a);

var a = 5;
```

---

## Medium

Why does this print `3` three times?

```javascript
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
```

How would you fix it?

---

## Hard

Implement a function that creates a private counter using closures:

```javascript
const counter = createCounter();

counter.increment();

counter.decrement();

counter.getValue();
```

The internal value should not be directly accessible from outside the function.

---

# Time Complexity

Most examples focus on JavaScript execution behavior rather than algorithmic complexity.

For the closure counter:

- `increment()` → **O(1)**
- `decrement()` → **O(1)**
- `getValue()` → **O(1)**

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. Why is `var` initialized to `undefined`?
2. What is the Temporal Dead Zone?
3. Why are function declarations callable before they're written?
4. What is variable shadowing?
5. What is lexical scope?
6. How do closures work?
7. Why does `var` behave differently from `let` in loops?
8. What's the difference between block scope and function scope?
9. Why doesn't a closure lose access to outer variables?
10. What's the difference between `ReferenceError` and `TypeError` in the context of hoisting?

---

## Coding

11. Build a private counter using closures.
12. Rewrite a `var` loop using `let`.
13. Demonstrate variable shadowing with nested scopes.
14. Explain the execution of a function declaration vs. a function expression.
15. Write an example that triggers the TDZ.

---

## Debugging

16. A function prints `undefined` instead of the expected global variable. How could local hoisting be the cause?
17. A callback inside a loop always logs the final loop value. Why?
18. A variable declared with `let` throws a `ReferenceError` before its declaration. Explain the execution phases leading to the error.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Hoisting
        ↓
Bindings Created
Before Execution

----------------------------

var
        ↓
Hoisted
Initialized → undefined

----------------------------

let / const
        ↓
Hoisted
TDZ Until Initialization

----------------------------

Function Declaration
        ↓
Fully Hoisted

----------------------------

Function Expression
        ↓
Depends on Variable

----------------------------

Closure
        ↓
Remembers
Lexical Scope

----------------------------

Scope Chain
        ↓
Local
↓
Outer
↓
Global
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Predict outputs involving `var`, `let`, and `const`.
- ✅ Explain hoisting without saying "JavaScript moves code."
- ✅ Describe the Temporal Dead Zone.
- ✅ Trace scope chains and variable shadowing.
- ✅ Explain and implement closures.
- ✅ Debug common interview questions involving execution context.

---

# Mini Mock Interview

Without running the code, explain the output:

```javascript
var x = 1;

function outer() {
    console.log(x);

    var x = 2;

    return function inner() {
        console.log(x);
    };
}

const fn = outer();

fn();

console.log(x);
```

Your explanation should include:

1. The Global Execution Context.
2. The Function Execution Context for `outer()`.
3. Hoisting.
4. Scope lookup.
5. Closures.
6. The final output.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 12.2 — JavaScript Interview Challenge II: `this`, Call, Apply, Bind, Arrow Functions, Objects & Prototypes**, where you'll tackle some of the most confusing and frequently tested JavaScript interview questions.

questions.questionText: Predict the output of the following scope code snippet:
questions.explanation: `var x = y = 5;` is interpreted as `y = 5; var x = y;`. `y` becomes a global variable (number) because there is no declaration, while `x` is function-scoped inside the IIFE (its type is undefined outside).

questions.questionText: Which statements describe closures accurately? (Select all that apply)
options: They retain references to parent scope variables.
They are created when nested functions are defined.
They copy variables by value into memory.
They cause ReferenceErrors inside the TDZ.
questions.explanation: Closures hold live references to their outer scope variables. They do not copy values, which is why changes are reflected live.

questions.questionText: What keyword is function-scoped rather than block-scoped?
questions.explanation: `var` declarations are hoisted to the nearest enclosing function scope.
