# Module 12 — JavaScript & React Interview Challenges

# Lesson 12.2 — JavaScript Interview Challenge II: `this`, `call()`, `apply()`, `bind()`, Arrow Functions, Objects & Prototypes

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the most tested JavaScript interview topics)

---

# 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters

Many JavaScript interviews include questions like:

- "What is `this`?"
- "What will this code print?"
- "What's the difference between `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`?"
- "Why don't arrow functions have their own `this`?"
- "How does the prototype chain work?"

These questions test your understanding of how JavaScript works under the hood.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Predict the value of `this`.
- Explain the four binding rules of `this`.
- Use `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`.
- Understand arrow functions and lexical `this`.
- Explain prototypes and prototype inheritance.
- Solve common interview questions.

---

# The Four Rules of `this`

When JavaScript executes a function, it determines `this` using these rules (highest applicable rule wins):

```text
1. new Binding
        ↓
2. Explicit Binding (call/apply/bind)
        ↓
3. Implicit Binding (object.method())
        ↓
4. Default Binding
```

---

# Challenge 1 — Default Binding

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this);
}

greet();
```

### Output

In a browser (non-strict mode):

```text
Window
```

In strict mode:

```text
undefined
```

### Why?

The function is called by itself, so default binding applies.

---

# Challenge 2 — Implicit Binding

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John",

    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

user.greet();
```

### Output

```text
John
```

### Why?

The object before the dot (`user`) becomes `this`.

---

# Challenge 3 — Losing `this`

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John",

    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

const fn = user.greet;

fn();
```

### Output

```text
undefined
```

(or the global object's `name` in non-strict environments if one exists)

### Why?

The function is no longer called as a method of `user`. Default binding applies.

---

# Challenge 4 — `call()`

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this.name);
}

const user = {
    name: "Alice"
};

greet.call(user);
```

### Output

```text
Alice
```

### Why?

`call()` explicitly sets `this`.

---

# Challenge 5 — `apply()`

```javascript
function introduce(city, country) {
    console.log(this.name, city, country);
}

const user = {
    name: "John"
};

introduce.apply(user, ["Lagos", "Nigeria"]);
```

### Output

```text
John Lagos Nigeria
```

### Why?

`apply()` is like `call()`, but it accepts arguments as an array.

---

# Challenge 6 — `bind()`

```javascript
function greet() {
    console.log(this.name);
}

const user = {
    name: "Sarah"
};

const bound = greet.bind(user);

bound();
```

### Output

```text
Sarah
```

### Why?

`bind()` doesn't call the function immediately.

It returns a **new function** with `this` permanently bound.

---

# Difference Between `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`

| Method | Executes Immediately? | Arguments |
|---------|-----------------------|-----------|
| `call()` | ✅ Yes | Comma-separated |
| `apply()` | ✅ Yes | Array |
| `bind()` | ❌ No | Comma-separated (returns a new function) |

---

# Challenge 7 — Arrow Function

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John",

    greet: () => {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

user.greet();
```

### Output

```text
undefined
```

(in most module/strict environments)

### Why?

Arrow functions **do not create their own `this`**.

They inherit `this` from the surrounding lexical scope.

---

# Challenge 8 — Arrow Inside Method

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John",

    greet() {
        const inner = () => {
            console.log(this.name);
        };

        inner();
    }
};

user.greet();
```

### Output

```text
John
```

### Why?

The arrow function inherits `this` from `greet()`, where `this` is `user`.

---

# Challenge 9 — Regular Function Inside Method

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John",

    greet() {
        function inner() {
            console.log(this.name);
        }

        inner();
    }
};

user.greet();
```

### Output

```text
undefined
```

(or the global object's `name` in non-strict mode)

### Why?

`inner()` is a regular function, so it gets its own `this` based on how it's called.

---

# Challenge 10 — Constructor Function

```javascript
function Person(name) {
    this.name = name;
}

const p = new Person("Alice");

console.log(p.name);
```

### Output

```text
Alice
```

### Why?

Using `new` creates a new object and binds `this` to it.

---

# Challenge 11 — Prototype

```javascript
function Person(name) {
    this.name = name;
}

Person.prototype.sayHi = function () {
    console.log("Hi", this.name);
};

const p = new Person("John");

p.sayHi();
```

### Output

```text
Hi John
```

### Why?

`sayHi()` isn't stored on each object.

It's stored once on `Person.prototype`, and all instances share it.

---

# Challenge 12 — Prototype Lookup

```javascript
function Animal() {}

Animal.prototype.sound = "Roar";

const lion = new Animal();

console.log(lion.sound);
```

### Output

```text
Roar
```

### Why?

JavaScript doesn't find `sound` on `lion`, so it looks up the prototype chain.

---

# Prototype Chain

```text
lion
  │
  ▼
Animal.prototype
  │
  ▼
Object.prototype
  │
  ▼
null
```

Property lookup starts on the object itself and moves up the chain until it finds the property or reaches `null`.

---

# Challenge 13 — Shadowing a Prototype Property

```javascript
function Animal() {}

Animal.prototype.type = "Mammal";

const dog = new Animal();

dog.type = "Pet";

console.log(dog.type);
```

### Output

```text
Pet
```

### Why?

The object's own property takes precedence over the prototype property.

---

# Challenge 14 — Checking Ownership

```javascript
function Person() {}

Person.prototype.age = 25;

const p = new Person();

console.log(p.hasOwnProperty("age"));
```

### Output

```text
false
```

### Why?

`age` exists on the prototype, not directly on `p`.

---

# Challenge 15 — Object Creation

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John"
};

console.log(user.__proto__ === Object.prototype);
```

### Output

```text
true
```

### Why?

Object literals inherit from `Object.prototype`.

---

# Common Interview Mistakes

### Mistake 1

Thinking `this` refers to the function itself.

`this` depends on **how the function is called**, not where it's defined (except for arrow functions).

---

### Mistake 2

Using arrow functions as object methods when you need dynamic `this`.

---

### Mistake 3

Thinking `bind()` executes the function.

It returns a new bound function.

---

### Mistake 4

Thinking every object has its own copy of prototype methods.

Prototype methods are shared among instances.

---

# Under the Hood

```text
new Person("John")

↓

Create Empty Object

↓

Bind this

↓

Execute Constructor

↓

Link to Prototype

↓

Return Object
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What determines the value of `this`?

> It's determined by how the function is called, following the binding rules: `new`, explicit (`call`/`apply`/`bind`), implicit (object method), then default.

---

### Why don't arrow functions have their own `this`?

> They lexically capture `this` from the surrounding scope instead of creating a new binding.

---

### What's the difference between `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`?

> `call()` and `apply()` invoke the function immediately. `bind()` returns a new function with `this` permanently bound. `apply()` takes arguments as an array.

---

### What is the prototype chain?

> It's JavaScript's inheritance mechanism. When a property isn't found on an object, JavaScript searches its prototype, then that prototype's prototype, and so on until `null`.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Explain:

```javascript
const obj = {
    name: "Alex",
    greet() {
        console.log(this.name);
    }
};

obj.greet();
```

---

## Medium

Fix this:

```javascript
const user = {
    name: "John",

    greet() {
        setTimeout(function () {
            console.log(this.name);
        }, 1000);
    }
};
```

Expected output:

```text
John
```

(Hint: consider using an arrow function or `bind()`.)

---

## Hard

Implement your own simplified version of `bind()`.

Example usage:

```javascript
function greet(city) {
    console.log(this.name, city);
}

const user = {
    name: "Alice"
};

const bound = myBind(greet, user);

bound("London");
```

---

# Time Complexity

- Property lookup: Average **O(1)** on the object, though prototype traversal may continue up the chain if needed.
- `call()`, `apply()`, `bind()`: **O(1)** for normal usage (ignoring the work done inside the function).

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What are the four binding rules of `this`?
2. Why don't arrow functions have their own `this`?
3. What's the difference between `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`?
4. What does `new` do internally?
5. What is a prototype?
6. How does the prototype chain work?
7. Why are prototype methods memory efficient?
8. What does `hasOwnProperty()` check?
9. What happens when a property exists on both an object and its prototype?
10. Why is `this` inside a callback often different from `this` in the outer method?

---

## Coding

11. Build a constructor function with prototype methods.
12. Rewrite a callback using an arrow function to preserve `this`.
13. Implement a simplified `bind()`.
14. Demonstrate prototype inheritance.
15. Show property shadowing with prototypes.

---

## Debugging

16. A method loses its `this` when assigned to another variable. Why?
17. An arrow function used as an object method prints `undefined`. Explain.
18. A property can't be found on an object. Describe how JavaScript searches the prototype chain.

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
this Binding Priority
        ↓
new
↓
call / apply / bind
↓
object.method()
↓
default

----------------------------

Arrow Function
        ↓
Lexical this

----------------------------

call()
        ↓
Immediate
Arguments separated

----------------------------

apply()
        ↓
Immediate
Arguments as array

----------------------------

bind()
        ↓
Returns New Function

----------------------------

Prototype Chain
        ↓
Object
↓
Prototype
↓
Object.prototype
↓
null
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Predict the value of `this` in different scenarios.
- ✅ Explain the four binding rules.
- ✅ Use `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()` correctly.
- ✅ Explain why arrow functions behave differently.
- ✅ Describe the prototype chain.
- ✅ Explain JavaScript inheritance in interviews.

---

# Mini Mock Interview

Without running the code, explain the output:

```javascript
function Person(name) {
    this.name = name;
}

Person.prototype.sayName = function () {
    console.log(this.name);
};

const user = new Person("Olalekan");

const fn = user.sayName;

fn();

user.sayName();
```

Your explanation should cover:

1. What `new` does internally.
2. Where `sayName` is stored.
3. Why `fn()` behaves differently from `user.sayName()`.
4. How `this` is determined in each call.
5. How the prototype chain is involved.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 12.3 — JavaScript Interview Challenge III: Asynchronous JavaScript, Event Loop, Promises, Async/Await & Microtasks**, one of the most important—and frequently misunderstood—topics in modern JavaScript interviews.

questions.questionText: Predict the output of the following code snippet:
questions.explanation: `getX()` returns an arrow function. Arrow functions bind `this` lexically. When `getX()` is called as a method on `obj`, its `this` is bound to `obj`. The returned arrow function inherits this bind, outputting `10`.

questions.questionText: Which methods establish or update prototype links? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: `Object.create()` creates a new object with a specified prototype. `Object.setPrototypeOf()` alters prototypes. `getPrototypeOf()` only reads them.

questions.questionText: What standard property on objects references the constructor function's prototype object?
questions.explanation: Objects link to their prototypes via the `__proto__` reference (under-the-hood internal property `[[Prototype]]`).

lessons.content:
# Module 12 — JavaScript & React Interview Challenges

# Lesson 12.3 — JavaScript Interview Challenge III: Asynchronous JavaScript, Event Loop, Promises, Async/Await & Microtasks

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (One of the most frequently asked JavaScript interview topics)

---

# 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters

If there's one topic that separates beginner and experienced JavaScript developers, it's understanding the **Event Loop**.

Interviewers love questions like:

- "What prints first?"
- "Why does `Promise.then()` run before `setTimeout()`?"
- "What is the difference between the Call Stack and the Event Loop?"
- "Explain the execution order."

These questions test whether you truly understand how JavaScript executes asynchronous code.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Explain the Event Loop.
- Predict asynchronous execution order.
- Understand Call Stack, Web APIs, Task Queue, and Microtask Queue.
- Explain Promises and `async/await`.
- Solve common async interview questions.

---

# 1. JavaScript is Single-Threaded

JavaScript executes one piece of code at a time.

It has:

- One Call Stack.
- One main execution thread.

Example:

```javascript
console.log("A");

console.log("B");

console.log("C");
```

Output:

```text
A
B
C
```

Simple.

But asynchronous operations change the picture.

---

# 2. The JavaScript Runtime

JavaScript itself doesn't provide timers or network requests.

The runtime environment (browser or Node.js) provides them.

```text
JavaScript Runtime

┌─────────────┐
│ Call Stack  │
└─────────────┘
        │
        ▼
┌─────────────────────┐
│ Browser / Node APIs │
│ setTimeout          │
│ fetch               │
│ DOM Events          │
└─────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
┌──────────────┐
│ Task Queues  │
└──────────────┘
        │
        ▼
   Event Loop
```

---

# 3. Call Stack

The Call Stack keeps track of which function is currently executing.

Example:

```javascript
function one() {
    two();
}

function two() {
    console.log("Hello");
}

one();
```

Stack:

```text
Call Stack

↓

one()

↓

two()

↓

console.log()

↓

Empty
```

Functions are pushed onto the stack and popped off when finished.

---

# 4. `setTimeout`

Interview Question:

```javascript
console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("B");
}, 0);

console.log("C");
```

### Think First...

⬇️

### Output

```text
A
C
B
```

### Why?

Execution:

```text
Call Stack

↓

console.log("A")

↓

setTimeout()

↓

Browser Timer

↓

console.log("C")

↓

Stack Empty

↓

Event Loop

↓

Task Queue

↓

console.log("B")
```

Even with a delay of `0`, the callback cannot run until the current call stack is empty.

---

# 5. Promises

Interview Question:

```javascript
console.log("A");

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("B");
});

console.log("C");
```

### Output

```text
A
C
B
```

But **why**?

Because Promise callbacks go to the **Microtask Queue**.

---

# 6. Task Queue vs Microtask Queue

JavaScript has different queues.

```text
Queues

Microtasks
│
├── Promise.then()
├── catch()
├── finally()
└── queueMicrotask()

-----------------------

Tasks (Macrotasks)
│
├── setTimeout()
├── setInterval()
├── DOM Events
└── Message Events
```

Rule:

> **Microtasks always run before the next task (macrotask).**

---

# 7. Event Loop Order

After the Call Stack becomes empty:

```text
Call Stack Empty

↓

Run ALL Microtasks

↓

Run ONE Task

↓

Run ALL New Microtasks

↓

Run ONE Task

↓

Repeat
```

This execution order is a favorite interview topic.

---

# Challenge 1

```javascript
console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C"));

console.log("D");
```

### Output

```text
A
D
C
B
```

### Why?

1. Synchronous code runs first.
2. Promise callback (microtask).
3. `setTimeout` callback (task).

---

# Challenge 2

```javascript
setTimeout(() => console.log(1), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(2));

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3));

console.log(4);
```

### Output

```text
4
2
3
1
```

---

# Challenge 3

```javascript
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("Promise");
});

console.log("End");
```

### Output

```text
Start
End
Promise
Timeout
```

---

# 8. Async/Await

`async/await` is syntax built on top of Promises.

Example:

```javascript
async function greet() {
    return "Hello";
}

greet().then(console.log);
```

Output:

```text
Hello
```

Even though it looks synchronous, an `async` function always returns a Promise.

---

# Challenge 4

```javascript
async function test() {
    console.log(1);

    await Promise.resolve();

    console.log(2);
}

console.log(3);

test();

console.log(4);
```

### Output

```text
3
1
4
2
```

### Why?

`await` pauses the async function.

The remainder of the function is scheduled as a microtask.

---

# Challenge 5

```javascript
async function test() {
    return 5;
}

test().then(console.log);
```

Output:

```text
5
```

Because:

```javascript
return 5;
```

is equivalent to:

```javascript
return Promise.resolve(5);
```

inside an `async` function.

---

# Challenge 6

```javascript
async function test() {
    throw new Error("Oops");
}

test().catch(err => console.log(err.message));
```

Output:

```text
Oops
```

Throwing inside an `async` function rejects the returned Promise.

---

# 9. Promise Chaining

```javascript
Promise.resolve(2)
    .then(x => x * 2)
    .then(x => x + 1)
    .then(console.log);
```

Output:

```text
5
```

Each `.then()` receives the previous result.

---

# 10. Error Handling

Using Promises:

```javascript
fetchData()
    .then(...)
    .catch(...)
```

Using `async/await`:

```javascript
try {
    const data = await fetchData();
}
catch (err) {
    console.log(err);
}
```

Both handle asynchronous errors, but `async/await` often reads more like synchronous code.

---

# 11. Common Interview Mistakes

### Mistake 1

Believing `setTimeout(..., 0)` runs immediately.

It doesn't.

It runs **after** the current call stack is empty and after pending microtasks.

---

### Mistake 2

Thinking Promises execute before synchronous code.

Synchronous code always finishes first.

---

### Mistake 3

Confusing the Call Stack with the Event Loop.

The Event Loop coordinates execution after the Call Stack becomes empty.

---

### Mistake 4

Thinking `await` blocks the entire program.

It only pauses the current `async` function.

Other JavaScript can continue executing.

---

# Under the Hood

Example:

```javascript
console.log(1);

setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3));

console.log(4);
```

Execution:

```text
Call Stack
↓

1

↓

setTimeout → Browser API

↓

Promise → Microtask Queue

↓

4

↓

Call Stack Empty

↓

Microtask Queue

↓

3

↓

Task Queue

↓

2
```

Output:

```text
1
4
3
2
```

---

# Interview Perspective

### What is the Event Loop?

> The Event Loop monitors the Call Stack and task queues. When the Call Stack is empty, it executes pending microtasks first, then tasks.

---

### Why do Promise callbacks run before `setTimeout`?

> Promise callbacks are placed in the Microtask Queue, which has higher priority than the Task Queue.

---

### Does `await` block JavaScript?

> No. It pauses only the current `async` function and schedules the remaining code as a microtask once the awaited Promise settles.

---

### What does an `async` function return?

> It always returns a Promise.

---

### What happens if an `async` function throws an error?

> The returned Promise is rejected with that error.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Predict the output:

```javascript
console.log(1);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(2));

console.log(3);
```

---

## Medium

Explain the output:

```javascript
setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("Promise"));

console.log("End");
```

---

## Hard

Without running it, determine the output:

```javascript
console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("B");

    Promise.resolve().then(() => {
        console.log("C");
    });
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("D");
});

console.log("E");
```

Also explain:

1. Call Stack.
2. Browser APIs.
3. Microtask Queue.
4. Task Queue.
5. Event Loop execution.

---

# Time Complexity

The Event Loop concepts describe execution order rather than algorithmic complexity.

Promise resolution and queue scheduling are generally treated as **O(1)** operations for interview purposes.

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. What is the Call Stack?
2. What is the Event Loop?
3. What is the Task Queue?
4. What is the Microtask Queue?
5. Why do Promise callbacks execute before `setTimeout` callbacks?
6. Does `await` block the entire JavaScript runtime?
7. What does an `async` function always return?
8. How are errors handled in `async` functions?
9. Why doesn't `setTimeout(..., 0)` execute immediately?
10. What's the difference between synchronous and asynchronous code?

---

## Coding

11. Convert a Promise chain into `async/await`.
12. Write an `async` function that fetches data and handles errors.
13. Demonstrate Promise chaining.
14. Show the execution order of synchronous code, Promises, and timers.
15. Create an example with nested microtasks and explain the output.

---

## Debugging

16. A developer expects `setTimeout(..., 0)` to run before a Promise callback. Explain why that's incorrect.
17. An `async` function seems to "pause." What exactly is paused?
18. A Promise rejection isn't being handled. How can you fix it using both `.catch()` and `try...catch`?

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
JavaScript Runtime
        ↓
Call Stack
        ↓
Browser / Node APIs
        ↓
Queues
        ↓
Event Loop

----------------------------

Priority

Synchronous Code
        ↓
Microtasks
(Promise.then, catch, finally, await)
        ↓
Tasks (Macrotasks)
(setTimeout, setInterval, DOM Events)

----------------------------

async Function
        ↓
Always Returns Promise

----------------------------

await
        ↓
Pauses Current Async Function
Not Entire JavaScript
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Explain the Event Loop confidently.
- ✅ Predict execution order involving synchronous code, Promises, and timers.
- ✅ Distinguish between the Microtask Queue and Task Queue.
- ✅ Explain how `async/await` works internally.
- ✅ Handle asynchronous errors correctly.
- ✅ Reason through interview questions without running the code.

---

# Mini Mock Interview

Without running the code, explain the output:

```javascript
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("Timer");

    Promise.resolve().then(() => {
        console.log("Microtask");
    });
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("Promise 1");
});

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("Promise 2");
});

console.log("End");
```

Your explanation should include:

1. The Call Stack.
2. The Browser API.
3. The Microtask Queue.
4. The Task Queue.
5. Every step the Event Loop takes.
6. The final output.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 12.4 — JavaScript Interview Challenge IV: Arrays, Objects, Maps, Sets & Common Coding Problems**, where you'll solve practical algorithm and data structure questions that appear in JavaScript interviews, with an emphasis on writing clean, efficient solutions.

questions.questionText: Predict the output order of this asynchronous code snippet:
questions.explanation: `1` and `4` run synchronously. The resolved promise enters the Microtask Queue and runs next (`3`). `setTimeout` enters the Callback Queue and runs last (`2`).

questions.questionText: Which statements are true about the Event Loop? (Select all that apply)
options: Microtasks execute immediately after the current call stack clears.
Macrotasks (timeouts) run in the next loop ticks.
The loop blocks browser execution when promises resolve.
Event loop executes multiple async callbacks in parallel.
questions.explanation: Microtasks run immediately when call stack empties. Macrotasks are executed one-per-loop-turn (tick). JavaScript remains single-threaded; callbacks execute sequentially, never in parallel.

questions.questionText: What queue receives callbacks from resolved Promises?
questions.explanation: Promise `.then()` and `.catch()` callbacks are routed to the Microtask Queue.

lessons.content:
# Module 12 — JavaScript & React Interview Challenges

# Lesson 12.4 — JavaScript Interview Challenge IV: Arrays, Objects, Maps, Sets & Common Coding Problems

> **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆
>
> **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely Common)

---

# 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters

If you've done JavaScript interviews before, you've probably seen questions like:

- "Remove duplicates from an array."
- "Find the first non-repeating character."
- "Group users by age."
- "Flatten this array."
- "What's the difference between `Map` and `Object`?"
- "When should you use a `Set`?"

These questions test both your JavaScript knowledge and your problem-solving ability.

---

# Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

- Choose between `Array`, `Object`, `Map`, and `Set`.
- Solve common coding interview problems.
- Analyze time and space complexity.
- Write clean, optimized JavaScript solutions.

---

# Choosing the Right Data Structure

| Structure | Best For |
|-----------|----------|
| Array | Ordered collections |
| Object | Simple key-value pairs with string/symbol keys |
| Map | Key-value pairs with keys of any type and predictable iteration order |
| Set | Unique values |

Choosing the right structure often makes your solution simpler and faster.

---

# Challenge 1 — Remove Duplicates

### Problem

```javascript
const nums = [1,2,3,2,1,5];
```

Expected:

```javascript
[1,2,3,5]
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
const unique = [...new Set(nums)];

console.log(unique);
```

### Complexity

- Time: **O(n)**
- Space: **O(n)**

---

# Challenge 2 — Count Frequencies

### Problem

Count how many times each word appears.

```javascript
const words = [
    "apple",
    "banana",
    "apple",
    "orange",
    "banana",
    "apple"
];
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
const counts = {};

for (const word of words) {
    counts[word] = (counts[word] || 0) + 1;
}

console.log(counts);
```

Output:

```javascript
{
    apple: 3,
    banana: 2,
    orange: 1
}
```

---

### Complexity

- Time: **O(n)**
- Space: **O(n)**

---

# Challenge 3 — First Non-Repeating Character

```javascript
"javascript"
```

Expected:

```text
j
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
function firstUnique(str) {
    const counts = {};

    for (const char of str) {
        counts[char] = (counts[char] || 0) + 1;
    }

    for (const char of str) {
        if (counts[char] === 1) {
            return char;
        }
    }

    return null;
}
```

---

### Complexity

- Time: **O(n)**
- Space: **O(n)**

---

# Challenge 4 — Group Users

```javascript
const users = [
    { name: "John", age: 20 },
    { name: "Jane", age: 20 },
    { name: "Bob", age: 30 }
];
```

Expected:

```javascript
{
    20: [
        { name: "John", age: 20 },
        { name: "Jane", age: 20 }
    ],
    30: [
        { name: "Bob", age: 30 }
    ]
}
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
const grouped = users.reduce((acc, user) => {
    if (!acc[user.age]) {
        acc[user.age] = [];
    }

    acc[user.age].push(user);

    return acc;
}, {});
```

---

# Challenge 5 — Flatten an Array

Input:

```javascript
[1,[2,[3,[4]]]]
```

Expected:

```javascript
[1,2,3,4]
```

---

### Solution 1 (Modern)

```javascript
const flat = arr.flat(Infinity);
```

---

### Solution 2 (Recursive)

```javascript
function flatten(arr) {
    let result = [];

    for (const item of arr) {
        if (Array.isArray(item)) {
            result.push(...flatten(item));
        } else {
            result.push(item);
        }
    }

    return result;
}
```

---

# Challenge 6 — Find the Maximum Value

```javascript
const nums = [4,10,2,99,1];
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
const max = Math.max(...nums);
```

Or:

```javascript
const max = nums.reduce((a, b) => Math.max(a, b));
```

---

# Challenge 7 — Intersection of Two Arrays

```javascript
const a = [1,2,3,4];

const b = [3,4,5,6];
```

Expected:

```javascript
[3,4]
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
const setB = new Set(b);

const result = a.filter(num => setB.has(num));
```

---

### Complexity

- Time: **O(n + m)**
- Space: **O(m)**

---

# Challenge 8 — Check if Two Arrays are Equal

```javascript
[1,2,3]

[1,2,3]
```

Simple solution:

```javascript
function equal(a, b) {
    if (a.length !== b.length) {
        return false;
    }

    return a.every((value, index) => value === b[index]);
}
```

> This compares values in order. It doesn't perform a deep comparison of nested objects or arrays.

---

# Challenge 9 — Find Missing Number

Input:

```javascript
[1,2,3,5]
```

Expected:

```text
4
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
function missing(arr) {
    const n = arr.length + 1;

    const expected = (n * (n + 1)) / 2;

    const actual = arr.reduce((sum, num) => sum + num, 0);

    return expected - actual;
}
```

---

# Challenge 10 — Reverse a String

```javascript
"hello"
```

Expected:

```text
olleh
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
function reverse(str) {
    return str.split("").reverse().join("");
}
```

---

# Challenge 11 — Palindrome

```javascript
"racecar"
```

---

### Solution

```javascript
function palindrome(str) {
    return str === str.split("").reverse().join("");
}
```

---

# Challenge 12 — `Map`

```javascript
const map = new Map();

map.set("name", "John");

map.set(1, "Number");

map.set({}, "Object");
```

Unlike objects:

- Keys can be any type.
- Maintains insertion order.
- Provides methods like `set()`, `get()`, `has()`, and `delete()`.

---

# Challenge 13 — `Set`

```javascript
const set = new Set();

set.add(1);

set.add(1);

set.add(2);
```

Output:

```text
{1,2}
```

A `Set` stores only unique values.

---

# Challenge 14 — Object vs Map

| Object | Map |
|---------|-----|
| Keys are strings or symbols | Keys can be any type |
| Simpler syntax | Rich API |
| Good for plain objects | Better for dynamic key-value storage |

---

# Challenge 15 — `for...of` vs `for...in`

```javascript
const arr = [10,20,30];
```

### `for...of`

```javascript
for (const value of arr) {
    console.log(value);
}
```

Output:

```text
10
20
30
```

---

### `for...in`

```javascript
for (const index in arr) {
    console.log(index);
}
```

Output:

```text
0
1
2
```

- `for...of` iterates over **values**.
- `for...in` iterates over **enumerable property keys** (array indices in this case).

---

# Common Interview Mistakes

### Mistake 1

Using nested loops when a `Set` or `Map` would reduce the complexity.

---

### Mistake 2

Using an `Object` when keys aren't strings or symbols.

Use a `Map` instead.

---

### Mistake 3

Comparing arrays with:

```javascript
[1,2] === [1,2]
```

Output:

```text
false
```

Arrays are compared by reference, not by value.

---

### Mistake 4

Using `for...in` when you intended to iterate over array values.

---

# Under the Hood

Frequency Counter Pattern:

```text
Array

↓

Loop Once

↓

Object / Map

↓

Store Counts

↓

Loop Again (if needed)

↓

Answer
```

This pattern appears in many interview problems because it often reduces time complexity from **O(n²)** to **O(n)**.

---

# Interview Perspective

### When would you use a `Map` instead of an `Object`?

> When keys aren't limited to strings or symbols, or when you need a richer API and predictable insertion order.

---

### Why use a `Set`?

> To efficiently store unique values and perform membership checks.

---

### What's the difference between `for...of` and `for...in`?

> `for...of` iterates over iterable values, while `for...in` iterates over enumerable property keys.

---

### How would you remove duplicates from an array?

> A concise approach is `const unique = [...new Set(array)]`.

---

# Live Coding Questions

## Easy

Remove duplicate values from an array.

---

## Medium

Group products by category using `reduce()`.

---

## Hard

Given:

```javascript
const users = [
    { id: 1, name: "John" },
    { id: 2, name: "Jane" },
    { id: 3, name: "Bob" }
];

const orders = [
    { userId: 2, total: 50 },
    { userId: 1, total: 100 }
];
```

Return:

```javascript
[
    { id: 1, name: "John", total: 100 },
    { id: 2, name: "Jane", total: 50 },
    { id: 3, name: "Bob", total: null }
]
```

**Hint:** Build a lookup with a `Map` keyed by `userId` to avoid nested loops.

---

# Time Complexity Summary

| Problem | Time |
|---------|------|
| Remove Duplicates | O(n) |
| Frequency Counter | O(n) |
| Group By | O(n) |
| Intersection | O(n + m) |
| Flatten (Recursive) | O(n) |
| Reverse String | O(n) |
| Palindrome | O(n) |
| Find Max | O(n) |

---

# Practice Exercises

## Knowledge

1. When should you use an `Array`?
2. When is a `Map` preferable to an `Object`?
3. What is a `Set` used for?
4. Why are arrays compared by reference?
5. What's the difference between `for...of` and `for...in`?
6. How does the frequency counter pattern work?
7. Why is `reduce()` useful for grouping?
8. What's the complexity of removing duplicates with a `Set`?
9. Why use a lookup table instead of nested loops?
10. When is `flat(Infinity)` useful?

---

## Coding

11. Remove duplicates from an array.
12. Count character frequencies in a string.
13. Find the first unique character.
14. Group users by age.
15. Flatten a deeply nested array.

---

## Debugging

16. A developer compares two arrays with `===` and gets `false` even though they contain the same values. Explain why.
17. An algorithm uses nested loops to check for duplicates. How can a `Set` improve it?
18. A `Map` lookup unexpectedly returns `undefined`. What are some possible causes (e.g., wrong key type or using a different object reference as the key)?

---

# Interview Cheatsheet

```text
Choose the Right Structure
        ↓
Array → Ordered data
Object → Simple key-value pairs
Map → Any key type + rich API
Set → Unique values

----------------------------

Common Patterns
        ↓
Frequency Counter
Lookup Table
Grouping
Filtering
Deduplication

----------------------------

Performance
        ↓
Prefer O(n)
Avoid O(n²) When Possible

----------------------------

Arrays
        ↓
Compared by Reference
Not by Value
```

---

# Mastery Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- ✅ Choose the right data structure for a problem.
- ✅ Use `Map` and `Set` effectively.
- ✅ Solve common array and object interview questions.
- ✅ Analyze time and space complexity.
- ✅ Replace inefficient nested-loop solutions with lookup-based approaches.

---

# Mini Mock Interview

You're given a list of 100,000 customer records and 80,000 purchase records.

Each purchase has a `customerId`.

Your task is to produce a new array where each customer includes their total purchase amount.

Explain:

1. Why a nested loop is a poor solution.
2. Which data structure you'd use.
3. The algorithm.
4. The time complexity.
5. The space complexity.
6. How your solution would scale as the dataset grows.

---

## Coming Next

Reply **Next** for **Lesson 12.5 — React Interview Challenge I: Hooks, State Management, Component Design & Real-World React Problems**, where you'll tackle React-specific interview questions involving hooks, rendering behavior, state updates, performance optimization, and component architecture.

lessons.objective: Complete coding challenge on custom React hooks, state management, and component architecture designs.
lessons.content:
# Module 12 — JavaScript & React Interview Challenges # Lesson 12.5 — React Interview Challenge I: Hooks, State Management, Component Design & Real-World React Problems > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (The most common React interview topic) --- # 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters If you interview for any React role, you'll almost certainly be asked about: - Hooks - State updates - Component re-renders - `useEffect` - `useMemo` - `useCallback` - Custom Hooks - State management - Performance optimization Interviewers often present code snippets and ask you to explain what happens or how you'd improve them. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Predict React rendering behavior. - Explain Hooks clearly. - Identify unnecessary re-renders. - Optimize React components. - Build reusable Custom Hooks. - Answer common React interview questions. --- # Challenge 1 — `useState` Updates ```jsx function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); function handleClick() { setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1); } return ( <>

{count}

); } ``` ### Question After clicking the button once, what is displayed? --- ### Answer ```text 1 ``` ### Why? Both updates use the same captured value of `count`. React batches the updates. They are effectively: ```jsx setCount(1); setCount(1); ``` --- # Challenge 2 — Functional Updates ```jsx function handleClick() { setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(c => c + 1); } ``` ### Output ```text 2 ``` ### Why? Each update receives the latest state. Execution: ```text 0 ↓ 1 ↓ 2 ``` --- # Challenge 3 — `useEffect` ```jsx useEffect(() => { console.log("Mounted"); }, []); ``` Question: How many times does it run? --- ### Answer ```text Once after the component mounts. ``` An empty dependency array means the effect runs after the initial render and not again unless the component is unmounted and mounted again. --- # Challenge 4 — Dependency Array ```jsx useEffect(() => { console.log(count); }, [count]); ``` Question: When does it run? --- ### Answer Whenever `count` changes. --- # Challenge 5 — Missing Dependencies ```jsx useEffect(() => { fetchUser(id); }, []); ``` Question: What's wrong? --- ### Answer If `id` changes, the effect won't re-run. A better version is: ```jsx useEffect(() => { fetchUser(id); }, [id]); ``` If `fetchUser` comes from props or another hook, ensure its stability or include it if appropriate. --- # Challenge 6 — Infinite Loop ```jsx useEffect(() => { setCount(count + 1); }); ``` ### What happens? The effect runs after every render, updates state, triggers another render, and repeats indefinitely. --- ### Fix ```jsx useEffect(() => { setCount(c => c + 1); }, []); ``` Only do this if incrementing on mount is actually intended. --- # Challenge 7 — `useMemo` ```jsx const expensive = useMemo(() => { return calculate(items); }, [items]); ``` Question: Why use `useMemo`? --- ### Answer It avoids recalculating an expensive value unless `items` changes. --- # Challenge 8 — `useCallback` ```jsx const handleClick = useCallback(() => { save(); }, [save]); ``` Question: Why? --- ### Answer It provides a stable function reference, which is useful when passing callbacks to memoized child components or when a hook depends on the callback. --- # Challenge 9 — `React.memo` ```jsx const Child = React.memo(function Child() { console.log("Render"); return

Child

; }); ``` Question: When can React skip rendering `Child`? --- ### Answer When its props have not changed and React determines the memoized output can be reused. --- # Challenge 10 — Custom Hook ```jsx function useCounter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); function increment() { setCount(c => c + 1); } return { count, increment }; } ``` Why use a Custom Hook? --- ### Answer To reuse stateful logic across components without duplicating code. --- # Challenge 11 — Controlled Component ```jsx setName(e.target.value)} /> ``` This is a: ```text Controlled Component ``` Because React controls the input's value. --- # Challenge 12 — Uncontrolled Component ```jsx ``` The value is managed by the DOM rather than React state. --- # Challenge 13 — List Keys ```jsx users.map(user => ( )); ``` Why use `key`? --- ### Answer Keys help React identify which items have been added, removed, or reordered during reconciliation. --- # Challenge 14 — Bad Key ```jsx users.map((user, index) => ( )); ``` What's the issue? --- ### Answer If the list changes order or items are inserted/removed, React may reuse component instances incorrectly, leading to unexpected UI behavior or state mismatches. Prefer stable, unique IDs whenever possible. --- # Challenge 15 — Context Question: When should you use Context? --- ### Answer For data shared across many components, such as: - Theme - Authentication - Locale - User preferences Avoid putting rapidly changing or unrelated state into a single Context, as it can trigger unnecessary re-renders for consumers. --- # Challenge 16 — Lifting State Up Suppose: ```text Parent ├── Search └── Results ``` Where should the search state live? ### Answer In the closest common ancestor (`Parent`), so both `Search` and `Results` can access it via props or context if appropriate. --- # Challenge 17 — State Mutation ```jsx items.push(newItem); setItems(items); ``` What's wrong? --- ### Answer The array is mutated in place. React state should be treated as immutable. Correct: ```jsx setItems(prev => [...prev, newItem]); ``` --- # Challenge 18 — Multiple State Variables ```jsx const [name, setName] = useState(""); const [age, setAge] = useState(20); ``` Question: Should these be combined? --- ### Answer Not necessarily. Keep state separate when values change independently. Combine related values into one object only when it makes updates clearer and they naturally belong together. --- # Common Interview Mistakes ### Mistake 1 Using `useMemo` everywhere. Only use it when there's a measurable benefit. --- ### Mistake 2 Ignoring the dependency array. Missing dependencies can cause stale values or skipped updates. --- ### Mistake 3 Mutating state directly. Always create new arrays or objects. --- ### Mistake 4 Using array indexes as keys for dynamic lists. --- ### Mistake 5 Using Context for all state management. Context is not a replacement for every state management need. --- # Under the Hood When state changes: ```text State Update ↓ Schedule Render ↓ Component Function Executes ↓ Virtual DOM Produced ↓ Reconciliation ↓ DOM Updated ``` Understanding this flow helps explain rendering behavior and optimization techniques. --- # Interview Perspective ### Why are functional state updates sometimes necessary? > Because they always receive the latest state, avoiding issues with batched updates or stale closures. --- ### When should you use `useMemo`? > To memoize expensive calculations when profiling shows recomputation is a bottleneck. --- ### What's the difference between `useMemo` and `useCallback`? > `useMemo` memoizes a computed value. `useCallback` memoizes a function reference. --- ### Why shouldn't you mutate state? > React relies on detecting state changes through new references. Mutating existing objects or arrays can prevent expected updates and make bugs harder to track. --- ### When should you create a Custom Hook? > When multiple components need to share the same stateful logic. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Build a counter using `useState`. --- ## Medium Create a reusable `useToggle` Custom Hook. Example: ```jsx const { value, toggle } = useToggle(); ``` --- ## Hard Build a searchable product list that: - Debounces user input. - Memoizes expensive filtering. - Prevents unnecessary child re-renders. - Cleans up timers properly. - Uses stable keys. - Explains why each optimization is used. --- # Time Complexity | Operation | Complexity | |-----------|------------| | State update | Typically O(1) to schedule; actual rendering cost depends on the component tree | | Array append (immutable) | O(n) because a new array is created | | `useMemo` lookup | O(1) for dependency comparison, excluding the cost of recomputation | | Context consumer update | Depends on the number of consumers that re-render | --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. Why do two `setState(count + 1)` calls often produce a single increment? 2. When does `useEffect` run? 3. Why is the dependency array important? 4. What causes an infinite effect loop? 5. When should you use `useMemo`? 6. When should you use `useCallback`? 7. Why are keys important in lists? 8. Why avoid mutating state? 9. When is Context appropriate? 10. What problem do Custom Hooks solve? --- ## Coding 11. Create a `useCounter` hook. 12. Create a `useToggle` hook. 13. Build a controlled form. 14. Memoize an expensive filter. 15. Lift state to a parent component shared by two children. --- ## Debugging 16. A component re-renders more often than expected. How would you investigate? 17. A `useEffect` doesn't run when a prop changes. What might be wrong? 18. A list displays incorrect data after reordering. How could unstable keys be responsible? --- # Interview Cheatsheet ```text React State ↓ Immutable Updates ---------------------------- useState ↓ Functional Updates When Depending on Previous State ---------------------------- useEffect ↓ Runs After Render Controlled by Dependencies ---------------------------- Performance ↓ React.memo useMemo useCallback ---------------------------- Reusability ↓ Custom Hooks ---------------------------- Lists ↓ Stable Unique Keys ``` --- # Mastery Checklist Before moving on, make sure you can: - ✅ Explain React's rendering lifecycle. - ✅ Predict `useState` update behavior. - ✅ Use `useEffect` correctly with dependencies. - ✅ Distinguish `useMemo` from `useCallback`. - ✅ Build and reuse Custom Hooks. - ✅ Explain list keys and immutable state updates. - ✅ Optimize React components without premature optimization. --- # Mini Mock Interview You're given a React application with these problems: - A search box sends a request on every keystroke. - A child component re-renders even when its props appear unchanged. - A list uses array indexes as keys. - State is mutated directly before calling `setState`. - A `useEffect` fetches user data but never updates when the `userId` prop changes. For each issue: 1. Explain why it's a problem. 2. Describe how you would fix it. 3. Discuss any trade-offs. 4. Explain how you would verify that your solution works. --- ## Coming Next Reply **Next** for **Lesson 12.6 — React Interview Challenge II: Advanced React, Architecture, Performance, System Design & Senior-Level Scenarios**, where you'll tackle complex interview questions involving large-scale React applications, architecture decisions, performance tuning, state management strategies, and real-world frontend system design.

questions.questionText: Why is it dangerous to mutate React state directly without setState?
options: React is unaware of the mutation and will not trigger a re-render.
questions.explanation: React tracks state updates via dispatcher calls. Direct mutations do not trigger re-renders, causing views to go out of sync with data.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are valid React hook rules? (Select all that apply)
options: Only call hooks at the top level of your functional component.
Only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks.
Hooks can be called inside conditional statements.
Hooks can be called inside loops.
questions.explanation: Hooks must run in the exact same order on every render, so calling them inside conditionals, loops, or nested functions is forbidden.

questions.questionText: What is the common name for React components that receive props, return JSX, and have no state of their own?
questions.explanation: Stateless or presentational components focus entirely on rendering UI based on incoming props.

lessons.content:
# Module 12 — JavaScript & React Interview Challenges # Lesson 12.6 — React Interview Challenge II: Advanced React, Architecture, Performance, System Design & Senior-Level Scenarios > **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ > > **Interview Frequency:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Senior Frontend / Full-Stack Interviews) --- # 🚨 Why This Lesson Matters Junior interviews focus on: - `useState` - `useEffect` - Components Mid-level interviews ask: - Performance - Architecture - Reusability Senior interviews ask: - **Why did you design it this way?** - **How would this scale to millions of users?** - **How would you organize a large React codebase?** - **How would you improve performance without sacrificing maintainability?** This lesson focuses on those higher-level discussions. --- # Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: - Design scalable React applications. - Organize large projects. - Optimize rendering. - Choose the right state management approach. - Discuss frontend architecture confidently. - Answer senior-level React interview questions. --- # Challenge 1 — Large Project Structure Imagine you're building an e-commerce platform. How should the project be organized? A common feature-based structure: ```text src/ ├── app/ │ ├── router/ │ ├── providers/ │ └── store/ │ ├── features/ │ ├── auth/ │ ├── cart/ │ ├── products/ │ ├── checkout/ │ └── profile/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── hooks/ │ ├── services/ │ ├── utils/ │ ├── layouts/ │ ├── assets/ │ └── types/ ``` ### Why? Group related files by **feature**, not by file type. Feature-based organization scales better as the application grows. --- # Challenge 2 — State Management Where should state live? ```text Component ↓ Parent ↓ Context ↓ Global Store ``` Choose the **smallest scope** that solves the problem. --- ## Local State ```jsx const [open, setOpen] = useState(false); ``` Good for: - Modals - Toggles - Forms - Local UI state --- ## Context Good for: - Theme - Authentication - Language - User preferences Avoid storing frequently changing application data in a single context because it can trigger unnecessary re-renders for consumers. --- ## Global Store Examples include: - Redux Toolkit - Zustand - Jotai - Recoil (where applicable) Use when many unrelated parts of the application need shared state. --- # Challenge 3 — Preventing Re-renders Given: ```jsx function Parent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( <> ); } ``` Question: Will `Child` re-render? ### Answer Yes. Whenever `Parent` renders, React also renders its children by default. --- ## Optimization ```jsx const Child = React.memo(function Child() { return
Child
; }); ``` Now React can skip rendering `Child` if its props haven't changed. --- # Challenge 4 — Expensive Lists Suppose you have: ```jsx products.filter(...) ``` running on every render. Better: ```jsx const filtered = useMemo(() => { return products.filter(...); }, [products]); ``` Only use `useMemo` when profiling indicates the computation is expensive enough to justify memoization. --- # Challenge 5 — API Layer Bad: ```jsx useEffect(() => { fetch("/users"); }, []); ``` Better: ```text Component ↓ Service ↓ API Client ``` Example: ```javascript // services/userService.js export async function getUsers() { return api.get("/users"); } ``` Then: ```jsx useEffect(() => { getUsers(); }, []); ``` Benefits: - Easier testing - Centralized API logic - Reusability --- # Challenge 6 — Custom Hooks Bad: The same fetching logic appears in five components. Better: ```jsx function useUsers() { // fetching logic } ``` Reuse stateful logic through a Custom Hook. --- # Challenge 7 — Error Boundaries Question: Can `try...catch` catch React rendering errors? Answer: No. React rendering errors should be handled using an **Error Boundary**. Example: ```jsx ``` Error Boundaries catch errors during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors of descendant class components. They do **not** catch errors in event handlers or asynchronous callbacks. --- # Challenge 8 — Lazy Loading Instead of: ```jsx import Dashboard from "./Dashboard"; ``` Use: ```jsx const Dashboard = React.lazy(() => import("./Dashboard")); ``` With: ```jsx }> ``` Benefits: - Smaller initial bundle. - Faster first load. --- # Challenge 9 — Code Splitting Split by: - Route - Feature - Large components - Admin-only pages Don't eagerly load code users may never need. --- # Challenge 10 — Virtualization Rendering: ```text 100,000 rows ``` is slow. Instead: Render only visible rows using virtualization libraries (e.g., `react-window` or similar). --- # Challenge 11 — Optimistic UI User clicks: ```text Like ❤️ ``` Instead of waiting: ```text Click ↓ Server ↓ Update UI ``` Do: ```text Click ↓ Update UI Immediately ↓ Send Request ↓ Rollback if Failed ``` This improves perceived performance. --- # Challenge 12 — Authentication Typical flow: ```text Login ↓ Access Token ↓ Refresh Token ↓ Protected Routes ``` Keep authentication logic centralized and handle token refresh gracefully. --- # Challenge 13 — Folder Design Avoid: ```text components/ hooks/ pages/ utils/ ``` containing hundreds of unrelated files. Prefer: ```text features/ auth/ dashboard/ users/ ``` Each feature can contain: ```text components/ hooks/ services/ types/ tests/ ``` This keeps related code together. --- # Challenge 14 — React Query / Server State Question: Should fetched server data live in `useState`? Not always. Server state libraries such as **TanStack Query (React Query)** provide: - Caching - Refetching - Loading state - Error state - Background synchronization These tools are designed specifically for server state. --- # Challenge 15 — Performance Strategy If an application feels slow: Don't immediately add memoization everywhere. Instead: 1. Measure with React DevTools Profiler. 2. Find the bottleneck. 3. Optimize the slow part. 4. Measure again. Optimization should be evidence-based. --- # System Design Interview ## Design a Chat Application Features: - Conversations - Messages - Online users - Typing indicator - Read receipts - Notifications Suggested structure: ```text features/ chat/ components/ hooks/ services/ socket/ types/ ``` --- ## State Local: - Input text - Emoji picker - Modal visibility Global: - Current user - Active conversation - Authentication Server: - Messages - Conversation history - User profiles --- # Challenge 16 — Dashboard Architecture Dashboard contains: - Charts - Tables - Notifications - Filters Question: Should all data be stored in one Context? Answer: No. Separate concerns. Example: ```text Charts ↓ Chart Data ---------------- Notifications ↓ Notification State ---------------- Filters ↓ Filter State ``` This reduces unnecessary updates. --- # Challenge 17 — Explain Reconciliation Question: What is React Reconciliation? Answer: Reconciliation is React's process of comparing the previous rendered tree with the new one to determine the minimum set of DOM updates required. Keys play an important role in helping React match list items correctly. --- # Challenge 18 — Explain Hydration Question: What is hydration? Answer: Hydration is the process where React attaches event handlers and makes server-rendered HTML interactive on the client. This is commonly used in frameworks like Next.js. --- # Common Senior Interview Mistakes ### Mistake 1 Using global state for everything. Keep state as local as possible. --- ### Mistake 2 Optimizing before measuring. Always profile first. --- ### Mistake 3 Putting API calls directly into many components. Centralize data access. --- ### Mistake 4 Ignoring bundle size. Lazy-load when appropriate. --- ### Mistake 5 Mixing server state with client UI state unnecessarily. Use tools suited to each type of state. --- # Under the Hood Typical request flow: ```text User Click ↓ Component ↓ Service ↓ API ↓ Response ↓ Cache (optional) ↓ State Update ↓ Render ↓ DOM Update ``` --- # Interview Perspective ### How would you structure a large React application? > I prefer feature-based organization because it keeps related components, hooks, services, tests, and types together, making the codebase easier to navigate and scale. --- ### When should you use Context? > For application-wide values such as theme, authentication, or locale—not as a replacement for all state management. --- ### When should you use a global store? > When multiple unrelated parts of the application need to share and update the same client-side state. --- ### How do you optimize React performance? > Profile first, identify bottlenecks, then apply targeted optimizations such as memoization, code splitting, virtualization, or reducing unnecessary renders. --- ### What is the difference between server state and client state? > Client state represents UI state managed by the application (e.g., modals or selected tabs). Server state comes from an external source and often requires caching, synchronization, and refetching strategies. --- # Live Coding Questions ## Easy Create a reusable `useFetch` hook. --- ## Medium Refactor repeated API logic into a service layer and Custom Hook. --- ## Hard Design the frontend architecture for a SaaS application with: - Authentication - Billing - Notifications - Dashboard - Admin panel - Analytics - Real-time updates Explain: - Folder structure - State management - Data fetching - Routing - Performance strategy - Testing approach --- # Practice Exercises ## Knowledge 1. Why is feature-based architecture preferred for large projects? 2. When is Context appropriate? 3. When should you introduce a global state library? 4. Why use a service layer? 5. What problems do Custom Hooks solve? 6. What is code splitting? 7. Why use lazy loading? 8. What is virtualization? 9. What is optimistic UI? 10. What is hydration? --- ## Coding 11. Build a `useFetch` hook. 12. Lazy-load a route. 13. Create an Error Boundary. 14. Implement optimistic updates for a "like" button. 15. Refactor repeated fetch logic into a service and hook. --- ## Debugging 16. A page re-renders excessively after every context update. How would you reduce unnecessary renders? 17. The initial JavaScript bundle is very large. What strategies would you use to reduce it? 18. A list with 50,000 rows is slow to render. What techniques would you apply? --- # Interview Cheatsheet ```text State Scope ↓ Local ↓ Parent ↓ Context ↓ Global Store ---------------------------- Architecture ↓ Feature-Based Structure ---------------------------- Performance ↓ React.memo useMemo useCallback Lazy Loading Code Splitting Virtualization ---------------------------- Data ↓ Service Layer Custom Hooks Server State Library ---------------------------- Optimization ↓ Profile First Optimize Second ``` --- # Mastery Checklist Before moving on, make sure you can: - ✅ Design scalable React applications. - ✅ Explain state management trade-offs. - ✅ Separate client state from server state. - ✅ Optimize rendering based on measurements. - ✅ Organize code using a feature-based architecture. - ✅ Discuss senior-level frontend design decisions confidently. - ✅ Explain reconciliation, hydration, lazy loading, and code splitting. --- # Final Mock Interview You are asked to design the frontend for a project similar to **Slack** or **Microsoft Teams**. Requirements: - Authentication - Real-time messaging - File uploads - Notifications - Search - User profiles - Settings - Offline support - Responsive design - High performance with thousands of messages Be prepared to explain: 1. Folder structure. 2. Routing strategy. 3. State management choices. 4. Server state management. 5. WebSocket integration. 6. Performance optimizations. 7. Error handling. 8. Caching strategy. 9. Testing approach. 10. How your design would scale as the application grows. --- # 🎉 End of Module 12 Congratulations! You have completed the **JavaScript & React Interview Challenges** module. By this point, you should be comfortable with: - JavaScript execution model - Closures, scopes, prototypes, and `this` - Asynchronous JavaScript and the Event Loop - Arrays, Objects, Maps, and Sets - React Hooks and rendering behavior - React performance optimization - Frontend architecture and system design - Common interview coding challenges - Senior-level React interview discussions You're now well-equipped to tackle JavaScript and React interviews ranging from junior to senior levels.

questions.questionText: Which are React optimization techniques? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Component caching (`React.memo`), value caching (`useMemo`), callback reference caching (`useCallback`), and dynamic lazy bundle splitting are all standard React optimizations.

questions.questionText: What is the term for syncing virtual DOM changes with the actual DOM?
questions.explanation: Reconciliation is the process of generating new Virtual DOM trees and diffing them to update the Real DOM.
